intro.heading: Four options, and the one most families compare badly
paragraphs: A parent in Ras Al Khaimah who decides their child needs IB help is rarely choosing between tutoring and nothing. They are choosing between four things that cost different amounts, cover different ground and solve different problems. The school's own after-hours support is usually free and usually taught by the same teacher whose explanation did not land the first time. A tuition centre is cheaper per hour and runs at a group pace. A freelance tutor who drives over is the most convenient and the most constrained by who happens to live nearby. A specialist over live video is matched on subject knowledge and has no radius at all.

The reason this comparison goes wrong is that families compare on price per hour, which is the least informative number available. A group class at AED 80 an hour that covers Standard Level content while your child is failing a Higher Level Paper 3 is more expensive than a AED 250 session that fixes the Paper 3 problem, because the first one buys nothing. The useful comparison is cost per problem solved, and that requires knowing what the problem is before shopping.

Ras Al Khaimah makes the comparison sharper than Dubai does. The private-school set here is small and concentrated around Al Nakheel, Al Hamra and Mina Al Arab. The emirate has its own regulator, the Department of Knowledge, which approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. And specialist subject teachers are genuinely scarce locally — a parent in Al Marjan Island looking for a Chemistry Higher Level specialist is not choosing between several; they are often choosing between one who is driving distance away and nobody.

That scarcity is the honest case for remote delivery, and it is a stronger case here than anywhere else in the UAE. IB Gram matches Ras Al Khaimah families to subject specialists who teach one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE — home visits are a service offered only in India — so a family who specifically wants someone at the kitchen table should use the local market, and this page tells them what that market charges and what to check before they do.

The rest of the page works through each alternative in turn: what it costs, what it covers, when it is the right answer, and what it cannot do. Then the IB-specific detail that decides whether specialism matters at all for your child — assessment weightings, where the Internal Assessment sits, the Higher Level papers that carry the grade. Then the regulatory position in this emirate, the academic-honesty boundary, and a frank table of how the decision usually resolves by subject and year group.

There is no version of this page that concludes tutoring is always the answer. For a Diploma Programme student in Year 12 who has not yet sat a timed paper, the right first step costs nothing: ask the school for the subject's assessment outline and attempt one past paper. Several families who read that sentence will not need anything else, and that is a fine outcome.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-tutor.programmesIntro: The IB runs as a continuum, and a Ras Al Khaimah family may be dealing with any stage of it — or with a child moving between an IB school and a British-curriculum one, which is its own piece of work. What a tutor does differs completely by stage.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led, transdisciplinary and assessed internally rather than by examination. Support at this stage is about reading fluency, number sense and the language of inquiry rather than about subject content. Families often arrive asking for tutoring and leave with a reading plan, which is usually the right trade.
programmes.countryNote: In Ras Al Khaimah the PYP cohort is small and concentrated in a handful of schools around Al Hamra and Khuzam. Because transitions into the emirate often happen mid-year, the most common PYP request here is not academic support but settling a child who has moved from a very different system into an inquiry classroom.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, on a 1-8 scale. The criterion language is explicit and most students never learn to read it properly, which is where marks sit. MYP Year 5 ends with the Personal Project, a process-heavy piece of independent work that needs supervision rather than teaching.
programmes.countryNote: MYP students in Ras Al Khaimah frequently sit alongside peers heading for IGCSE at a different school, and parents compare the two routes constantly. The practical difference for a tutoring plan is that MYP rewards criterion fluency and extended process work, while the IGCSE route rewards timed-paper technique.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three normally at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Each subject is graded 1-7 with bonus points from TOK and the Extended Essay. Higher Level courses carry extra content and, in most sciences, an additional paper. This is where almost every tutoring request in the emirate originates.
programmes.countryNote: A Ras Al Khaimah Diploma student is typically in a small cohort — sometimes the only person in the year taking a given Higher Level subject. That has a real consequence: there is no classmate to compare an Internal Assessment draft against and no second teacher to ask. Remote one-to-one fills precisely that gap.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: A smaller IB route combining DP courses with a career-related study and a core of personal and professional skills. Rare in the UAE and rarer in the northern emirates, but worth naming because families comparing options sometimes encounter it and find almost nothing written about how support works.
programmes.countryNote: Where a Ras Al Khaimah student is on a career-related route, the DP courses inside it are assessed identically to the full Diploma, so subject tutoring is the same work. The difference is the reflective project, which needs process supervision rather than content teaching.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-tutor.subjectsIntro: These are the IB subjects Ras Al Khaimah families ask for most, with what each one assesses and where specialism genuinely changes the outcome. Levels are given because the Higher Level papers, not the subject label, are what a specialist is for.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Algebraic fluency, calculus and proof, with Higher Level adding substantial depth and a third paper. The Higher Level cohort in a small RAK school is often two or three students, so a student who falls behind has nobody to work alongside. The Internal Assessment exploration is where many lose easy marks on mathematical communication.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics and technology-led problem solving, with the graphical display calculator integral to assessment rather than incidental. Students choose it expecting an easier route and meet a heavy statistics load. Course choice has university consequences, so the AA against AI decision deserves a conversation before Year 12 rather than during it.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Higher Level adds depth across energetics, kinetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms. The reliable mark loss is in calculation chains — moles through to yield — and in explaining mechanism rather than reciting it. One of the two scarcest Higher Level specialisms in the northern emirates.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mechanics, fields, circuits and the Higher Level extensions, with data analysis assessed throughout. Students who are comfortable with the algebra still lose marks on uncertainty treatment and on explaining a graph's gradient as a physical quantity. Practical skills carry into both the Internal Assessment and the written papers.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content-heavy with command terms that reward precision. Higher Level adds depth in metabolism, plant biology and genetics. Extended-response questions are where the grade moves, and they respond quickly to teaching that is about structuring an answer rather than about learning more facts.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Microeconomics, macroeconomics, the global economy and, at Higher Level, additional quantitative content and an extra paper. Diagram accuracy earns marks explicitly. The Internal Assessment commentaries require current articles and a tight word limit, and editing discipline is most of the skill.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Assessed through case-study response and, at Higher Level, a longer written paper plus extra content. Evaluation marks decide the grade: a student who knows every tool and never judges a decision stays mid-band. UAE students usually have strong commercial intuition and need the mark-scheme structure.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 guided analysis, Paper 2 comparative essay, the Individual Oral and, at Higher Level, the HL Essay. Marks sit in analysis of how meaning is made rather than in what the text says. Strong readers often underperform because they summarise.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: For students working in English as an additional language, assessed across reading, writing, listening and oral components. Text-type conventions are assessed explicitly, so a candidate must produce a blog that reads like a blog and a formal letter that reads like one. Highly trainable in a short block.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: Arabic runs as an IB language and, separately, as a federally mandated school subject in the UAE. Arabic A assumes first-language fluency with literary analysis; Arabic B is the acquisition route. Non-native-household Arab students commonly need Arabic A support, and it is a thin specialism across the emirates.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Assessed by the exhibition and a prescribed-title essay, contributing bonus points alongside the Extended Essay. Students struggle because it rewards argument rather than content, and because nobody at a small school has time to read drafts. Supervision and questioning are the whole of the support here.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: A 4,000-word independent research piece in a chosen subject, supervised at school. Support means helping a student narrow a question, plan a method and interrogate their own draft. The boundary is firm: the research and the writing are the student's, and a supervisor signs off on that.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-tutor.regionsTitle: Ras Al Khaimah, area by area — what support is realistically available
ras-al-khaimah/ib-tutor.regionsIntro: RAK is spread out, and that geography is the main reason the four options resolve differently here than in a dense city. These notes describe what local provision actually looks like in each area and how long the drive is to an alternative.

regions.name: Al Nakheel
regions.note: The commercial centre, where most of the emirate's tuition centres and institute signage sits. Families here have the shortest drive to a group class, which makes the centre option genuinely competitive for broad revision.

regions.name: Al Hamra Village
regions.note: Gated coastal community with a concentration of international-school families. Local one-to-one tutors do exist here but the pool is small, and Higher Level science cover is the recurring gap families describe.

regions.name: Mina Al Arab
regions.note: Waterfront villas and townhouses, growing fast, with a long drive to Al Nakheel at school-run times. The travel cost of a centre class is high enough from here that one-to-one at home or online usually wins on time alone.

regions.name: Al Marjan Island
regions.note: Low-density and reclaimed, with an unusually high proportion of households in hospitality and construction management working irregular hours. Evening session timing is the deciding constraint rather than cost.

regions.name: Al Dhait
regions.note: Large established residential district, south and north, where a substantial share of local families live. The second cluster of tuition centre provision after Al Nakheel, and the most price-sensitive part of the emirate.

regions.name: Khuzam
regions.note: Central and close to school provision, with short school runs. Afternoon sessions from 4pm are realistically available here, which is not true of the coastal communities.

regions.name: Al Qusaidat
regions.note: Older residential area to the north with a largely local Emirati population. Arabic A support and mandatory-subject support come up more often here than Higher Level sciences do.

regions.name: Julphar
regions.note: Dense mixed-use area near the old town and the corniche, with apartment households and frequent mid-year arrivals. Short, twice-weekly sessions suit this group better than a single long block.

regions.name: Seih Al Uraibi
regions.note: Inland and industrial in parts, with a long commute to the coastal schools. Late-evening slots after 7.30pm are the norm, which rules out most centre timetables.

regions.name: Al Mamourah
regions.note: Residential and quiet, with families who often commute towards Umm Al Quwain or Sharjah for work. A tutor needing to arrive by 6pm is frequently the thing that breaks a plan here.

schoolClusters.note: The emirate's international-school provision is concentrated in a small number of campuses around Al Hamra, Khuzam and Al Nakheel, overseen by the RAK Department of Knowledge, which approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Diploma cohorts are small, which is why a single missing subject teacher is felt so sharply.

schoolClusters.note: When a programme or a subject combination is not offered locally, RAK families look south. The drive is long enough that it is a relocation or a boarding conversation rather than a commute, and it is one of the three alternatives families weigh against tutoring.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-tutor.modesIntro: Three shapes of engagement cover almost every request from this emirate. The distinction that matters is not hourly rate but whether the engagement has an end point, because an open-ended arrangement with no review date is how families end up paying for momentum rather than progress.

modes.title: Single-subject weekly, one Higher Level course
modes.description: One session a week on the subject where the gap is widest, running alongside school. The tutor works from the student's returned assessments and the school's assessment outline, so the hour targets what the class is doing rather than a generic syllabus order. The default choice for a Year 12 Diploma student.

modes.title: Internal Assessment supervision block
modes.description: Four to eight sessions around an Internal Assessment, exploration or commentary, timed to the school's internal deadline. The work is process supervision: narrowing a question, checking a method is viable, reading the criteria out loud against the student's own draft and asking what evidence supports each claim.

modes.description: A finite block ahead of a Diploma examination session, built backwards from the school's own paper dates. Content teaching stops; the hours go to timed papers, mark-scheme analysis and the two topics the baseline showed were costing most. Usually twice weekly, and it ends on a fixed date.

sections.heading: The four options, side by side
paragraphs: Before any detail, here is the comparison a Ras Al Khaimah parent is actually making. Four models, four cost structures, four different things they are good at. The right answer depends on one variable more than any other: how specialised the subject is. For a Standard Level subject taught by a competent teacher at a school with an after-hours clinic, the free option often works. For Higher Level Chemistry in a cohort of three, it does not, because the constraint is availability of expertise rather than hours.

The second variable is whether the problem is content or technique. A student who does not understand equilibrium needs teaching. A student who understands equilibrium and loses nine marks a paper to command terms and timing needs marked papers and a conversation about pacing. Group classes handle the first case reasonably and the second case badly, because technique diagnosis is individual by definition.

The third variable is the calendar. Eight weeks from a session, every model except the finite intensive is the wrong shape. Weekly open-ended tutoring started in March for a May session is a structure optimised for a problem the family no longer has. This is where most money gets wasted in this market, and it is entirely avoidable by starting from the date and working backwards.

Read the table as a decision aid rather than a sales argument. Two of the four rows are things IB Gram does not sell, and they are listed with their genuine advantages because a parent who picks the wrong model will stop paying anyone within a term.

sections.heading: Alternative one: the support the school already owes you
paragraphs: The first thing worth doing costs nothing. Ask the subject teacher for three specific items: the assessment outline for the course, the student's own marked work from the last two assessments, and whether an after-hours clinic or departmental drop-in runs. In a small Ras Al Khaimah cohort the teacher usually knows the student's weak topics precisely and has not been asked to say so in writing.

This option has a real advantage no paid tutor can match. The teacher sets and marks the internal assessments the student is actually judged on through the year, and supervises the Internal Assessment. Alignment with the school's own deadlines and expectations is total. Where a student's problem is that they missed a fortnight of content or did not understand one taught topic, the free route is frequently sufficient.

Its limits are structural rather than a criticism. A teacher with a full timetable cannot mark a weekly set of timed past papers for one student. A teacher who explained a topic in a way that did not land is not guaranteed to have a second explanation available. And in a cohort of two or three Higher Level students, there is no second specialist in the building to ask.

There is also a boundary families should know about. Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules bar private and charter school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE private tuition work permit carries a code of conduct that also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. Asking your child's own teacher for paid lessons is asking them to do something they should decline — but asking for the free clinic and the marked work is entirely appropriate.
bullets: Ask for the assessment outline in writing, by subject
Ask which two topics the teacher would prioritise and why
Ask whether a departmental clinic or drop-in exists and when
Do not ask the class teacher for paid private sessions

sections.heading: Alternative two: a tuition centre group class
paragraphs: Tuition centres cluster in Al Nakheel and Al Dhait, and for a family in those areas the group class is a serious option. Per hour it is the cheapest paid route by a wide margin, the premises are supervised, and for a student who simply needs structured revision hours in a room without a phone, that structure is worth real money.

The constraint is the pace. A group class teaches to the median of the room, which means a student well behind spends the hour lost and a student well ahead spends it waiting. For IB subjects the problem compounds, because Standard Level and Higher Level students are frequently combined to fill a class, and the Higher Level extensions — the extra papers, the additional content — are exactly what the Higher Level student needed covering.

Centres are also the part of the market where it is worth asking the licensing question directly. An operation with premises and staff in the UAE is a different legal entity from an individual tutor: a training institute in Dubai requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit, with initial approval first and annual renewal requested at least 30 days before expiry. In Ras Al Khaimah the Department of Knowledge regulates private education in the emirate and approves fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Ask a centre what it holds and from whom.

Practical advice: a centre class works best as a complement rather than a replacement. A student taking a group revision class for breadth and a small number of one-to-one sessions on their two worst topics often gets more for the same money than either route alone. Nobody in this market will tell you that, because nobody sells both.

sections.heading: Alternative three: a freelance tutor who drives to the villa
paragraphs: IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; that service exists only in India. So this section is about the local market rather than about us, and it is written to be useful to a family who decides to go that route.

The appeal is obvious and legitimate. No technology, a parent in the next room, a student who stays on task, and a relationship that builds over months. For students in Years 7 to 10, and for any child who needs physical presence to focus, an in-home tutor is frequently the better choice, and a family who has already concluded that should not be argued out of it.

The constraints are geography and verification. In Ras Al Khaimah the distances between Mina Al Arab, Al Marjan Island, Al Dhait and Al Qusaidat are significant, and the pool of tutors willing to drive to a given address for a 7pm session is a small subset of the pool that exists at all. That subset is selected for proximity, not for Higher Level subject depth, and market rates for an in-home visit run roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel priced in.

Verification is the part most families skip. An individual providing private tuition in the UAE needs the MoHRE private tutor work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students. Those tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws — no fine schedule is published, so treat quoted amounts with suspicion. Because the permit is free, there is no cost reason for a tutor not to hold one, which makes asking a reasonable question rather than an awkward one.

sections.heading: Alternative four: a subject specialist over live video
paragraphs: The argument for remote one-to-one in Ras Al Khaimah is not that it is modern or convenient. It is that it changes which tutors exist. Over video the selection pool is everyone who teaches Chemistry Higher Level and is free at 7.30pm Gulf Standard Time, rather than everyone who teaches anything and lives within twenty minutes of Mina Al Arab. In an emirate where a Diploma cohort can be a dozen students, that difference is the whole proposition.

The format also does things a kitchen table cannot. A past paper annotated on screen is saved and revisited. A mark scheme sits beside the student's own answer in the same field of view. An explanation of the one calculation they keep failing can be recorded and watched again on Thursday. Written parent updates are easy because the work product already exists in a shared place.

The honest weakness is engagement, and it varies enormously by student. A self-directed Year 13 student loses nothing online. A distractible Year 8 student may lose a great deal, and no amount of software fixes that. The mitigations are real but modest: shorter sessions, a visible written plan, work set and marked between sessions, and a free trial lesson so a family judges the format on their own child rather than on a claim in marketing copy.

What this model is best at is narrow and worth stating plainly: Higher Level courses, Internal Assessment supervision, Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay process work, scarce languages, and finite pre-session intensives. What it is worst at is substituting for adult presence in a room. A family who needs the second thing should buy the second thing.

sections.heading: Why Higher Level specialism decides the answer
paragraphs: Whether specialism matters is not a matter of opinion; it follows from how the Diploma is assessed. Each subject is graded 1-7 from a combination of externally examined papers and internally assessed work, and Higher Level courses carry additional content and, in most sciences, an extra paper weighted substantially. A tutor who knows the subject broadly can help with the Standard Level core and be of limited use on the Higher Level extensions, which is where the grade difference between a 5 and a 7 usually sits.

The Internal Assessment is the other reason. Across subjects it typically carries something in the region of a fifth to a quarter of the subject grade, and it is assessed against named criteria with published mark allocations. Students lose marks there not because the science is wrong but because the criteria were never read closely — a method inadequately justified, an evaluation that lists limitations without weighing them, a communication criterion ignored entirely. Reading criteria properly with a student is a specific skill and a short piece of work.

Then there are the bonus points. Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay together contribute additional points on top of the six subject grades, and both are supervised at school with very limited individual attention available in a small cohort. A student at a large Dubai school has a dedicated Extended Essay coordinator and a shelf of exemplars. A student in a RAK cohort of fifteen may have neither.

The practical upshot: for Standard Level subjects taught well, the free or cheap options often suffice. For Higher Level sciences and mathematics, for Arabic A, for Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay, specialist attention is the thing that is scarce locally and the thing remote delivery supplies. That is the entire decision, and it can be made subject by subject rather than all at once.

sections.heading: What each option costs in AED, with sources
paragraphs: Most pages ranking for UAE tutoring queries publish no price. The two that do quote in US dollars. The figures below are market figures from competitors' own published pages and from Bestimate's 2026 Dubai tutoring cost table, and they are presented as the market rather than as our price list. IB Gram's own position is a free trial lesson and a quote after the diagnostic, because the hours required for a Year 12 weekly slot and for a ten-week Higher Level intensive are not comparable.

Ras Al Khaimah runs below Dubai at the mid-market end, by something in the order of ten to twenty per cent, and the budget end is thinner because there are fewer university students to supply it. At the specialist end the gap narrows to almost nothing, because a Higher Level Chemistry specialist is scarce everywhere and prices accordingly. That compression is the reason the cost comparison between models matters more here than the comparison between emirates.

Monthly packages circulate widely. Observed figures include AED 799 per month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 per month for four two-hour in-home sessions. Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour session run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. Compare packages on sessions and session length, not on the headline monthly figure.

One piece of useful context for a fee conversation: KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in Dubai for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package. Ras Al Khaimah sets fees through its own Department of Knowledge, so that announcement does not apply here, but it is the reference point many UAE families are working from.

sections.heading: The Department of Knowledge, and how Ras Al Khaimah differs
paragraphs: Most UAE tutoring content is written about Dubai and quietly assumes Dubai's regulator. A Ras Al Khaimah family should know the actual position. Private education in this emirate is regulated by the Department of Knowledge, which approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. That is a broader remit than inspection alone, and it is the same scope the Sharjah Private Education Authority holds in Sharjah.

Elsewhere the map differs again. The Knowledge and Human Development Authority is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in Dubai. The Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in Abu Dhabi. And the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Five bodies, one country — and a parent moving between emirates should expect the reporting and the fee process to change with the border.

Federal rules reach into every emirate's timetable. Private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the ministry's general regulations. In Dubai, KHDA has set out the detail: separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, with combined classes strictly prohibited; Standard Arabic as the language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs; and instructional time calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, with any mandatory-subject lesson advised to run at least 25 minutes. Those mandatory subjects take real hours out of a Diploma student's week.

The planning consequence is concrete. A Diploma student in Ras Al Khaimah is carrying six IB subjects, Theory of Knowledge, an Extended Essay, CAS, and mandatory UAE subjects. Any tutoring plan built as though the IB load were the whole load will be abandoned by November. Two tutored subjects is usually one too many for this timetable, and saying so is more useful than selling the second one.

sections.heading: The academic-honesty line, stated once and clearly
paragraphs: This search results page contains operators selling finished Internal Assessments. One has been observed advertising completed work at AED 3,750. That is an academic-integrity breach and an IB malpractice trigger, and the consequence falls on the student, not the seller. A family should know where the line sits so they do not cross it by accident while buying what they think is ordinary help.

The line is authorship. Assessed work — the Internal Assessment, the Extended Essay, the Theory of Knowledge essay and exhibition, any coursework — must be the student's own. A tutor may teach the underlying skill, discuss a plan the student has made, read the published criteria aloud with them, ask questions about a draft the student has written, and give feedback the student then acts on. A tutor may not author any portion of what is submitted, and a legitimate provider will not offer to.

The same principle covers materials. Syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes, grade-boundary tables and subject guides belong to the IB, Cambridge and Pearson. They can be referenced in a lesson and linked from their official sources. Supplying them as a downloadable pack is copyright infringement, and for unreleased material it is a malpractice exposure attaching to the candidate. An offer to send you a folder of restricted material tells you something about the operation.

This is a genuine differentiator rather than a disclaimer. Reading the criteria letter by letter with a student, asking why a limitation matters, making them justify a method out loud — that work moves Internal Assessment marks substantially and leaves the authorship entirely with the student. It is also the part of the job most group settings cannot do at all.

sections.heading: How the decision usually resolves, and what to do first
paragraphs: In practice the four options sort themselves by year group and by subject, and the sorting is reasonably predictable. Younger students with a content gap and a school clinic available should use the school. Students who need revision hours in a supervised room and are in Al Nakheel or Al Dhait should look at a centre. Students in Years 7 to 10 who need an adult present should use the local in-home market, having asked about the MoHRE permit. Diploma students with a Higher Level problem, an Internal Assessment deadline or a scarce language should look for a specialist, and in this emirate that means remote.

The first concrete step costs nothing in any of those branches. Obtain the subject's assessment outline from the school. Have the student attempt one real past paper under timed conditions. Get it marked against the published scheme, with the loss attributed by question and by cause. That document tells you whether the problem is content, technique or timing, and the three have different answers and different price tags.

If the answer points towards specialist one-to-one, the sequence from there is a short diagnostic conversation, then a free trial lesson on the actual subject — one lesson, one subject, no payment taken — then a written plan naming two priority topics rather than six. Where the specialism is thin, which for the northern emirates means Higher Level Chemistry, Higher Level Physics and Arabic A in particular, we give a realistic match time rather than filling the slot with a generalist.

And the plan gets reviewed. At six weeks the student re-sits a comparable paper, it is marked the same way, and the two breakdowns are compared. Sessions go up, down, sideways to a different subject, or stop. Stopping because the problem is solved is a legitimate outcome, and a provider unwilling to name it is not giving you advice.

Match the model to the problem: content, technique, supervision or specialism

process.title: Name the subject and the level
process.description: Tell us the subject, whether it is Higher or Standard Level, the school, and the date you are working towards. A Higher Level Chemistry problem in Year 13 twelve weeks out and a Standard Level Economics drift in Year 12 need different tutors, different session lengths and different numbers of hours.

process.title: Bring the school's own evidence
process.description: The most useful thing a parent can supply is the subject's assessment outline plus the student's last two marked pieces of school work. That is better diagnostic material than any questionnaire, because it shows what the school assesses and how this student is losing marks against it.

process.title: A free trial lesson, one subject
process.description: One full one-to-one lesson over live video at no cost, on the subject you actually need, with no card details required. A trial that is an hour of tutor talk has told you nothing. Expect the student to attempt real questions and the tutor to name two specific things to fix.

process.title: A written plan with two priorities
process.description: The plan names the level, the two priority topics, the session slot in Gulf Standard Time and the dates of the timed papers. Two topics fixed properly moves a grade; six touched lightly does not. It is written down so you can check what happens against what was promised.

process.title: Review at six weeks against a re-marked paper
process.description: The student re-sits a comparable paper and it is marked the same way, so the conversation uses two mark breakdowns rather than impressions. The outcome may be more sessions, fewer, a different subject, or none. All four are real answers and we will say which one the evidence supports.

whyPoints.title: We name the alternatives we do not sell
whyPoints.description: The school clinic, the centre group class and the local in-home tutor are listed on this page with their genuine advantages, because a family that picks the wrong model stops paying anyone within a term. Telling you when the free option is sufficient is better business than selling into a mismatch.

whyPoints.title: Specialists, not a driving radius
whyPoints.description: Over live video the pool is everyone who teaches that course and is free in Gulf Standard Time evening hours, rather than everyone within twenty minutes of Mina Al Arab. In an emirate where a Higher Level cohort can be three students, that is the whole proposition.

whyPoints.title: Internal Assessment work done properly
whyPoints.description: Criteria are read letter by letter with the student against their own draft, with questions rather than corrections. Authorship stays entirely with the student. This is the part of the work that moves marks most and that group settings cannot do at all.

whyPoints.title: Finite engagements with review dates
whyPoints.description: Internal Assessment blocks end when the school's deadline does. Pre-session intensives end on a fixed date. Weekly work gets a six-week review against a re-marked paper. An arrangement with no end point and no measure is how families pay for momentum rather than progress.

whyPoints.title: Regulatory facts, sourced and emirate-correct
whyPoints.description: Ras Al Khaimah is regulated by the Department of Knowledge, not KHDA, and this page says so with the source. Every regulatory statement here is attributable to u.ae, KHDA, MoHRE or the exam board that published it, and unverified items are marked unverified rather than smoothed over.

whyPoints.title: Coverage limits disclosed up front
whyPoints.description: Higher Level Chemistry, Higher Level Physics and Arabic A are thin specialisms in UAE evening hours. Where the match will take a week, we say a week. Where only an inconvenient slot exists, we say that and let you decide. Nobody else in this market discloses a coverage limit.

faqs.question: We live in Al Nakheel — what are our actual options for IB support in Ras Al Khaimah?
faqs.answer: Four, and Al Nakheel is the one area of the emirate where all four are genuinely available. The school's own after-hours support costs nothing and should be tried first. Tuition centres cluster in and around Al Nakheel, so a group class is a short drive and the cheapest paid hour you will find. A freelance tutor visiting the villa is viable because you are central, though the pool is selected by proximity rather than subject depth. A specialist over live video is matched on the course itself. Which one is right depends on whether the problem is missing content, weak technique, poor concentration or an unavailable specialism.

faqs.question: Is a tuition centre in Ras Al Khaimah cheaper than one-to-one for IB Diploma subjects?
faqs.answer: Cheaper per hour, almost always. Cheaper per problem solved, often not. A centre class teaches to the median of the room, and IB classes are frequently filled by combining Standard and Higher Level students, which means the Higher Level extension content your child needed is the part least likely to be covered properly. For broad revision hours in a supervised room the economics are excellent. For a diagnosed mark loss on a specific paper they are poor, because individual diagnosis is the one thing a group format cannot do. Many families get the best value from a centre class for breadth plus a few targeted one-to-one sessions.

faqs.question: Can my child's own IB teacher at school tutor them privately in Ras Al Khaimah?
faqs.answer: They should decline, and it is better for everyone if the question is not asked. Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules prohibit private and charter school staff from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE private tuition work permit carries a code of conduct that also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. What is entirely appropriate is asking that teacher for the subject's assessment outline, for your child's marked work, for the two topics they would prioritise, and for access to any free departmental clinic. That costs nothing and is frequently the most valuable conversation of the year.

faqs.question: How does the Department of Knowledge differ from KHDA for a Ras Al Khaimah family?
faqs.answer: They are separate authorities for separate emirates with different remits. Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge regulates private education in the emirate and approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Dubai's KHDA is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education there. Most UAE tutoring and schooling guidance you find online is written about Dubai and silently assumes KHDA's framework, including its inspection cadence and fee announcements. Those do not apply in Ras Al Khaimah. Fee and curriculum questions here go to your school and to the Department of Knowledge, and a relocation across emirates means a different regulator.

faqs.question: Why are IB Higher Level subject tutors hard to find locally in Ras Al Khaimah?
faqs.answer: Arithmetic. The emirate's international-school provision is concentrated in a small number of campuses, and a Diploma cohort can be a dozen or two students, of whom perhaps three take Chemistry at Higher Level. The population of locally resident teachers who have taught that course at that level is correspondingly tiny, and those who exist are generally employed full time. A tutor selected by driving distance is therefore selected from a pool that mostly does not include the specialism you want. Remote one-to-one changes the selection criterion from geography to subject, which is why it matters more here than in Dubai.

faqs.question: What does an IB tutor cost per hour in Ras Al Khaimah?
faqs.answer: Market rates run roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour for a university-student tutor online, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor, AED 180 to 500 for an in-home visit with travel priced in, and AED 200 to 450 or more for an IB subject specialist. The premium end reaches AED 650. Those figures come from providers' own published pages and from Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table, not from us, and Ras Al Khaimah sits modestly below Dubai in the mid band while matching it at the specialist end. IB Gram quotes after a diagnostic, following a free trial lesson.

faqs.question: Does my child need a Higher Level specialist, or will a general maths tutor do?
faqs.answer: It depends on where the marks are being lost. If the problem is algebraic fluency, arithmetic slips or unwritten method, a strong general mathematician fixes that efficiently and cheaply. If the problem sits in the Higher Level extension content or in the additional Higher Level paper, a generalist will work hard and under-deliver, because familiarity with that paper's conventions is the thing being bought. The way to find out costs nothing: get one real past paper marked against the published scheme with the loss attributed by question. The breakdown tells you which kind of tutor you need, and it is often the cheaper one.

faqs.question: How much of the IB Diploma grade comes from the Internal Assessment?
faqs.answer: It varies by subject, but across most Diploma courses the internally assessed component carries roughly a fifth to a quarter of the subject grade, with the remainder from externally examined papers. Confirm the exact weighting for your child's subjects from the school's own assessment outline, since it differs between courses and levels. What is consistent is that the Internal Assessment is marked against named criteria with published mark allocations, and that students lose marks there for process reasons — a method inadequately justified, limitations listed but never weighed, a communication criterion ignored — rather than for not knowing the subject.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with my son's Extended Essay without crossing the IB's honesty rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the boundary is authorship. A tutor can help a student narrow a research question, sanity-check whether a method is viable in the time available, read the assessment criteria aloud with them, ask hard questions about a draft the student has written, and give feedback the student then acts on. A tutor cannot author any part of what is submitted, and no legitimate provider offers to. The school supervisor signs an authenticity declaration, so the record has to be honest. Operators in this market advertise completed work; the consequence of using one falls on the candidate, not the seller.

faqs.question: We are considering moving our daughter to a Dubai IB school. Is tutoring the cheaper alternative?
faqs.answer: Usually by a wide margin, but they solve different problems. Relocating buys a larger cohort, more subject choices, a dedicated Extended Essay structure and a deeper bench of teachers. Tutoring buys specialist attention on specific components while everything else stays as it is. If the issue is that your child's school does not offer the subject combination she needs, tutoring cannot fix that. If the issue is that she is strong in five subjects and losing ground in Higher Level Chemistry, a finite specialist block is the proportionate answer and costs a fraction of a school move.

faqs.question: How quickly can an IB tutor be matched for a Ras Al Khaimah student?
faqs.answer: For common Standard Level subjects and mathematics, usually within a few days. For Higher Level Chemistry, Higher Level Physics and Arabic A, the honest answer is sometimes a week or more, because those are thin specialisms in UAE evening hours and we would rather say so than put a generalist in the slot. Where a specialist exists but only at a time that does not suit, we tell you the time and let you decide. A realistic match date is more useful than an optimistic one, particularly if you are working backwards from an examination session.

faqs.question: Is online IB tutoring workable around Ras Al Khaimah school hours?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the scheduling is easier than the in-home alternative because there is no tutor travel to accommodate. Sessions run in Gulf Standard Time, and families from the coastal communities commonly use slots from 6.30pm onwards, while households in Khuzam and central areas with short school runs often prefer 4.30pm. Shorter sessions twice a week tend to survive a term better than a single long block. During Ramadan, sessions typically move to the early afternoon or to a post-Iftar slot, and planning that shift a fortnight ahead works considerably better than improvising week by week.

faqs.question: What happens in a trial lesson, and is there a condition attached to it?
faqs.answer: The condition is stated plainly: one lesson, one subject, no payment and no card details. The lesson itself is a full one-to-one session over live video on the subject you actually need, not a sales call. What you should expect is the student attempting real questions from their own course, the tutor marking or discussing that work in the session, and a clear statement at the end of the two specific things that need fixing first. A trial that consists of an hour of tutor explanation has told you very little about the match.

faqs.question: My child takes Maths AI SL but wants to study engineering. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: It can be, and it is better discovered now than in a university application. Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation is a legitimate, demanding course, but engineering and several quantitative degrees commonly expect Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level, and admissions requirements differ by university and by country. Check the stated entry requirements for the specific universities on your list, including the UAE institutions, before assuming. Where a change of course is still possible the school decides, and where it is not, a bridging plan in the final year plus an honest conversation about course choice is the realistic route.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send tutors to homes in Ras Al Khaimah?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service exists only in India. Tutoring for UAE families is delivered one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. If what you want is specifically an adult in the room — and for younger or easily distracted students that is a reasonable thing to want — the local Ras Al Khaimah market supplies it at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel priced in. Ask any tutor you engage whether they hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, which is free of charge and valid for two years.

faqs.question: Which schools in Ras Al Khaimah offer the IB programmes?
faqs.answer: IB provision in the emirate is concentrated in a small number of campuses around Al Hamra, Khuzam and Al Nakheel, with the broader international-school set including British and Indian curriculum schools alongside them. Rather than rely on any third-party list, check the IB's own programme finder and the RAK Department of Knowledge's school information, because programme authorisation changes and a school offering the Middle Years Programme does not necessarily offer the Diploma. Ask any school directly which programmes it is currently authorised for and which Higher Level subjects it actually runs this year, since the second question is the one that affects your child.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-tutor.closingHeading: Compare the four, then start with the free one
ras-al-khaimah/ib-tutor.closingBody: The decision in front of you is not whether to hire a tutor. It is which of four models fits the problem you actually have, and the only way to know that is to get one real past paper marked against the published scheme and read where the marks went. Ask the school for the assessment outline first; it costs nothing and sometimes it is enough. If the breakdown points to a Higher Level gap, an Internal Assessment deadline or a specialism your school cannot staff, a free trial lesson over live video is available before any payment, and the first conversation is about the diagnosis rather than a package.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-tutor-near-me.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach single IB subjects at a named level over live video, one-to-one. Each starts with a marked baseline rather than a lesson, because a plan written before the diagnosis is a guess, and a guess costs you the first three weeks.

intro.heading: Three questions, in this order
paragraphs: Every useful tutoring conversation answers three questions in sequence. Where is the student now, precisely enough to be measured? Where do they need to be, expressed as marks on named components rather than as a grade? And what do the weeks in between contain, week by week, with a checkpoint that would reveal if it were not working? Most families start at the third question, buy hours, and never establish the first two. That is why tutoring often feels unmeasurable.

The first question has a free answer. Ask the school for the subject's assessment outline, and have your child attempt one real past paper under timed conditions. Get it marked against the published scheme, with every lost mark attributed by question and by cause. That document is the diagnosis. It routinely shows that the problem is narrower than it felt — two topics and a timing failure rather than a whole syllabus — and occasionally shows that no tutor is needed at all.

The second question is where most plans go wrong. A parent says the target is a 6. A plan can only be built on something more specific: the baseline shows nine marks lost to one topic, six to command-term mismatch, and four to the last question never being reached. Those three numbers are the plan. Expressed that way, a target becomes a set of tasks with a plausible timescale, and it becomes obvious whether the timescale available is enough.

The third question is the content of this page. A twelve-week plan and a six-week plan are different instruments, not the same instrument in different sizes. Twelve weeks allows content teaching, then technique, then timed rehearsal. Six weeks does not: it is triage, and attempting a twelve-week structure in six weeks produces a student who has revised everything and practised nothing. Which one applies depends only on the calendar.

On proximity: the search phrase asks for a tutor nearby, and in Ras Al Khaimah that is the wrong filter for Diploma subjects. The emirate's international provision sits in a small number of campuses and a Higher Level cohort can be three students, so the locally resident specialist pool is tiny. Over live video the pool becomes everyone who teaches that course and is free in Gulf Standard Time evening hours. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE — home visits are a service we offer only in India — and for a timeline-driven problem the speed of finding the right specialist matters more than the distance to the nearest one.

What this page will not do is suggest that more weeks always produce more grade. There is a point at which a student is not short of teaching but short of sleep, and there is a point in the year at which the right recommendation is to stop paying for sessions. Both appear later in the page, with the honest version of what to do instead.
bullets: The diagnosis is a marked paper with the loss attributed by question and cause
A target is only usable when expressed as marks on named components
Twelve weeks allows teaching then technique; six weeks is triage only
Two priority topics fixed properly beats six topics touched lightly
Checkpoints at four, eight and twelve weeks, with the measure agreed in advance
Assessed work stays the student's own authorship whatever the deadline pressure

ras-al-khaimah/ib-tutor-near-me.programmesIntro: The timeline looks different at each stage of the IB, because the deadlines that constrain it are different. A PYP year has no fixed external date; a DP2 year has almost nothing but. Find your stage below before reading the plans.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: No external examinations and no fixed deadline, which changes the entire logic of a timeline. Progress is measured in reading fluency, number confidence and willingness to attempt unfamiliar work. The right unit of time is a term rather than a block of weeks, and the right outcome is often a routine rather than a tutor.
programmes.countryNote: For a Ras Al Khaimah family the practical PYP question is usually a mid-year arrival from a different system. The timeline there is about settling rather than catching up: six to eight weeks of light, regular support while the child learns what an inquiry classroom expects of them.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Criterion-assessed on a 1-8 scale with published descriptors, so the timeline can be anchored to real evidence: the student's own criterion judgements before and after. MYP Year 5 adds the Personal Project, which is a deadline with a process rather than a paper to revise for.
programmes.countryNote: MYP Year 4 and 5 are the cheapest years in which to fix a problem, because nothing external is at stake yet and the habits transfer directly into the Diploma. A family in this emirate who acts here rather than in DP2 spends a fraction as much for a larger effect.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Two years with a dense internal calendar: Internal Assessments across six subjects, a 4,000-word Extended Essay, the Theory of Knowledge exhibition and essay, CAS, and then the examination session. Every one of those has a school deadline that sits earlier than the IB's own. Almost all timeline pressure in this emirate originates here.
programmes.countryNote: A Ras Al Khaimah Diploma student is often the only person in the year taking a given Higher Level subject, so there is no classmate whose draft or revision pace provides a reference point. That absence is why a plan with explicit weekly checkpoints matters more here than at a large school.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: Diploma courses combined with a career-related study and a core including the reflective project. The DP courses inside it carry the same assessment and therefore the same timeline; the reflective project adds a separate deadline with a process rather than an examination.
programmes.countryNote: Local provision for the career-related core is effectively absent in the northern emirates, so the reflective project in particular tends to be supervised remotely or not at all. Build its deadline into the plan early rather than discovering it in the final term.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-tutor-near-me.subjectsIntro: Below is how long things usually take, by subject. These are typical ranges from the work we see rather than promises, and they assume the baseline diagnosis has already identified two priority topics. Nobody can state a timescale for a student they have not assessed.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Method-selection problems and unwritten working are the fastest wins — often visible within four sessions, because they are habits rather than knowledge. Genuine content gaps in Higher Level calculus or proof take longer, typically eight to twelve weeks of weekly work alongside school.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics interpretation and calculator-output reasoning respond quickly, often in six sessions, because the technique is explicit. The exploration needs its own four to six session block timed to the school's draft deadline rather than squeezed into weekly work.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Calculation chains and mechanism explanation are the usual targets and take eight to twelve weeks to shift reliably at Higher Level. The scarcest specialism in the northern emirates, so book earlier than you think you need to — a week's match delay eats a week of a six-week plan.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Uncertainty treatment and graph interpretation are discrete, teachable skills that move within four to six sessions. Conceptual gaps in fields or circuits take a term. The two are easy to tell apart from a marked baseline and should not be treated as one problem.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Extended-response structure and terminology precision are the recoverable marks, and they move fast — sometimes within three sessions of marked practice. If the baseline shows breadth of content missing instead, that is a term of work rather than a block.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy is a short, high-yield fix. The commentaries are a deadline rather than a skill gap and need a dedicated block of four to six sessions timed to the school's submission date, with editing to the word limit taking longer than the writing.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Evaluation marks are the entire gap for most students, and once the pattern is named it tends to move within five or six sessions of marked case-study practice. Content revision beyond that is rarely what the baseline actually calls for.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Moving from summary to analysis is a habit change and takes longer than families expect — eight to twelve weeks of regular written practice with feedback. The Individual Oral is a separate, shorter piece of work with a fixed school date.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Text-type conventions are explicit and trainable, frequently inside four sessions. Oral components benefit from recorded rehearsal across a six-week run-up. One of the faster subjects to show measurable movement.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: Arabic A literary analysis at the higher grades is a term of work and a thin specialism across the emirates, so the booking lead time is the binding constraint rather than the teaching time. Arabic B acquisition work responds faster and more predictably.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Deadline-shaped rather than skill-shaped. The exhibition and the prescribed-title essay each need a short block of questioning sessions placed before the school's draft date. Weekly year-long support is almost never the right instrument here.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: The timeline that goes wrong most often. A question narrowed in DP1 and a method tested early turns 4,000 words into a manageable task; a question still broad in DP2 turns it into a crisis. Four to eight supervision sessions, placed early, are worth more than twelve placed late.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-tutor-near-me.regionsTitle: Ras Al Khaimah — how soon a session can realistically start
ras-al-khaimah/ib-tutor-near-me.regionsIntro: On a timeline, the question about your area is not scenery but speed: how quickly a session can be in the diary and at what hour it can run. These notes describe that, area by area.

regions.name: Al Nakheel
regions.note: Central, short school runs, and the fastest area in the emirate to get a session running. Slots from 4.30pm are realistic, which means a six-week plan can use two sessions a week without colliding with a commute.

regions.name: Khuzam
regions.note: Close to school provision with minimal travel after the last bell. The earliest practical start times in the emirate, so an intensive block with two weekday sessions fits here more easily than anywhere else.

regions.name: Al Dhait
regions.note: Large and established across north and south, with the emirate's most price-sensitive households. Timeline conversations here are usually about total cost over twelve weeks rather than about the hourly rate.

regions.name: Al Hamra Village
regions.note: Gated and coastal, with a later school finish and a real drive home. Sessions generally start from 5.30pm, so a two-session week works best split across a weekday evening and a weekend morning.

regions.name: Mina Al Arab
regions.note: Expanding waterfront community with a meaningful commute to the centre at peak hours. Removing tutor travel is what makes a 6pm start possible, and on a six-week plan that single hour of flexibility is the difference between twelve sessions and eight.

regions.name: Al Marjan Island
regions.note: Causeway access, low density, many households on irregular hospitality and development schedules. Fixed weekly slots are fragile here, so plans are built with a floating second session rather than two fixed ones.

regions.name: Al Qusaidat
regions.note: Northern and largely local-resident, with Arabic A and mandatory-subject requests predominating. Those are the specialisms with the longest booking lead times, so the timeline here starts with the match rather than the teaching.

regions.name: Julphar
regions.note: Dense mixed-use near the old town, apartment households, frequent mid-year arrivals. A student joining in Year 12 from another system needs assessment-instrument work first, which is a six-week job before subject content begins.

regions.name: Seih Al Uraibi
regions.note: Inland with the longest school commutes in the emirate. Sessions begin after 7.30pm, which limits a weekday plan to one session and pushes the second to the weekend.

regions.name: Al Mamourah
regions.note: Quiet and residential, with households commuting south. Weekend mid-mornings are the least-cancelled hour of the week here, and a plan built on them survives a term better than one built on weekday evenings.

sections.heading: "Near me" is the wrong filter for a Diploma subject here
paragraphs: The phrase deserves a direct answer before the timeline starts. A parent searching for a tutor nearby is usually optimising for two things: speed of starting, and the assumption that local means available. In Ras Al Khaimah the second assumption breaks for Diploma subjects, and when it breaks it costs the first thing too.

The arithmetic is unforgiving. The emirate's international provision sits in a small number of campuses. A Diploma cohort can be a dozen or two students, of whom perhaps three take a given subject at Higher Level. The number of locally resident people who have taught that course at that level is therefore very small, and those who exist are generally employed full time. Searching within a driving radius does not produce a shortlist; it often produces nobody, and three weeks spent discovering that is three weeks removed from a twelve-week plan.

Over live video the filter changes from residence to availability: everyone who teaches that course and is free at a workable hour in Gulf Standard Time. For a family working to a date, that is the faster route to the right person as well as the better one. The honest exception is a younger or easily distracted student, where physical presence is the product — and for that, the local in-home market exists at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel priced in.

IB Gram does not provide home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service exists only in India. Saying so at the top rather than in a footnote is the point. What we do provide is one-to-one live video in Gulf Standard Time with late-evening slots, which is also the only format in which the specialism you need can usually be found inside a week.

sections.heading: Step one: establishing where your child is now
paragraphs: The baseline is one real past paper, attempted under timed conditions, marked against the published scheme, with every lost mark attributed by question and by cause. It is free if the school provides the material, it takes an afternoon, and it is the only thing that converts a vague worry into a plan. A family that does this and nothing else is better placed than one that buys twenty hours without it.

What makes it useful is the attribution rather than the score. A total of 42 out of 70 tells you almost nothing. The same paper broken down — nine marks lost on one topic, six to command-term mismatch, four to the final question never being reached, three to arithmetic slips — tells you the shape of the problem, and the shape dictates the instrument. Topic loss needs teaching. Command-term loss needs twenty minutes with a mark scheme. Unreached questions need a timing rehearsal, not more content.

Two cautions. First, use a paper for the correct course and level, because practising the wrong level's conventions trains the wrong habits. Second, insist on timed conditions. An untimed paper hides the single most common failure in this programme, which is a student who knows enough and runs out of time, and it is a failure that responds to practice within weeks.

Interpretation matters as much as marking. A student losing marks across every topic evenly has a different problem from one losing nine marks in one place, and the second is far more tractable. The table below is how we read a baseline, and it is deliberately published so a family can read their own.

sections.heading: Step two: turning a target grade into marks
paragraphs: Parents arrive with a grade and plans need marks. A target of 6 in a subject is not actionable; the same target expressed as "recover the nine marks on that topic, stop losing six to command terms, and reach the final question" is a set of tasks with a plausible timescale. The translation is done from the baseline paper plus the school's assessment outline, and it takes one conversation.

The translation also exposes whether the target is reachable in the time available. Nineteen recoverable marks spread across three identifiable causes, with twelve weeks and a weekly session, is a sensible proposition. The same nineteen marks with four weeks left is not, and the right response is to say so and to pick the largest single cause rather than to sell the full plan and under-deliver on it.

There is a second, less comfortable use for the translation. Sometimes the baseline shows a student is already close to their target and losing marks to nerves and timing rather than to knowledge, in which case the recommendation is three sessions of timed rehearsal and nothing else. Sometimes it shows a student two grades below target with six weeks left, where the honest plan is to protect the grade they can get rather than chase the one they cannot. Both are real outcomes and both get said.

Nobody can promise a grade, and nothing on this page should be read as doing so. What can be promised is a measurement: the same kind of paper, re-sat and marked the same way at six weeks, so that the question of whether it is working has an answer that does not depend on anyone's opinion.

sections.heading: The twelve-week plan, week by week
paragraphs: Twelve weeks is the shortest period in which content, technique and rehearsal all fit without crowding each other. The structure below is the one we use, and it is published in full because a family should be able to check what is happening against what was promised. Deviation from it is fine; silent deviation is not.

The first phase is content, and it is deliberately narrow: two priority topics drawn from the baseline, taught properly, with work set and marked between sessions. Resisting the urge to cover everything is the hardest part of the plan and the most important. A student who has fixed two topics and practised them under time pressure outperforms one who has been reminded of twelve.

The second phase moves to the mark scheme. Past answers get rewritten against the published scheme, command terms get separated, and the student starts predicting the mark allocation before answering. This phase produces the largest measurable movement in most subjects and it cannot happen first, because a student has to know something before they can learn to display it.

The third phase is rehearsal: full papers under timed conditions, marked and attributed, with the timing discussed as a tactical problem rather than a personal failing. By week twelve the student should have sat at least three complete timed papers and know their own time budget per question. The checkpoint at week eight exists precisely so that a plan which is not working can be changed before the rehearsal phase, which is the point at which it becomes too late.

sections.heading: Six weeks, and the discipline of triage
paragraphs: When the papers are six weeks away, the twelve-week structure is not a plan, it is a wish. There is no time for a content phase that covers two topics and then a separate technique phase. Attempting it produces a student who has revised a great deal and rehearsed nothing, which is the worst configuration available going into an examination.

Triage means choosing one thing. The baseline identifies the single largest recoverable loss, the block addresses that, and timed papers start in week two rather than week ten. Sessions go to twice weekly where the diary allows, because the limiting factor is calendar weeks rather than willingness. Everything else on the syllabus is explicitly out of scope, and that has to be agreed rather than assumed.

The second discipline is stopping. The final ten days before a paper are not teaching time. They are consolidation, sleep and light rehearsal of known material, and introducing new content in that window reliably reduces performance. A provider still selling sessions in that fortnight is selling to the parent's anxiety rather than to the student's need.

Six-week plans can work well, and they work best when the honest framing is accepted at the start: this recovers marks, it does not cover the syllabus, and the target may need adjusting. A family told that at the beginning is satisfied at the end. A family promised a transformation is not, whatever actually happens. One practical note on booking: in a six-week block the match time is part of the plan, so a week spent finding a Higher Level specialist is a sixth of the block gone, and the baseline paper should be sat while that search is still running rather than afterwards.

sections.heading: The two-year Diploma timeline, counted backwards
paragraphs: Most of the crises that produce a frantic search for a tutor were visible eighteen months earlier. Laid out as a timeline, the Diploma has a small number of points at which a cheap intervention prevents an expensive one, and almost all of them sit in DP1 where nothing feels urgent yet.

The Extended Essay is the clearest example. A research question narrowed in the first year, with a method tested against real data early, turns 4,000 words into a manageable piece of work. The same essay with a broad question still unresolved in the second year becomes a crisis that consumes time the student needed for Higher Level revision. Four supervision sessions placed early are worth more than twelve placed late, and they cost a third as much.

Subject and level choices are the second. A student in Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation who wants a quantitative degree, or a student at Standard Level in a subject their intended course expects at Higher Level, has a problem that is solvable in DP1 and much harder afterwards. Checking stated university entry requirements in the first year rather than during the application is free and prevents the most painful conversations in this job.

The third is the Internal Assessment cluster. Across six subjects the school's internal deadlines bunch, and in that fortnight a student has no capacity for anything else. A family who knows the dates in advance converts that from an emergency into a planned block of supervision. Ask the school in writing for its internal deadline calendar in the autumn term; it is the single most useful document available and it is rarely volunteered.

sections.heading: What progress looks like at four, eight and twelve weeks — and what it does not
paragraphs: Progress in this work is not linear and families should be warned about that in advance rather than reassured after the fact. The first visible change is usually behavioural: working shown, questions attempted rather than skipped, a willingness to sit a timed paper. That appears within two to four sessions and it is a real signal even though it does not move a score yet.

The second change is diagnostic rather than numerical. At around six to eight weeks the lost marks move from one cause to another — a student who was losing marks to unwritten method starts losing them to the harder end of the topic instead. That looks like no progress on a total and is in fact substantial progress, which is exactly why the checkpoint compares two attributed breakdowns rather than two percentages.

A plateau between weeks four and eight is common and is not by itself a reason to change tutor. A plateau at twelve weeks, with the same attributed losses in the same places, is. The difference between the two is the reason checkpoints are set in advance: a measure agreed at the start cannot be rationalised afterwards by whoever is being paid.

Occasionally a score drops after tutoring starts. The usual cause is that the student is now attempting the harder questions they previously skipped, and attempting them badly before attempting them well. It should be explained at the time rather than hidden, and if it persists past the eight-week checkpoint it is a genuine problem and we will say so.
bullets: Weeks 2-4: behavioural change — working shown, questions attempted

sections.heading: When the honest answer is to start later, or not at all
paragraphs: There are four situations in which the right recommendation is not to buy tutoring, and a page that cannot name them is a sales page. The first is when the baseline shows the student is close to target and losing marks to timing alone. The fix is three sessions of timed rehearsal, or sometimes just the school's own past papers and a stopwatch. Selling a term of weekly sessions into that diagnosis is taking money for a problem that does not exist.

The second is when the student is not short of teaching but short of time. A Diploma student carrying six subjects, mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies, an Extended Essay and CAS does not always have an hour spare. Adding a session to a saturated week produces a cancelled session and a guilty student. The correct intervention there is a conversation with the school about load, not a tutor.

The third is the ten days before an examination. New content in that window reduces performance rather than improving it, and a provider still booking sessions through it is responding to a parent's anxiety. Stop deliberately, and say in advance that you are going to.

The fourth is when the problem is not academic. A student who has stopped working across every subject simultaneously usually has something else going on, and tutoring is a poor instrument for it. The useful move is a conversation with the school's pastoral lead. We would rather lose that booking than take it, and a provider unwilling to say that out loud is one to be careful with.
bullets: Close to target with a timing failure: three rehearsal sessions, not a term
A saturated week: a conversation about load, not another hour in it

sections.heading: What a timeline costs, rather than what an hour costs
paragraphs: Comparing providers on an hourly rate is how families end up spending more for less. The useful figure is the total cost of the plan that fits their calendar, and that is calculable in advance. Market rates for a qualified subject tutor online run roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with an IB specialist at AED 200 to 450 or more and the premium end reaching AED 650; an in-home visit runs AED 180 to 500 with travel priced in. Those figures come from providers' own published pages and from Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table rather than from us.

Multiply those by the plan rather than by the month. A twelve-week weekly plan is twelve sessions. A six-week triage at twice weekly is ten to twelve. A deadline block is four to eight. Expressed that way, the deadline block is frequently the cheapest effective intervention available and the one families never consider, because nobody sells it.

Monthly packages circulate at AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits. Divide by total teaching minutes before comparing, and be aware that a monthly commitment removes the ability to stop at the six-week checkpoint, which is the one thing you most want to retain if the plan turns out to be wrong.

IB Gram quotes after the diagnostic rather than publishing a price list, because the hours a plan needs are a function of the baseline. What is fixed is the free trial lesson — one lesson, one subject, no payment and no card details — and the review date. A provider that will not tell you the total before you start, or that has no checkpoint at which you can stop, is selling an open-ended commitment.
