sections.heading: Deadline pressure is where honesty rules get broken
paragraphs: The academic-honesty line matters most at exactly the moment a timeline is tightest. A student with an Internal Assessment due on Thursday and a tutor trying to be helpful on Wednesday evening is the scenario in which a feedback session becomes an editing session. The rule does not bend for deadlines: assessed work must be the student's own.

What legitimate support looks like under pressure is narrower and more useful than it sounds. The published criteria get read aloud with the student. The tutor asks what evidence supports each claim and whether the limitation listed actually matters. The student types every word. Version history in a shared document records who wrote what, which protects the candidate rather than surveilling them.

The market pressure is real. Operators in this search results page sell completed Internal Assessments, with finished work advertised at around AED 3,750. The school supervisor signs an authenticity declaration, so the exposure sits with the student as an IB malpractice matter while the seller carries nothing. A family that knows this in week one cannot be sold it in week eleven.

The same applies to materials. Syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes, grade-boundary tables and subject guides belong to the IB, Cambridge and Pearson, and should be downloaded by the family from the board's own site rather than supplied by a tutor as a folder. The offer of a drive full of restricted material, which arrives more often as a deadline approaches, is information about the operation rather than a benefit.
bullets: The student types every word, including under deadline pressure

sections.heading: Starting this week
paragraphs: If the date you are working towards is more than twelve weeks away, the first step is free and does not involve us. Ask the school for the subject's assessment outline, the internal deadline calendar and your child's last two pieces of marked work, then have them sit one real past paper under timed conditions. Marked and attributed, that paper is the plan. Several families who do this discover the problem is three sessions wide.

If the date is closer than twelve weeks, the sequence compresses but does not change. Baseline first, still. Then the single largest recoverable loss, then timed papers from week two. A plan without a baseline is a plan built on a guess, and in a six-week block there is no room to discover in week four that the guess was wrong.

Then a free trial lesson: one lesson, one subject, no payment and no card details. What you should see is the student attempting real questions and the tutor finishing with two specific named things to fix. Then a written plan with the week-by-week structure, the session slot in Gulf Standard Time, and the checkpoint date and measure agreed before the first paid hour.

And the honest items. Higher Level Chemistry, Higher Level Physics and Arabic A are thin specialisms in UAE evening hours, so if your timeline is short, the match time matters and we will give you a real one rather than an optimistic one. We provide no home visits in the UAE. We hold no regulator approval and claim none. And at the checkpoint we will tell you what the two marked papers show, including when they show that you can stop.

process.title: Put the date at the top of the page
process.description: Write down the date you are working towards — a mock, an Internal Assessment deadline, the examination session as your school's IB coordinator states it. Everything else follows from the number of weeks available, and choosing a plan shape without that number is how families buy the wrong instrument.

process.title: Baseline one real paper, under time
process.description: A past paper for the correct course and level, attempted under timed conditions and marked against the published scheme with the loss attributed by question and cause. This is the diagnosis. Untimed papers hide the most common failure in the programme, which is knowing enough and running out of time.

process.title: Translate the target into marks
process.description: Convert the grade you want into specific recoverable marks on named causes. Nineteen marks across three causes with twelve weeks available is a plan. The same nineteen with four weeks is not, and the right response is to pick the largest cause rather than to promise the full recovery.

process.title: Free trial lesson, one subject
process.description: One full one-to-one session over live video at no cost, no card details, with the condition stated in advance. Expect the student to attempt real questions and the tutor to name two specific things to fix. An hour of explanation tells you almost nothing about whether the match works.

process.title: Agree the plan and the checkpoint in writing
process.description: The week-by-week structure, the two priority topics, the session slot in Gulf Standard Time, and the checkpoint date with the measure that will be used. Agreeing the measure before the first paid hour is what stops it being rationalised later by the person being paid.

process.title: Checkpoint, then decide
process.description: At six weeks a comparable paper is re-sat and marked the same way, and the two attributed breakdowns are compared. The decision is to continue, to change the priority, to change the tutor, or to stop. Stopping because the problem is solved is a legitimate and reasonably common outcome.

whyPoints.title: A diagnosis before a plan
whyPoints.description: No lesson is planned until a real paper has been marked and the loss attributed by question and by cause. The first three weeks of most tutoring arrangements are spent discovering what a single marked paper would have shown in an afternoon, and that is three weeks a timeline cannot spare.

whyPoints.title: The plan is published week by week
whyPoints.description: The twelve-week and six-week structures are set out on this page in full, including what is deliberately out of scope. A family should be able to check what is happening against what was agreed, and silent deviation from a plan is the thing that makes tutoring feel unmeasurable.

whyPoints.title: Checkpoints agreed in advance
whyPoints.description: The review date and the measure are fixed before the first paid hour: a comparable paper, re-sat, marked the same way, two attributed breakdowns compared. A measure agreed at the start cannot be reinterpreted at the end by whoever is being paid for the sessions.

whyPoints.title: Speed of match treated as part of the timeline
whyPoints.description: On a six-week plan, a week spent finding a tutor is a sixth of the plan. Higher Level Chemistry, Higher Level Physics and Arabic A are thin specialisms in UAE evening hours, so we give a real match time rather than an optimistic one and let you plan around it.

whyPoints.title: We will tell you not to buy
whyPoints.description: Close to target with a timing failure, a saturated week, the final ten days before a paper, or a collapse across every subject at once — in each of those the right answer is not tutoring, and this page names all four. A provider that cannot name them is a sales page.

whyPoints.title: Cost quoted as a plan, not an hour
whyPoints.description: Market rates are published here with their sources, and plan totals are set out by shape so you can see what twelve sessions or four actually comes to. A monthly commitment that removes your ability to stop at the checkpoint is the one structure we would advise against anywhere.

faqs.question: We searched for an IB tutor near me — does it matter that the tutor is not in Ras Al Khaimah?
faqs.answer: For Diploma subjects, usually not, and in this emirate insisting on it works against you. International provision here sits in a few campuses and a Higher Level cohort can be three students, so the number of locally resident people who have taught that course at that level is very small. Searching within a driving radius frequently produces nobody, and the weeks spent finding that out come out of your plan. Over live video the filter becomes availability rather than residence, which is both wider and faster. The genuine exception is a younger student who needs an adult physically present.

faqs.question: My son has eight weeks before his papers. Is it too late to start?
faqs.answer: No, but the plan has to be triage rather than a compressed version of a longer one. Eight weeks allows a baseline paper in week one, one named priority rather than two, timed papers from week two, and a deliberate stop in the final ten days. What it does not allow is covering the syllabus, and accepting that at the start is what makes the outcome satisfactory. Expect to recover marks on the largest identifiable cause rather than to transform a grade. If your target needs nineteen marks across three causes, the honest version is that eight weeks addresses the biggest one.

faqs.question: How long does it take to move an IB subject grade?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on what the baseline shows, which is why nobody should answer this before marking a paper. Technique losses — unwritten method, command-term mismatch, unreached final questions — often move within two to six sessions because they are habits. A genuine content gap in one or two topics takes four to eight weeks. Breadth missing across a whole syllabus takes a term or more. Internal assessment criteria problems take four to eight focused sessions. A provider who quotes a timescale before seeing a marked paper is guessing, and the guess is usually optimistic.

faqs.question: What should we expect to see after four sessions?
faqs.answer: Behavioural change rather than score movement. By session four a student should be showing their working, attempting questions they previously skipped, and willing to sit a timed paper. Those are real signals even though a total mark may not have shifted yet, and they are the things to ask about. What you should also have by then is written evidence: marked work returned with the loss attributed by question. If after four sessions nothing has been marked and nothing has been set between sessions, that is a problem with the arrangement rather than with your child.

faqs.question: What if the grade goes down after we start tutoring?
faqs.answer: It happens, and the usual cause is benign: the student is now attempting the harder questions they used to skip, and attempting them badly before attempting them well. A total can fall while the attributed losses improve, which is why checkpoints compare breakdowns rather than percentages. It should be explained to you at the time rather than discovered at a report evening. If the same attributed losses are still sitting in the same places at the eight-week checkpoint, that is a genuine problem, and the right responses are changing the priority topic, changing the tutor, or stopping.

faqs.question: How many weeks of support does a Chemistry Internal Assessment need?
faqs.answer: Four to eight sessions, placed before the school's internal draft deadline rather than after it. The work is not teaching chemistry; it is reading the published criteria letter by letter with the student against a draft they have written, asking what evidence supports each claim, and testing whether the method will survive contact with the data. Most marks are lost on process criteria rather than on chemistry. Get the school's internal deadline in writing first, because it sits earlier than the IB's own upload date, and a block timed to the wrong date is a block wasted.

faqs.question: When in DP1 should we start thinking about the Extended Essay?
faqs.answer: Earlier than feels necessary, because this is the single most common timeline failure in the programme. A research question narrowed in the first year, with the method tested against real data before the summer, turns 4,000 words into a manageable task spread over months. The same essay with a broad question unresolved in the second year becomes a crisis that consumes revision time for Higher Level subjects. Two to four supervision sessions in DP1 are worth more than twelve in DP2 and cost a fraction as much. The school supervisor remains the formal supervisor throughout.

faqs.question: My daughter is in MYP Year 5. Should we start before the Diploma begins?
faqs.answer: If there is a gap, this is the cheapest year in which to close it. Nothing external is at stake yet, the criteria are published so progress is measurable, and the habits that matter in the Diploma — showing method, reading command terms, sitting timed work without panic — transfer directly. A term of light weekly work in MYP Year 5 routinely prevents a crisis block in DP2 that costs several times as much. The Personal Project also provides a natural, low-stakes rehearsal for the process skills the Extended Essay will demand two years later.

faqs.question: Is it better to have one long session a week or two short ones?
faqs.answer: Two shorter sessions, in most cases, and the reason is retention rather than preference. A 45 or 60-minute session twice a week produces two opportunities to set work, two opportunities to mark it, and two points at which a misunderstanding gets caught. A single 120-minute block produces one of each and a tired student in the final half hour. The exception is timed-paper rehearsal, which needs a block long enough to sit a full paper. In practice, plans often run one shorter session midweek and one longer weekend slot.

faqs.question: How many total hours is a twelve-week plan, and what does that cost in AED?
faqs.answer: Twelve sessions at one a week, so twelve to eighteen hours depending on session length. At market rates of around AED 200 an hour for a qualified subject tutor that is roughly AED 2,400; at AED 350 for a specialist, roughly AED 4,200. Those market figures come from providers' published pages and Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table rather than from us. A four-session deadline block is AED 800 to AED 1,400 on the same basis and is frequently the better-value intervention. We quote after the diagnostic, because the hours needed depend on what the baseline paper shows.

faqs.question: When is the honest answer that we should not start tutoring at all?
faqs.answer: Four situations. When the baseline shows your child is close to target and losing marks to timing alone — three rehearsal sessions, or just past papers and a stopwatch. When the week is already saturated with six subjects, the mandatory UAE subjects, an Extended Essay and CAS, and the real need is a conversation with the school about load. In the final ten days before a paper, when new content reduces performance. And when a student has stopped working across every subject at once, which is usually pastoral rather than academic and needs the school, not a tutor.

faqs.question: Can we pause over the summer and resume in August?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for most students it is the right call. A genuine break improves the autumn term more than summer sessions do, and the exceptions are narrow: a student bridging a real gap before a new course begins, a student who has just changed curriculum, or an Extended Essay question that needs narrowing before DP2 starts. Where a summer block is justified, keep it short and specific — four to six sessions on a named objective, ending on a stated date. Open-ended summer tutoring with no target is the easiest money to waste in this market.

faqs.question: How far ahead should we book if we need a Higher Level Physics specialist?
faqs.answer: Treat the match as part of your timeline rather than as a formality. Higher Level Physics, Higher Level Chemistry and Arabic A are thin specialisms in UAE evening hours, so a week of match time is realistic and on a six-week plan that is a sixth of the plan gone. If your date is fixed, start the conversation as soon as the baseline paper is marked. Where a specialist exists only at a time that does not suit your household, we will tell you the time rather than substituting a generalist, and you can decide whether to move the slot or the expectation.

faqs.question: What should my child do in the three weeks between the last session and the papers?
faqs.answer: Consolidate what is already known, sit a small number of timed papers on material already covered, sleep properly, and learn nothing new. That last part is the one families resist and it is the most important. New content introduced inside the final fortnight reliably displaces what was already secure rather than adding to it. A plan should end with a stated final session rather than trailing off, and the last ten days belong to the student. A provider still booking sessions through that window is responding to anxiety rather than to need.

faqs.question: Should tutoring continue during the examination window itself?
faqs.answer: Generally no. During the papers a student is managing a schedule rather than learning, and an additional commitment competes with rest between examinations. There is one narrow exception: where a long gap sits between two papers in different subjects and the student wants a single rehearsal session on the later one, that can be useful. Otherwise the money is better kept for post-results decisions, which is when a planning conversation genuinely helps — retake options, enquiries about results, and what the next stage actually requires. Agree in advance that the plan stops, so it is a decision rather than a drift.

faqs.question: My child is predicted a 4 and needs a 6. Is that realistic in one term?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and the marked baseline is the only thing that can tell you. If the gap is concentrated — one topic consistently failed, method marks discarded, the final question never reached — then a term of weekly work addressing those causes is a credible proposition, because those are the fastest-moving losses. If the baseline shows marks lost evenly across every topic, the gap is breadth and a term is unlikely to close two grades. Nobody can promise a grade and we will not. What we will give you is a measurement at six weeks, and an honest statement if the evidence says the target needs adjusting.

ras-al-khaimah/ib-tutor-near-me.closingHeading: Put the date down, then mark one paper
ras-al-khaimah/ib-tutor-near-me.closingBody: The useful order is always the same: the date you are working towards, then a real past paper sat under timed conditions and marked with the loss attributed by question and cause, then the plan shape that fits the weeks remaining. Everything else is detail. The first two steps cost nothing if the school supplies the material, and they regularly reveal that the problem is three sessions wide rather than a term. If specialist help is what the paper points to, a free trial lesson over live video is available — one lesson, one subject, no payment taken — and you will get a real match time rather than an optimistic one.

intro.heading: The question behind the search: how many weeks are left, and what has to happen in them
paragraphs: A parent types home tutor because that is the familiar phrase for one-to-one attention. The thing being bought, though, is almost never the travel. It is the sequence: somebody reads the evidence, says where the student currently stands, names the grade that is realistic, and lays out what each of the remaining weeks has to contain. Nine times out of ten, when a family in Al Dhait or Mina Al Arab asks about a home tutor, that sequence is what they want and nobody has yet given it to them.

So start with the arithmetic. A Year 11 student in Ras Al Khaimah sitting a June series in the summer term has roughly twenty-four teachable weeks from the start of the autumn term, minus the winter break, minus Ramadan's altered evenings, minus the school's own mock fortnight, minus the week nobody works after Eid. The honest figure is closer to nineteen or twenty. That is enough to clear four or five recurring error types in a subject and to raise a grade by a band, and it is not enough to re-teach two years of content. Knowing which of those two jobs you are buying changes everything about how the weeks are spent.

In-home tuition is a real market here and worth describing properly. Published market rates for in-home one-to-one across the UAE run roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour including travel, against roughly AED 150 to 300 for qualified online teaching and AED 200 to 450 for exam-board specialists. Those are provider figures, not ours. In an emirate where residential areas are spread across about forty kilometres of coast and inland belt, the travel inside that fee is not a rounding error: a tutor who drives from the city to Al Hamra Village and back has spent an hour of their evening on the road, and that hour is in your rate whether it is itemised or not.

IB Gram's answer is to drop the travel and keep the one-to-one. Teaching happens online, over live video, with one tutor and one student, and we do not send a tutor to a home anywhere in the UAE; in-home visiting is a service we run only in India. The practical gain is subject depth. A student in Al Rams needing Extended-tier Chemistry 0620 gets a chemistry teacher rather than whoever is willing to make the drive, and the hour you pay for is an hour of teaching.

The rest of this page is the timeline. What the first two weeks look like, what has to be true by week six, what changes at week twelve, what the final eight weeks contain, and how the Ras Al Khaimah calendar - winter break, Ramadan, Eid, the school's mock window - cuts into the plan. There is also a short section on when a physical presence in the room genuinely is the better answer, because sometimes it is, and pretending otherwise would be a sales pitch rather than advice.

ras-al-khaimah/igcse-home-tutor.programmesIntro: The plan looks different at each stage, because the amount of time left is different. These are the four points in a Ras Al Khaimah student's route where families most often start, with what the weeks realistically contain at each one.

programmes.name: IGCSE Year 10, the first of the two years
programmes.description: The year nobody treats as urgent and the year with the most leverage. Content is being met for the first time, so a weekly hour spent on the topic currently being taught in class prevents the gap rather than repairing it. A Year 10 plan is measured in terms rather than weeks: three or four topics a term, each closed properly before the next one starts.
programmes.countryNote: Ras Al Khaimah schools generally set internal examinations at the end of Year 10 that decide the tier a student is entered for in Year 11. That makes the summer term of Year 10 the real decision point for Core or Extended, and it is the moment at which a term of targeted work changes which grades are available at all.

programmes.name: IGCSE Year 11, the exam year
programmes.description: Two phases, divided by the mock fortnight. Before mocks, the work is content and method: closing the gaps that the autumn term exposes while there is still room. After mocks, the work is almost entirely timed questions marked against the published scheme, with the topic list shrinking each week as errors are cleared. The second phase cannot repair what the first one ignored.
programmes.countryNote: Entry decisions in this emirate are usually finalised in the autumn term of Year 11, months before anyone sits a paper, and a Cambridge June series needs its final entries from the centre in the spring, well before revision peaks. A family starting in October still has influence over the entry itself; one starting in April has influence only over the preparation. The November series exists as the resit route, not as a way to reopen a decision already made.

programmes.name: November resit and private-candidate routes
programmes.description: A missed grade is not a twelve-month problem if the board offers a second series. Pearson runs International GCSE in May or June and again in November; Cambridge runs June and November. A resit plan is short and specific: the paper that cost the grade, the four topics inside it that lost the most marks, and six to ten weeks of timed practice rather than a repeat of the whole course.
programmes.countryNote: The November 2026 Pearson International GCSE final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, with November 2025 results reaching students on 22 January 2026. Ras Al Khaimah families need to confirm early whether their school's exam centre is entering candidates for that series, because a private-candidate entry elsewhere has its own earlier deadline.

programmes.name: The step after Year 11: A Level or IB Diploma
programmes.description: The transition is a timeline problem of its own. IGCSE rewards accurate recall and method; both post-16 routes reward argument, independent research and assessment against published criteria. The students who struggle in the first term of Year 12 are rarely the ones who lacked content - they are the ones who had never been asked to produce a sustained piece of their own reasoning.
programmes.countryNote: Because Ras Al Khaimah has both an IB continuum campus on the southern coast and A Level provision in the city, a summer of bridging work in mathematics is the most common request here. A single hour a week through July and August closes the gap between Extended IGCSE and the first weeks of either route.

ras-al-khaimah/igcse-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: What a plan contains differs by subject, because the marks are lost in different places. For each subject below the description names what the remaining weeks should actually be spent on rather than restating the syllabus.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: Weeks one to four on method and accuracy, weeks five onward on the multi-step questions at the back of the paper. A student who writes no working cannot be awarded method marks, and that single habit is worth more in six weeks than any new topic.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics (Cambridge 0606)
subjects.description: Calculus, trigonometric identities and series, taken alongside 0580. The timeline here is unforgiving because the content is genuinely new rather than revisited, so a plan that starts after the mock fortnight is usually a plan to secure a pass rather than to chase the top band.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 / Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Single tier at Pearson
subjects.description: Moles and stoichiometry first, always, because they appear across both papers and because a student who can lay out a calculation in steps stops losing whole questions. Organic chemistry comes next if the target is the top band, and data-handling practice runs alongside throughout.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 / Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Single tier at Pearson
subjects.description: Circuits and moments take the first fortnight of most plans. Then the describe-an-experiment questions, which follow a pattern the mark scheme rewards: a named measurement, a repeated reading, a stated control. That pattern is learnable in three sessions.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 / Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Single tier at Pearson
subjects.description: Content volume makes this the subject where a plan has to be ruthless. Weeks are allocated by mark weight rather than by syllabus order, and answer length is drilled against the mark allocation, because short answers to four-mark questions are the commonest leak.

subjects.name: Co-ordinated Sciences (Cambridge 0654)
subjects.description: The first job is scoping: establishing what the double award does not include, so the remaining weeks are not spent on single-science content that will never be examined. That audit takes one session and routinely saves a fortnight.

subjects.name: English as a First Language (Cambridge 0500 / Pearson 4EA1)
subjects.description: Two papers, two separate skills, so the weeks split. Reading work is summary discipline and close analysis of how a writer achieves an effect; writing work is structure, register and finishing within the time. Marking the student's own work against the criteria accelerates both.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510 and 0511)
subjects.description: Listening technique responds quickly to practice, which makes it a good early win in a short plan. Writing tasks are then drilled for purpose and audience, since answers that read well but miss the brief sit in the middle band.

subjects.name: Business Studies (Cambridge 0450 / Pearson 4BS1)
subjects.description: Application is the whole timeline. Weekly practice is one case study and one data-response question, marked for whether the answer refers to the business in front of it rather than to business in general.

subjects.name: Economics (Cambridge 0455)
subjects.description: Diagrams in week one, because they are quick marks and students lose them to missing labels. Then evaluation language, which is what separates the top two bands in the structured paper.

subjects.name: Computer Science (Cambridge 0478 / Pearson 4CP0)
subjects.description: Pseudocode and trace tables, practised rather than read, from the first session. Both are mechanical skills that improve with repetition, which makes them well suited to a short plan with weekly homework.

subjects.name: Geography (Cambridge 0460) and History (Cambridge 0470)
subjects.description: Source handling and the skills paper take priority because they are the most trainable components. Where a school runs coursework rather than the alternative paper, internal deadlines go into the plan before anything else.

ras-al-khaimah/igcse-home-tutor.regionsTitle: Travel time across Ras Al Khaimah, and what it does to a weekly slot
ras-al-khaimah/igcse-home-tutor.regionsIntro: These are the distances that make an in-home weekly booking hard to sustain in this emirate, and the session times that work in each area once the school run is finished. All figures are approximate and off-peak.

regions.name: Al Nakheel and Al Mairid
regions.note: The city core, where most weekday traffic sits. Short school runs mean a 4.30pm start is usually achievable, and this is the one part of the emirate where a tutor could plausibly see two families in an evening.

regions.name: Al Dhait North and Al Dhait South
regions.note: Residential districts inland of the city with a large school-age population. Fifteen minutes from the main city campuses, so a 5pm slot holds through the year; the earlier slots here are the first to be taken in September.

regions.name: Khuzam
regions.note: Inland and close to one of the emirate's main British-curriculum campuses, which makes the school run short and the homework window long. Families here often prefer two shorter sessions a week to one long one.

regions.name: Mina Al Arab and Hayat Island
regions.note: Coastal housing roughly twenty minutes south of the city. Siblings are often at campuses in opposite directions, so staggered slots forty minutes apart work better than consecutive ones.

regions.name: Al Hamra Village and Al Jazirah Al Hamra
regions.note: Half an hour south of the city centre with its own campuses on the doorstep. Short school run, long drive to everything else - which is why a visiting tutor's travel charge is highest here and a fixed online slot is easiest to protect.

regions.name: Al Marjan Island
regions.note: One causeway in and out. Any delay on the approach road adds twenty minutes, so a lesson that depends on nobody travelling is simply more reliable across a twenty-week plan.

regions.name: Al Qusaidat, Al Rams and Sha'am
regions.note: The northern strip towards the Oman border, where the school run alone can be twenty-five minutes each way. A 6pm start is realistic; a 4.30pm one usually is not, and that constraint shapes which tutors can hold the slot.

regions.name: Digdaga, Al Ghail and the inland belt
regions.note: Furthest from the school clusters and from any tutor pool. Connections are generally stable, and these are the households for whom the difference between a travelling tutor and a remote one is measured in hours rather than minutes.

sections.heading: What asking for a home tutor in this emirate actually gets you
paragraphs: In a dense city a home visit is a twenty-minute drive and a tutor can teach three families in an evening. Ras Al Khaimah is not that. Residential areas run from the northern strip at Al Rams down through the city districts to Mina Al Arab, Al Hamra Village and Al Marjan Island, and crossing that span in the early evening is a real journey. A tutor who commits to a Tuesday 5pm slot in Al Hamra and a Tuesday 7pm slot in Al Nakheel is committing to roughly an hour on the road between them, and that hour is priced into somebody's fee.

That changes the local economics in two ways. First, the published market range for in-home one-to-one in the UAE - roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour including travel, with monthly in-home packages advertised around AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour sessions - sits at the top of the market here rather than the middle, because distance is longer. Second, and more importantly, it shrinks the pool. The people willing to drive to Al Rams on a weekday evening are not selected for having taught Extended-tier Chemistry 0620; they are selected for living nearby and being free.

For a twenty-week plan, reliability matters as much as price. A visiting arrangement in a spread-out emirate loses sessions to traffic, to the tutor's own schedule and to the school holidays when they travel. A fixed online slot survives all three, and in a timeline where nineteen or twenty teachable weeks is the real budget, two lost sessions is ten per cent of the plan.

So the honest comparison is below, with market figures attributed to the market. IB Gram does not sell a home visit in the UAE; we teach the same one-to-one hour online and do not charge anybody for a drive. Where a family genuinely needs a person in the room - and that case exists - we would rather say so than take the booking, which is the subject of a later section on this page.

sections.heading: Step one: establishing where the student actually is
paragraphs: No plan can be written from a grade. A 5 in Pearson mathematics and a 5 in Pearson mathematics can be two completely different students: one who understands the content and loses marks to unfinished papers and missing method, and one who cannot handle algebraic manipulation and is scoring on the accessible questions only. The first needs six weeks of technique work; the second needs a term of teaching. The grade does not distinguish them. A marked script does, in about fifteen minutes.

What we ask for before the first session is specific: the two most recent marked mock scripts, one piece of recent class work with the teacher's comments, and the statement of entry showing the syllabus code and tier. From those, a tutor produces a ranked list of recurring errors - usually four or five - with a rough mark value attached to each. That list is the plan. It is also the thing to measure against later, which is why it goes to you in writing at the start rather than being described in conversation.

This step is where most tutoring arrangements go wrong, and the failure is quiet. Without evidence, a tutor defaults to the syllabus order and starts at the beginning, which feels productive and spends the first month on topics the student already knows. Six weeks in, the parent cannot tell whether anything has changed, because nothing was measured at the start. The diagnosis is not an administrative preliminary; it is the difference between a plan and a standing appointment.

For students in Years 7 to 9 the same logic applies with lighter evidence. Cambridge Checkpoint feedback, where the school uses it, maps onto the topics an IGCSE paper will test two years later, and a Year 8 report plus one piece of work is enough to find the arithmetic or writing gap that would otherwise become a grade ceiling in Year 11.

sections.heading: Step two: turning a target grade into something a week can contain
paragraphs: A target grade is not a plan; it is a wish with a number attached. The work of the second session is translating it into components. Each paper carries a share of the grade, and within each paper the marks sit in identifiable places: the short recall questions, the method-bearing middle, and the extended questions at the back that reward structure and stamina. A student aiming to move up a band almost never needs all three to improve. Usually one of them is where the band is being lost.

Take Cambridge science as the clearest case. The grade is built from a multiple-choice paper, a theory paper and either a practical test or the alternative-to-practical written paper, and each component rewards a different habit. A student losing marks on the practical component is not helped by more content revision; they need results tables, sources of error and controlled variables. A student losing marks across the theory paper's longer answers needs answer length matched to mark allocation and command words read properly. Same target grade, two unrelated plans.

We will not publish grade boundaries or claim a specific mark total produces a specific grade, because boundaries are set by the board after each series and vary. What a tutor can do honestly is show which component is leaking, estimate the marks available there, and say what the student has to be able to do by a given week to collect them. That is a check a parent can apply: if nobody can tell you where the marks are coming from, nobody has a plan.
The table below is the format we use for that conversation. It is judgement rather than published data, and it is written per student rather than per subject, but the shape is the same every time.

sections.heading: Step three: the weeks in between, counted backwards
paragraphs: Here is the sequence a Year 11 plan follows when there are roughly twenty-four weeks to a June series. It is written backwards from the exam because that is how deadlines work and forwards from today is how plans drift. The phases are not equal in length and the middle one is where most families underinvest.

Weeks twenty-four to seventeen are content and method. This is the only window in which new teaching is efficient, and it closes. Weeks sixteen to eleven are the mock fortnight and its aftermath: the school's internal examinations produce the single most useful document of the year, and the fortnight after them should be spent reading the script rather than celebrating or mourning the grade. Weeks ten to five are timed questions, topic by topic, with the error list rewritten weekly. Weeks four to one are full papers under conditions, past-paper pacing and the specific repairs that are still available.

The table sets this out with the evidence each phase should produce, because a plan you cannot audit is a plan you are trusting rather than following. If week six arrives and nobody can show you a shorter error list than week one's, the arrangement is not working, and that is a conversation to have in week six rather than in May.

One realism check. Few families start at week twenty-four. Most arrive somewhere in the middle, often just after a disappointing mock, which means the content phase has already gone. A plan starting at week ten is a legitimate plan - it is just a different one, with the content window closed and the work concentrated on collecting the marks the student can already reach. Saying that clearly at the start is better than discovering it in April.

sections.heading: The weeks the UAE calendar takes out of your plan
paragraphs: A twenty-four week plan is a fiction until the calendar is applied to it. The UAE academic year has a long winter break, a Ramadan period in which school days and household evenings both shorten, Eid holidays that remove a working week at short notice, and a school mock fortnight that absorbs the student's attention entirely. Build those in at the start and the plan holds. Ignore them and the plan quietly loses four or five weeks, which is most of a phase.

Ramadan is the one that needs real thought. School hours are reduced, families eat late, and a 5pm lesson that worked in January is the wrong slot in the fasting month. The workable options are an early-afternoon session straight after a shortened school day, or a post-Iftar slot in the evening, and both need to be agreed in advance rather than improvised in week one. Students generally do better with shorter, more frequent sessions during Ramadan than with the usual single long one.

The winter break is the other consequential gap, because it falls in the middle of the content phase for a June series and immediately before mocks at many schools. Families who use a short block of three or four sessions across that break tend to arrive at mocks with the content phase genuinely finished. Families who stop for three weeks usually spend the first fortnight of January recovering ground.

Summer matters for a different reason. July and August are when bridging work happens - Extended mathematics into the Diploma or an A Level, or English writing into a post-16 course - and they are also when many Ras Al Khaimah families travel. A slot can follow a family across time zones within reason, and saying at the outset which weeks will be missed is better than cancelling four sessions one at a time.

sections.heading: What the first month should look like, week by week
paragraphs: Week one is diagnosis and one piece of teaching. The tutor works through a mock script and a piece of class work, names the recurring errors, and then teaches the first of them so the session is not purely administrative. You receive the error list and the topic order the same day. Nothing else should happen in week one, and a tutor who spends it on general revision has skipped the only step that makes the rest efficient.

Weeks two and three are the first two errors on the list, in order of mark value rather than syllabus order. Each session follows the same shape: the student's practice from the previous week is marked at the start, the error is taught, and a short set of questions is agreed for the week ahead. By the end of week three a parent should be able to name what their child is working on, in specific terms, without asking the tutor.

Week four is the first checkpoint. The tutor reruns a subset of the original diagnostic questions and compares the result to week one. Two outcomes are normal: the first errors have cleared and the list is shorter, or they have not and the method needs changing. Both are useful. What is not acceptable is week four arriving with no comparison available, which is what happens when no baseline was recorded.

From week five the plan runs on its own rhythm until the mock window or the phase change at eight weeks out. The written note after each session is short on purpose - what was covered, what was practised, what is next - because a note nobody reads is worse than no note. Families who want more detail get a longer review at the six-week point, measured against the plan agreed in week one.

sections.heading: When a person in the room genuinely is the better answer
paragraphs: Online one-to-one is not the right format for every student, and pretending otherwise would be the sort of claim this page exists to avoid. There are cases where physical presence does something a screen cannot, and a family in Ras Al Khaimah weighing the two should know what they are.

The clearest is age and supervision. A student in Years 3 to 6 who cannot yet manage their own attention for forty minutes benefits from an adult in the room, and for that age group a local arrangement or a parent sitting in is usually better than a video call. The second case is a student with specific needs where reading the room, pacing and physical materials matter in ways a screen makes harder; some students with attention or processing differences work far better face to face, and some work better online because the environment is calmer and more controlled. It depends on the student, and a trial lesson is how you find out rather than a brochure.

The third case is practical equipment. Science practical skills belong in a laboratory, and no online arrangement replaces one. What online teaching does well is the assessed version of practical skill - results tables, error sources, controlled variables, the alternative-to-practical paper - which is where the marks actually are. The hands-on work stays at school.

For a secondary student working on a named IGCSE specification at a named tier, though, the trade-off generally runs the other way in this emirate. Presence in the room buys you whoever can drive to your area; a screen buys you whoever teaches the subject best. Over nineteen teachable weeks, that difference is usually larger than the difference between a chair and a camera. IB Gram does not offer the in-home option in the UAE at all, so if the first case above describes your child, we would rather tell you that than sell you a weekly slot.

sections.heading: If the timeline is shorter than eight weeks
paragraphs: Short plans are not bad plans, but they are different ones, and the first thing to do is abandon the ambition of covering the syllabus. With eight weeks or fewer the only rational strategy is to collect marks the student can already nearly reach, which means timed questions on the topics that appear most often, method presentation so partial credit is available, and pacing so the paper gets finished.

The second thing is to stop adding subjects. A family six weeks from a series with four subjects in trouble is tempted to book four tutors, and the result is usually twelve hours of teaching a week and no practice time, which makes things worse. Two subjects, properly worked, produce better outcomes than four skimmed. The choice between them is a mark-value calculation: which subject has the most reachable marks sitting unclaimed, and which one matters most for the next step after Year 11.

The third is to check the entry. Tier changes, subject additions and private-candidate entries close months before the exam - the centre files Cambridge final entries for a June series in the spring, and Pearson's November 2026 timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026, so entries for it were settled long before the autumn - which means by week eight those decisions are usually fixed. Knowing they are fixed is itself useful: it rules out the conversations that would otherwise absorb a week, and it tells the tutor to spend that week on papers instead.

And if the honest answer is that a target is out of reach in the weeks remaining, we will say so, and talk about the November series instead. Pearson and Cambridge both run one, which makes a resit a same-year option rather than a lost year. That conversation in April is uncomfortable; the same conversation in August is much worse.

faqs.question: We asked for a home tutor and you teach online. What do we lose by that?
faqs.answer: You lose a person in the room, which matters for younger children and for some students with specific needs. You gain three things. The hour is all teaching rather than partly travel. The tutor is chosen for having taught your child's specification at your child's tier rather than for living nearby, which in this emirate is the binding constraint. And the slot survives traffic, school holidays and the tutor's own commute across a twenty-week plan. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a UAE address at all; in-home visiting is offered only in India, so if presence in the room is essential we will tell you rather than take the booking.

faqs.question: How many teachable weeks do we really have before a June series?
faqs.answer: Count the calendar weeks, then subtract. From the start of the autumn term to a June series is roughly twenty-four weeks. Take out the winter break, the school's mock fortnight, the altered evenings of Ramadan and the week that disappears around Eid, and nineteen or twenty is the honest figure. That is enough to clear four or five recurring error types in a subject and to move a grade by a band. It is not enough to re-teach two years of content, which is why the first session is spent finding out which of those two jobs you are actually buying.

faqs.question: What should be different about the plan after a bad mock result?
faqs.answer: A bad mock is the most useful document of the year, so the week after it should be spent reading the script rather than reacting to the grade. Mark loss falls into three buckets: topics not known, method not shown, and papers not finished. Each needs a different response, and most students have all three in different proportions. The plan that follows is built from that split, with the biggest bucket taken first. What should not change is the number of subjects being tutored; the instinct after a bad mock is to add two more, and that usually removes the practice time that makes any of it work.

faqs.question: Do shorter sessions work better than our usual hour during the fasting month?
faqs.answer: For most students, yes. Concentration rather than available time is the limit during Ramadan, so two sessions of forty minutes generally produce more than one of ninety. The two slots that work in this emirate are early afternoon, straight after a shortened school day, or the evening once the family has eaten. Agree which one you want before the month starts rather than in its first week, because the slot is then held in that shape throughout and returns to the usual time afterwards. Plans built for the fasting month in advance rarely lose sessions; improvised ones usually do.

faqs.question: How will I know by week six whether this is working?
faqs.answer: Because there is a document from week one to compare against. The first session produces a ranked list of recurring errors with rough mark values; at week six the tutor reruns a subset of the original diagnostic questions and sets the new list beside the old one. Two outcomes are normal: the early errors have cleared, or they have not and the method needs to change. Both are information. The outcome to refuse is a week-six review with nothing to compare, which is what happens when no baseline was recorded at the start.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting in Year 10 rather than waiting for the exam year?
faqs.answer: It is the cheapest and most effective point to start, and the least popular. In Year 10 content is being met for the first time, so one hour a week on the topic currently being taught prevents the gap instead of repairing it, and a Year 10 student needs fewer hours than a Year 11 one for a larger effect. There is also a decision at stake: many Ras Al Khaimah schools use end-of-Year-10 internal examinations to set the tier for Year 11, and a Core or Foundation entry caps the grade before any exam is sat.

faqs.question: My daughter is five weeks from her first paper. What is realistic now?
faqs.answer: Collecting marks she can nearly reach, and nothing more ambitious. That means timed questions on the topics that appear most often, method presentation so partial credit is available, and pacing practice so the paper gets finished - the last two questions left blank is the commonest avoidable loss. Limit it to one or two subjects: a student with four tutors five weeks out has no practice time, and practice is where the marks come from. If a target grade is genuinely out of reach in five weeks, we will say so and talk about the November series instead.

faqs.question: Do you work to my child's school deadlines or your own schedule?
faqs.answer: The school's, in every case where they conflict. The student's internal mock dates, coursework deadlines where a school runs coursework rather than the alternative paper, and the dates the school sets for forecast grades all go into the plan at the start and take priority over the topic order. A tutor who teaches a topic sequence while a coursework deadline passes has helped with the wrong thing. If you can send the school's assessment calendar with the first enquiry, the plan is built around it rather than adjusted to it later.

faqs.question: How much practice should my son be doing between sessions?
faqs.answer: Between forty minutes and ninety a week for each subject being tutored, and it should be specific rather than general: the question set agreed at the end of the last session, done under something approaching exam conditions. This is where the progress actually happens. A student with three tutored hours a week and no practice moves more slowly than one with a single well-planned hour and the homework done, which is also why we resist adding subjects when a family is short of time.

faqs.question: Can we pause the plan during the school's own exam fortnight?
faqs.answer: Pausing is usually the wrong move, but changing the format is right. During mocks nothing new should be taught, and the sessions that help are short reviews between papers rather than teaching blocks. The fortnight immediately after mocks is the single most valuable week of the year, because the marked script is available and the error pattern is fresh. Families who stop entirely for three weeks around mocks typically spend the following fortnight recovering ground, which costs more than the sessions they saved.

faqs.question: Does the same tutor stay with us for the whole plan?
faqs.answer: That is the intention and it is why the trial lesson is with the tutor who would keep the slot rather than with a coordinator. Continuity matters more in a timeline-based plan than in ad-hoc tutoring, because each session starts from the last piece of marked work. If the match is wrong, say so after the first or second session and we will change it rather than persevering; if a tutor's availability changes mid-plan, you get the written error list and topic order so a new tutor starts from where the plan is, not from the beginning.

faqs.question: What happens to our slot if we travel out of Ras Al Khaimah in the summer?
faqs.answer: The slot can follow you where the time difference is workable, which it usually is for travel within the Gulf, to South Asia, to East Africa or to Europe. Sessions from a different time zone need the time agreed in advance rather than week by week, and a short written note of which weeks will be missed. Summer is also when most bridging work happens - Extended mathematics into a Diploma or A Level course - so a family travelling for six weeks often keeps two sessions a week rather than pausing, and arrives in September without the usual re-entry problem.

faqs.question: Is a longer session better value than two short ones?
faqs.answer: Rarely, for IGCSE students. Concentration on new material runs out well before ninety minutes for most fifteen-year-olds, and the last twenty minutes of a long session tend to be the least productive of the week. Two forty-five minute sessions usually produce more than one ninety-minute one, because there is practice between them and the second session can respond to how the practice went. The exception is the run-in phase, where a student sitting a full paper under time needs a block long enough to do it, followed by the marking in the next session.

faqs.question: What does the written plan actually contain?
faqs.answer: Five things: the ranked list of recurring errors with rough mark values, the topic order with week numbers, the number of sessions and their shape, the practice expected between sessions, and the dates already known to be unavailable - winter break, Ramadan arrangements, Eid, the school's mock fortnight. It runs to about a page. The point is not the document but the fact that it can be audited: at week six there is something specific to compare against, which an open-ended weekly booking never has.

faqs.question: Our son is in Year 11 at an Indian-curriculum school and taking some IGCSE subjects privately. Can that work?
faqs.answer: It can, and the timeline question becomes an entry question first. A private candidate needs an exam centre willing to accept the entry and has deadlines that fall earlier than a school candidate's, so the first step is confirming where the papers will be sat and by when the entry must be in. Teaching is then straightforward: the specification and tier are what matter, not the school. The practical components need care, since Cambridge sciences carry a practical test or alternative-to-practical paper and the centre's arrangements decide which one applies.

intro.heading: The subjects nobody books are where the cheap grades are
paragraphs: Almost every tutoring enquiry in the Northern Emirates concerns Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry or Biology. That is understandable, because those subjects feel hardest and carry the clearest post-16 consequences. It also means a typical Year 11 student is receiving help in four subjects and no help at all in four or five others, several of which are more responsive to a few hours of targeted work than any science is.

A grade is a grade. UAE equivalency on the British track counts five accredited subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from the count, and a post-16 offer counts the grades it asks for regardless of which subject produced them. A student two marks below a boundary in Business Studies loses exactly as much as one two marks below in Chemistry, and the Business Studies gap is usually cheaper to close.

Al Dhait is a large residential area south of Ras Al Khaimah city, predominantly villa housing across its northern and southern sections, with a straightforward run into the city's school cluster. The villas matter in one practical respect: a quiet room for a full timed paper is easier to arrange here than in the creek-side apartments, which makes the weekend block that revision needs more achievable.

Delivery is stated plainly. IB Gram teaches UAE families one-to-one over live video, on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. For IGCSE work that is an advantage rather than a compromise: the paper sits on a shared screen, gets annotated live against the published scheme, and the family keeps the annotated copy.

Two structural decisions get a section each on this page because they are taken early and cannot be undone: whether a student sits Double Award Science or three separate sciences, and how many subjects to enter in total. Both are usually settled by a school's default rather than by a conversation, and both have consequences a family should see before they are locked in.

Everything factual here should be confirmed against your own centre's entry and the current specification, because boards revise them. Pearson and Cambridge positions come from the boards' own exam-administration pages, read in October 2026. Past dates keep their year because that is what makes them checkable; future series are named by month only, so nothing here becomes wrong a year from now without anybody touching it. One correction worth making before anything else, because other pages in this market get it wrong: Cambridge offers the February and March series to candidates in India, and a centre in Ras Al Khaimah enters June and November. Revision guides written for an India audience circulate here freely, and a family that plans leave, travel and a revision schedule around those dates is planning around a window their child will never sit. Market rates, where they appear, are attributed to the provider that published them and dated to the month they were read.

subjects.description: A bridge subject for students heading to A Level Mathematics or a Higher Level Diploma course, introducing calculus and trigonometric identities. This is where a shaky Year 9 algebra foundation becomes impossible to hide.

sections.heading: Pearson Edexcel codes and the paper shapes behind them
paragraphs: Pearson's International GCSE suite is organised by code, and the code is the only reliable way to identify what a student is actually sitting. A school report that says Maths, Physics and Business tells a parent almost nothing about the assessment; 4MA1 Higher, 4PH1 and 4BS1 tells them everything they need to find the right past papers.

The shapes differ across the suite in ways that change preparation. Mathematics A sits two papers of equal weight with Foundation and Higher tiers. Physics, Chemistry and Biology each sit two written papers of unequal length, with the longer carrying the larger share and practical knowledge assessed inside them rather than through a separate component. Science Double Award runs as a single course awarding two grades. The humanities and business subjects carry their own codes and their own balance between source work, case application and extended writing.

Two practical points follow. First, a family should get the complete code list in writing, not just the codes for the subjects they are worried about, because the unexamined subjects are where the avoidable losses sit. Second, the grade scale is 9 to 1 rather than A* to G, which matters when a household also has a Cambridge candidate and ends up holding a certificate set in two currencies.

The table sets out the codes most commonly seen in this market with the paper shape and the characteristic loss. Confirm each one with your exams officer, because entries vary by centre and specifications are revised.

sections.heading: Double Award Science or three separate sciences?
paragraphs: This decision is usually made by a school's default timetable and almost never discussed with a family, which is a shame because it is one of the few genuinely strategic choices in an IGCSE course and it cannot be reversed after entries close.

Double Award Science covers biology, chemistry and physics content at reduced depth and awards two grades from one course. It occupies less timetable, which frees a slot for another subject, and it suits students whose interests lie elsewhere or who would spread themselves thin across three separate sciences. For equivalency purposes it contributes grades like any other subject, and for many post-16 routes it is entirely sufficient.

Three separate sciences cover more content, produce three grades, and keep science-specific post-16 doors open. Some A Level and Diploma Higher Level science courses expect the separate qualification, because the course assumes content only the separate syllabus covered. That is the asymmetry: Double Award rarely creates a problem for a student heading into humanities, and occasionally creates one for a student who changes their mind towards medicine or engineering in Year 12.

The honest framing is a conversation about likelihood rather than ambition. A student with no current interest in a science route loses little by taking Double Award and gains a timetable slot. A student who might plausibly want a science route should take the separate sciences even if they are currently undecided, because the cost of keeping the door open is a term of timetable and the cost of reopening it is a year. Ask the post-16 coordinator which entries their own courses require, in Year 10.

sections.heading: What grade boundaries actually do
paragraphs: Grade boundaries are the most misunderstood part of the system and the source of a specific kind of wasted anxiety. Families plan around a number they have seen from a previous series, and then feel cheated when it moves. It moves every time, by design.

A boundary is set after a series, once the board has seen how the cohort performed on that particular paper. If a paper turned out harder than intended, boundaries fall; if easier, they rise. The purpose is to keep the standard of the grade constant even though the difficulty of the paper varies. That means a raw mark from a past series cannot tell a student what grade the same mark would earn next time, and a target expressed as a raw mark is a target built on sand.

The practical consequence is to stop planning against boundaries and start planning against marks available. Every mark a student can reliably collect is worth having, regardless of where the line eventually falls, and the most reliably collectable marks are the ones that need no additional knowledge: a labelled axis, a shown method, a quoted figure from an extract, an ordered process. A student who collects those consistently is insulated from boundary movement in a way that a student aiming at a remembered number is not.

One related honesty point: no tutor should offer grade-boundary tables as downloads, and no provider can promise a grade, precisely because boundaries are set after the fact on the basis of that series' papers. Anybody offering a promised grade is either misunderstanding the mechanism or hoping it is not raised.

sections.heading: The subjects nobody tutors, and what their papers reward
paragraphs: Business, Economics, History, Geography and ICT between them account for a large share of a typical Year 11 entry list and almost none of the tutoring spend in this emirate. They also share a structural feature that makes them unusually responsive: in each, a substantial proportion of the marks depends on a specific writing move rather than on how much content a student has memorised.

In Business the move is application: using the business in the stimulus rather than reproducing a tool from memory. In Economics it is the diagram and the extract: labelled axes, the shift shown, the new equilibrium marked, and the figure quoted rather than paraphrased. In History it is supported judgement on the specific claim in the question, using the source rather than summarising it, instead of writing everything known about the period. In Geography it is case-study specificity: a named place with named figures earns what a general account of the process cannot. In ICT it is precise terminology and method rather than a finished artefact.

Each of those moves can be taught in four to six sessions, because the student usually knows enough content already and is losing marks on presentation of reasoning. That is a much better return per hour than the same spend on a science where content genuinely has to be built, and it is available to any family willing to look past the subjects that feel frightening.

sections.heading: The bridge subjects: Further Pure and Additional Mathematics
paragraphs: Students heading towards A Level Mathematics, a Higher Level Diploma mathematics course, or an engineering route often take an additional mathematics qualification alongside the main one. Pearson's Further Pure Mathematics 4PM1 and Cambridge's Additional Mathematics 0606 both serve that purpose, and both behave differently from the subject they sit alongside.

The difference is that they introduce calculus and trigonometric identities before a student has met them in any other context, and they do so assuming that algebraic manipulation is already automatic. A student who copes with the main mathematics paper by working carefully and slowly will struggle here, not because the ideas are beyond them but because the pace assumes fluency they do not yet have. That is the single most useful diagnostic for whether the bridge subject is the right choice: not whether the student is good at mathematics, but whether their algebra is fast.

For a family in Ras Al Khaimah there is a second consideration, which is availability. These are among the least widely taught courses in the emirate, so a student taking one may be in a very small class or effectively alone, with no peer group to calibrate against and sometimes no second opinion available locally on whether their work is where it should be.

Where the subject is the right choice, the preparation that works is unglamorous: short, frequent algebra sets until manipulation is automatic, then the new content. Attempting the calculus before the algebra is fluent produces a student who understands the concept and cannot execute it under time, which is the commonest pattern in this qualification.

sections.heading: Revision that works at this level
paragraphs: Most IGCSE revision is rereading, and rereading is close to useless. It feels productive because the material becomes familiar, and familiarity is mistaken for recall. The methods that work are less comfortable and take less time, which is an unusually good combination.

The first is retrieval: closing the book and writing down what can be remembered, then checking. It is unpleasant precisely because it exposes what is not known, which is the information the student needs. The second is spacing: returning to a topic after a gap rather than blocking it all in one evening, which produces better retention for the same total hours. The third is timed practice marked against the published scheme, which is the only method that tests the thing the examination tests.

The fourth, specific to this market and rarely mentioned, is working across subjects on a shared skill. Data and graph questions appear in Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Geography and Economics, and they reward the same handful of moves: read the scale, calculate rather than eyeball a gradient, quote the figure, state the trend with its cause. An hour spent on that skill improves five subjects at once, which no single-subject revision plan can match.

A practical note on materials. Work from papers and notes the student legitimately holds through their school. No tutor should reproduce or distribute syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes, grade-boundary tables or subject guides as downloads; the official source should be referenced and linked instead. That is a copyright matter and, for unreleased material, a malpractice exposure.
bullets: Retrieval beats rereading, and it is uncomfortable for the right reason.

sections.heading: How many subjects should a student enter?
paragraphs: Entry lists in this market range widely, and the number is usually inherited from a school's standard offer rather than chosen. It deserves a conversation, because more subjects is not straightforwardly better and fewer is not straightforwardly safer.

The floor is set by equivalency and by post-16 requirements. UAE equivalency on the British track counts five accredited subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from the count, so a student needs at least five countable subjects passed at that level, and in practice a margin above the minimum is sensible because one subject can always go wrong. Post-16 courses then specify their own subjects and grades, which is the real constraint for most families.

The ceiling is set by attention. A student entering a large number of subjects is spreading finite revision across all of them, and the marginal subject frequently costs more in other grades than it adds on its own. The honest test is whether the student can name why each subject is on the list. A subject taken because the timetable offered it, which nobody has revised and which nobody needs, is a liability rather than an asset.

One competitor page ranking for these queries tells UAE parents that six IGCSE subjects are required for equivalency. The published rule is five. Where this page states an equivalency figure it is taken from a sourced report, and families should confirm their own case with the Ministry of Education or the emirate's attestation channel. No tutoring provider performs or underwrites equivalency and tuition is not a requirement for it.

sections.heading: Honesty, materials and the permit
paragraphs: Three boundaries, stated plainly. The first is academic. A tutor may teach content, explain what a command term demands, work through past questions, mark answers against the published scheme and give written feedback on the student's own work. Where an IGCSE subject carries a coursework component, support means feedback on a draft the student has written, never production of the work.

The second is materials. No tutor should reproduce or distribute Cambridge, Pearson or IB syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes, grade-boundary tables or subject guides as downloads. The correct approach is to reference the official source and link to it, which is why there are no attachments on this page and why it repeatedly asks readers to confirm codes and structures with their own centre. Reproducing assessment material is a copyright matter, and for unreleased material a malpractice exposure.

The third is who may teach. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit: the MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students. MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published.

And a boundary on claims. No tutor can promise a grade, because boundaries are set after a series on the basis of that series' papers, which is the whole argument of the boundaries section above. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or licence from the Department of Knowledge, KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, Cambridge or Pearson, and claims none.
