sections.heading: Core or Extended, Foundation or Higher: the tier sets the ceiling
paragraphs: The single most consequential decision on an IGCSE entry form is the tier, and it is usually made by the school in the autumn of Year 11 without much conversation. In Cambridge mathematics, a Core entry means papers 1 and 2 and a grade range that stops at C. In Pearson's Mathematics A, a Foundation entry stops at grade 5. No amount of brilliant work in the exam hall lifts a student above the ceiling of the tier they were entered for.

That cuts both ways. An Extended or Higher entry for a student who is not ready produces a paper full of questions they cannot attempt, and the grade that comes back is often worse than the one a well-matched Core entry would have returned. The useful question in November of Year 11 is not which tier sounds better but which tier the student's last two mock scripts actually support, and whether the gap between them can be closed in the weeks remaining.

This is where a tutor earns their fee, and it has nothing to do with motivation. Read the mock script. Count the marks lost to topics the Core paper does not test. If most of the loss is in the Extended-only material, the conversation with the school is about readiness and timing. If the loss is spread across arithmetic, method presentation and misread command words, the tier is not the problem and a change of entry would hide a fixable issue rather than solve it.

For families weighing what comes after Year 11, the tier also closes doors quietly. A Core mathematics grade is rarely enough for an International A Level in the subject or for IB Analysis and Approaches, and in practice it narrows a Diploma choice to Applications and Interpretation. Raising the question in Year 10 rather than the term before the exam is the whole difference.

sections.heading: Where IGCSE marks actually go missing
paragraphs: Across the subjects Ras Al Khaimah families ask about most, the losses are predictable enough to list. In mathematics, the biggest single leak is method: an answer with no working earns nothing when the question says show your work, and exact-value questions punish students who reach for the calculator by habit. The second leak is the last four questions on the Extended papers, which are multi-step and are routinely left blank by students who ran out of time on earlier questions worth fewer marks.

In the sciences, the pattern is sharper. Chemistry grades are decided by moles and stoichiometry more than by any other topic; students who can set out a calculation in steps keep marks that others lose entirely. Physics loses marks on circuits, on moments, and on the describe-an-experiment questions, where the mark scheme wants a named measurement, a repeated reading and a stated control. Biology loses them on precision: the wrong process named, a two-mark answer given in half a sentence, a command word read as describe when it said explain.

In the essay and application subjects the leak is almost always the same thing. Business Studies candidates explain a concept correctly and never apply it to the business in the case study, so they sit in the middle band with accurate content. Economics candidates write good prose and draw an unlabelled diagram. English First Language candidates summarise when the question asked how the writer achieves an effect. Each of those is a technique problem with a short fix, which is why a tutor who marks against the published criteria moves a grade faster than one who re-teaches content the student already knows.

The diagnosis costs one session. Two marked mock scripts and the last few pieces of class work are enough to produce a list of four or five recurring errors, ranked by how many marks each one costs. That list is the teaching plan, and it is specific to the student rather than to the subject.

sections.heading: The entry deadline nobody puts in the calendar
paragraphs: Every family thinks about the exam date. Almost nobody thinks about the entry deadline, which sits months earlier and is the point at which tier changes, subject additions and private-candidate entries stop being possible. A UAE candidate has two realistic windows a year, and Pearson's International GCSE November 2026 series is the clearest worked example with published dates: the final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, and the results from the equivalent November 2025 series reached students on 22 January 2026 - roughly three months after the first paper, and the better part of a year after the entry for it had to be settled with the centre.

Read those dates in order and the planning implication is obvious. The decision about which tier a student is entered for has to be made while they are still mid-course, on the evidence of one mock rather than three. That is why a diagnostic session in October of Year 11 is worth more than four in May: it is the last point at which the information can still change the entry.

Pearson's calendar works the same way with different dates. The November 2026 International GCSE final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson also publishes provisional timetables well ahead of each series, which is the document to check rather than any date restated on a tutoring website, including this one.

One Cambridge detail catches UAE centres specifically. Every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and the timetable differs by zone. Cambridge states that it is essential to use the correct version for your zone and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. Ask your school's exams officer which zone it is in, and check the official timetable for that zone rather than a generic one.

sections.heading: Who regulates your child's school here, and why it changes the answer
paragraphs: Private education in Ras Al Khaimah is regulated by the emirate's own Department of Knowledge, which the UAE government's own guidance describes as regulating private education in the emirate. That is a different arrangement from Dubai, where the Knowledge and Human Development Authority oversees quality, and from Abu Dhabi and Al Ain, where the Department of Education and Knowledge supervises licensing and accreditation. Sharjah has its own authority, and the federal Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah.

The practical difference for a Ras Al Khaimah family is wider than inspection reports. Ras Al Khaimah's authority, like Sharjah's, approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Curriculum and fee approval sitting with the emirate regulator is why guidance written for Dubai parents, including anything framed around KHDA circulars, does not automatically describe your school's position.

At federal level the baseline is the same everywhere. Private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. So a British-curriculum student in Ras Al Khaimah is sitting Cambridge or Pearson papers in most subjects and carrying mandated Arabic and Islamic Education alongside them. Those mandated subjects have their own requirements and, in Dubai's published version of the rules, their own class-organisation and language-of-instruction constraints. Treat them as part of the timetable load when you plan tutoring hours, not as an afterthought.

None of this makes IB Gram a regulated school provider, and nothing on this page should be read that way. We hold no approval, licence or accreditation from any UAE regulator or examination board, and we never describe ourselves as approved by one. What a regulator does matters to you because it tells you where to read your school's inspection report and who approves its fees - not because any tutoring company is party to it.

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not do with coursework
paragraphs: IGCSE carries less assessed coursework than it used to, but it has not disappeared. Geography and History both offer coursework components that some UAE schools take and others replace with an alternative-to-coursework paper. Where coursework is sat, the rules about help are strict and the consequences of getting them wrong land on the student rather than the tutor.

A tutor may teach the skill the task assesses, explain the published criteria, model the method on a different example, ask questions about a draft the student has written, and point out where an argument is unsupported or a method is unsafe. A tutor may not write, redraft or complete any part of the work, and may not supply text for the student to use. We say this plainly because two of the sites competing for this search sell completed assessed work, one of them openly. That is a malpractice trigger for the student, and it is not a service IB Gram offers at any price.

The same boundary applies to the work that follows IGCSE. An Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay or a Theory of Knowledge essay in the Diploma must be the student's own; a tutor's role is to teach the criteria, question the reasoning and give feedback on the student's draft. Students moving from IGCSE to the Diploma meet this distinction for the first time in Year 12, and it is worth understanding before then.

One related point on materials. We do not host or distribute syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes or grade-boundary tables. They belong to Cambridge, Pearson and the IB, and reproducing them is a copyright problem. In lessons a tutor works from official material through the proper channels and links you to the publisher's own page, which is also where you should check anything date-sensitive.

sections.heading: Five subjects at grade E or 3: the equivalency rule parents get wrong
paragraphs: Families in Ras Al Khaimah planning a UAE university route eventually meet Ministry of Education equivalency, and the published British-track requirement is more specific than the version circulating in tutoring content. Students on the British track must show five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, together with one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than grade E, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade.

Two details inside that rule change decisions. First, Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects, so a student counting them towards the total may be a subject short without realising it. Second, the grade threshold is expressed on both scales, E or 3, which is why knowing whether your child sits Cambridge or Pearson matters even here. One competitor page ranking for these searches states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects; the published rule says five.

The American track is specified differently and is worth knowing if your household might switch systems. English proficiency is met by a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying. For the IB Diploma there is no points threshold we are willing to publish, because we have not read one on a Ministry source; ask the Ministry or your school's university counsellor rather than trusting a number on a tutoring site.

Equivalency is also not something a tutoring company performs, guarantees or speeds up. It is an administrative process run by the Ministry and the emirate's attestation channels, and tutoring is not a requirement for it. What tutoring can do is make the five subjects comfortably clear the threshold rather than sit on it, which is a different and more honest claim.

sections.heading: What happens if no specialist is free for your subject
paragraphs: Availability is the thing tutoring sites conceal and parents discover in week three. Our position is to say it in advance. For mainstream IGCSE subjects at both tiers - mathematics, the three sciences, English, business and economics - a match is usually available within a few days, and the trial lesson is with the tutor who would keep the slot rather than with a sales contact. For narrower combinations, the honest answer is sometimes a wait.

The combinations that take longest are predictable: Additional Mathematics 0606 at speed, Computer Science with a programming focus, Co-ordinated Sciences taught with the correct scope rather than from single-science material, and any subject needed at a specific hour that collides with the Gulf Standard Time evening peak. In those cases we will tell you the realistic wait, offer a different slot with the right specialist, or say that we cannot cover it well. The alternative - putting a generalist in front of an Extended-tier student and calling it a match - wastes a term that a Year 11 student does not have.

Timing in the week matters more here than families expect. Between about 4.30pm and 7.30pm Gulf Standard Time the demand curve for UAE families peaks, and the strongest subject specialists are booked first. A family in Al Hamra Village that fixes a Tuesday 5pm slot in September usually keeps the same tutor all year. A family that starts looking in April is choosing from what is left, in the term when it matters most.
If a subject cannot be covered properly, we would rather say so. There is no version of this where a student benefits from a tutor learning the specification alongside them in an exam year.

faqs.question: How do I tell whether my child needs an IGCSE tutor or just better study habits?
faqs.answer: Look at a marked paper rather than at the grade. If the lost marks cluster in one or two topics, that is a teaching problem and a tutor fixes it quickly. If they are scattered across missing method, misread command words and unfinished papers, it is a technique problem, which is also teachable but needs exam practice more than content. If the work is right but never finished, the issue is time management and a tutor is the expensive answer to a cheap problem. Send us a mock script and we will tell you which of the three you are looking at, before you commit to anything.

faqs.question: Is a group class at a Ras Al Khaimah tuition centre cheaper than one-to-one teaching?
faqs.answer: Per hour, yes. Published market rates for budget and group tuition in this region start around AED 45 to 150 an hour, while qualified one-to-one online teaching runs roughly AED 150 to 300 and exam-board specialists AED 200 to 450. Those are market figures, not our prices. The comparison that matters is cost per mark gained. A group of six moving at one pace is efficient for covering content and poor at finding the four specific errors costing your child marks. For a student who is behind on content, a class can work well; for one who knows the material and keeps losing marks, it rarely does.

faqs.question: My son's school runs free revision sessions. Why would I pay for a tutor as well?
faqs.answer: Often you should not. School clinics are free, run by the teacher who writes the mock, and aimed at the content most of the class is missing. Use them first. The gap they leave is individual diagnosis: a group of a dozen students cannot be taught from one student's error pattern, and the sessions stop when term stops. Paid teaching makes sense when the school's provision has been used and the marks are still leaking, when the subject needs a tier-specific specialist the school cannot spare, or when the student needs work in the holidays before a February or June series.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE subjects do Ras Al Khaimah families ask about most?
faqs.answer: Mathematics first, by a wide margin, and usually Extended or Higher tier in the autumn of Year 11. Chemistry and Physics come next, driven by students aiming at science routes after Year 11, and the losses there are concentrated in moles, circuits and the experiment-description questions. English as a First Language and English as a Second Language follow, then Business Studies and Economics. Additional Mathematics 0606 is the smallest group and the hardest to staff locally, which is exactly why remote matching matters: there may be no one in the emirate teaching it at the level a strong student needs.

faqs.question: Can one tutor take both Cambridge 0580 Maths and Cambridge 0625 Physics?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth asking rather than assuming. Maths and Physics overlap enough that one specialist can often carry both at IGCSE, and the shared session note helps because the algebra failing in Physics is usually the algebra failing in Maths. Chemistry and Biology are a different matter: the detail in each is specific enough that a single tutor covering all three sciences at Extended tier is usually spread too thin. Where we cannot staff a combination with one person, we say so and offer two tutors who share a plan rather than pretending one can do everything.

faqs.question: Does it matter that the tutor has never set foot in my child's school?
faqs.answer: Less than you would expect, because the examiner has never set foot in it either. What matters is the specification and the tier your child is entered for, the mark scheme the paper will be marked against, and the student's own error pattern. School knowledge helps with internal deadlines and the style of a particular department's mocks, and a good tutor asks about both in the first session. In a small emirate the alternative is real: insisting on someone who knows the campus often means accepting someone who has never taught the specification.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week does an Extended-tier Year 11 student usually need?
faqs.answer: One a week per subject for most of the year, moving to two in the eight to twelve weeks before a series if the marks are still leaking. More than two a week in the same subject is rarely useful: the limit is not teaching time but the practice a student does between lessons, and a student with four hours of tuition and no independent practice makes slower progress than one with a single well-planned hour. We would rather run one session a week for twenty weeks than four a week for five, and the cost usually works out lower as well.

faqs.question: What should I send before the first lesson so it is not wasted on diagnostics?
faqs.answer: Four things. The statement of entry or last report, so the tutor has the syllabus codes and tier. The two most recent marked mock scripts, which are worth more than any description of the problem. One piece of recent class work with the teacher's comments. And the internal deadlines, if coursework or an alternative-to-coursework paper is involved. With those, the first lesson teaches rather than interviews, and you get a ranked list of recurring errors out of it. Without them the first session is spent finding out what the papers would have shown in ten minutes.

faqs.question: Is it too late to start if the exams are five months away?
faqs.answer: No, and five months is a reasonable runway for a tiered subject. What changes with time pressure is the method: less content teaching, more timed questions and error review, and a topic list narrowed to what is costing the most marks. What a short runway cannot do is undo a tier decision, because final entries close months before the papers are sat. If you are five months out, the first useful step is reading a marked mock and checking what tier your child is entered for, in that order.

faqs.question: Do you teach the Core tier or only Extended?
faqs.answer: Both, and the distinction shapes the teaching completely. A Core entry caps the grade at C in Cambridge subjects and at 5 on Pearson's Foundation tier, so the plan is to make every mark on that paper reachable rather than to tour the Extended material. Students are often taught from Extended resources by default, which wastes weeks on content that will not be examined. If a Core-entered student is clearly capable of more, that is a conversation with the school in the autumn term, while the entry can still be changed, not a reason to teach them the wrong syllabus.

faqs.question: How does a tutor handle a science practical if the lessons are online?
faqs.answer: By teaching the component that is actually assessed. Cambridge sciences carry either a practical test or an alternative-to-practical written paper, and most UAE candidates sit one of those two under their school's arrangements; Pearson's international sciences assess practical understanding inside the written papers instead. Either way the marks go to reading a results table, identifying a source of error, naming a controlled variable and describing a repeated measurement. All of that is taught on screen with real data sets and past questions. The hands-on work happens in the school laboratory, where it should.

faqs.question: My daughter is in Year 9 and has not chosen her IGCSE options. Is tutoring premature?
faqs.answer: It is the cheapest point to intervene, and the least common. A Year 9 student needs one session a fortnight, not three a week, and the work is closing gaps in algebra, scientific writing and reading for command words before those gaps become grade ceilings. Cambridge Checkpoint feedback in March, May or October is a useful starting document. The option conversation itself is worth one session: whether to add Additional Mathematics, whether Co-ordinated Sciences or three separate sciences fits the timetable, and what each route leaves open after Year 11.

faqs.question: What does a private tutor in the UAE have to hold legally?
faqs.answer: A private tuition work permit from MoHRE, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and the eligible groups include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone offering private lessons without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule has been published, so ignore the amounts circulating online. Applications go through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system. Ask any tutor, local or remote, about their permit.

faqs.question: Do you give students past papers and mark schemes to keep?
faqs.answer: No, and nobody should. Past papers, mark schemes, syllabus documents and grade-boundary tables belong to Cambridge, Pearson and the IB, and redistributing them is a copyright problem rather than a grey area. In a lesson a tutor works from official material through proper channels and sends you to the publisher's own pages for anything you should hold yourself. Your school's exams officer can also tell you which material is available to candidates at your centre. A site offering a bundle of mark schemes as a download is telling you something about how it operates.

faqs.question: Is private tuition cheaper in the northern emirates than in Dubai?
faqs.answer: For in-home teaching, usually not in the way parents expect. The published market range for in-home one-to-one across the UAE is roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour including travel, and in a spread-out emirate the travel component is larger, not smaller, because a tutor covering Al Hamra Village and the city centre in one evening is paid for the drive. Online teaching costs the same wherever the family lives, which is why the gap between the two formats is wider here than in a dense city. Those are market figures from published provider rates, not our price list.

intro.heading: Nearest is a poor proxy for what your child needs
paragraphs: A near-me search is a request for convenience, and convenience is a reasonable thing to want. The trouble is that in Ras Al Khaimah the two questions a parent is really asking - who is close, and who can teach this - have different answers, and in some subjects they have no overlap at all. The emirate's private-school set is small and spread across roughly forty kilometres, from Al Qusaidat and the northern strip through the city districts to Al Hamra Village, Mina Al Arab and Al Marjan Island. The pool of people who have taught Extended-tier Chemistry 0620 or Additional Mathematics 0606 in that radius is not large, and for some syllabuses it is empty.

That is not a criticism of the emirate. It is arithmetic. Dubai has well over two hundred private schools and a tutoring market deep enough that a parent can insist on proximity and still find a specialist. The northern emirates have a fraction of that, so insisting on proximity means accepting whoever is both nearby and free, which selects for availability rather than for subject depth. In a Year 11 with nineteen or twenty teachable weeks left, that trade is expensive.

There is also a version of local that genuinely matters, and it is not the tutor's address. It is your child's examination centre. Entries are made through the school's centre, that centre is allocated to one of six Cambridge administrative zones, and the zone determines which version of the timetable applies - Cambridge states plainly that it cannot accept responsibility for a candidate who misses an exam after the wrong zone timetable was used. Which campus your child attends also decides which board they sit, whether coursework or an alternative paper applies, and when internal deadlines fall. All of that is local, and all of it is more consequential than a drive time.

IB Gram's answer to the near-me search is to be honest about both halves. Teaching is delivered online, over live video, one tutor and one student; we do not send a tutor to a home anywhere in the UAE, because in-home visiting is a service we run only in India. What we can do is match the specification exactly, hold a slot that survives the Ras Al Khaimah school run, and tell you before you pay whether your subject and tier are genuinely covered or whether the honest answer is a wait.

Below: the campus clusters near each area, a per-subject availability picture for the northern emirates, what families in different parts of the emirate actually ask for, the exam-centre questions worth asking your school this term, the regulator map for anyone crossing emirate lines for school, and a short checklist for vetting a local tutor if that is the route you choose.

ras-al-khaimah/igcse-tutor-near-me.programmesIntro: Which programme your child is on determines how far you would have to travel to find a local specialist in it. These are the four that Ras Al Khaimah families ask about, with the practical local picture for each.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: The most widely taught qualification in the emirate's British-curriculum schools, which makes mainstream subjects the easiest to cover locally: 0580 Mathematics, 0610 Biology, 0620 Chemistry, 0625 Physics, 0500 English First Language. Grades run A* to G, and most syllabuses are examined entirely at the end of Year 11.
programmes.countryNote: Because several campuses here enter different boards for different subjects, a tutor found locally may be fluent in one board and unfamiliar with the other. Check the entry code before the first lesson. The statement of entry from your school's exams officer settles it in seconds, and it is the document we ask for rather than the school name.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Grades 9 to 1, and specifications that differ in structure from Cambridge's: 4MA1 Mathematics A with Foundation and Higher tiers, 4PH1 Physics, 4CH1 Chemistry, 4BI1 Biology. The international sciences carry no separate practical examination, assessing practical understanding inside the written papers instead.
programmes.countryNote: Pearson's November series is the local detail worth knowing, because it turns a missed grade into a same-year problem rather than a twelve-month one. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Confirm with your school whether its centre is entering candidates for the series.

programmes.name: Lower secondary years before IGCSE
programmes.description: The years in which the gaps that later cost grades are formed: indices, rearranging formulae, writing a method, reading a command word. Support at this stage is light - one session a fortnight - and Cambridge Checkpoint tests in March, May and October give a diagnostic that maps onto what IGCSE papers will ask two years later.
programmes.countryNote: This is the one stage where proximity genuinely helps, because a younger student benefits from an adult nearby. Many families in Al Dhait and Khuzam use a parent in the next room rather than a tutor in the house, which works equally well with a remote session and costs nothing.

programmes.name: A Level and IB Diploma routes after Year 11
programmes.description: Both routes exist in or near the emirate, and the subject that decides between them is usually mathematics. An Extended-tier A* or 9 makes A Level Mathematics or IB Analysis and Approaches realistic; a middling Extended grade usually points towards Applications and Interpretation or a different combination.
programmes.countryNote: For post-16 work the local specialist pool thins out sharply, which is where a near-me search is least likely to help. Diploma Higher Level sciences and Analysis and Approaches are the clearest examples: families in Ras Al Khaimah asking for them locally are usually told no, and then told yes by someone who has not taught the course.

ras-al-khaimah/igcse-tutor-near-me.subjectsIntro: Availability is not uniform across subjects, so the near-me question has a different answer for each one. These notes say how easy each subject is to staff for families in the northern emirates and what the usual fallback is.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The best-covered subject in the market, locally and remotely, at both tiers. A match is usually available within days. The thing to check is not availability but whether the tutor knows which tier the student is entered for and which paper is sat without a calculator.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics (Cambridge 0606)
subjects.description: The hardest syllabus to staff in the northern emirates. Calculus, trigonometric identities and series at IGCSE level need somebody who has taught the course rather than someone comfortable with the content, and locally that person often does not exist.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 / Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Single tier at Pearson
subjects.description: Reasonably covered at Core and thinner at Extended, where moles, stoichiometry and organic chemistry decide the grade. A generalist science tutor can carry Core; Extended needs a chemist.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 / Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Single tier at Pearson
subjects.description: Available but frequently taught by mathematicians, which works for the calculation questions and less well for the describe-an-experiment marks. Ask specifically about the practical or alternative-to-practical component.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 / Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Single tier at Pearson
subjects.description: Well covered, and the subject where the difference between a specialist and a generalist shows up in precision: the right process named, answer length matched to the mark allocation, command words distinguished.

subjects.name: Co-ordinated Sciences (Cambridge 0654)
subjects.description: Easy to find someone willing and hard to find someone who knows the scope. A tutor who teaches it from single-science material wastes weeks on content that will not be examined, which is the commonest avoidable error in this subject.

subjects.name: English as a First Language (Cambridge 0500 / Pearson 4EA1)
subjects.description: Widely available. The useful question is whether the tutor marks against the published criteria, because the gap between a competent reader and an examiner-minded one is the difference between the middle and top bands.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510 and 0511)
subjects.description: Well covered in this emirate, where many students work in English at school and another language at home. Listening technique and task-purpose discipline are the two areas that respond fastest.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Economics (Cambridge 0450 and 0455)
subjects.description: Available, with a caveat: many tutors teach the content well and the application badly. Ask how they mark a case-study answer, since application and evaluation are where the top bands sit.

subjects.name: Computer Science and ICT (Cambridge 0478 and 0417)
subjects.description: Thin locally and better served remotely, particularly for pseudocode, trace tables and the practical software components of 0417, which need a shared screen rather than a shared desk.

subjects.name: Arabic and Islamic Education
subjects.description: Mandated alongside the international curriculum in UAE private schools, and the one area where local teaching is genuinely plentiful. Content for these subjects is set centrally and may not be varied without Ministry permission, so a tutor supports the school's material rather than replacing it.

subjects.name: Geography and History (Cambridge 0460 and 0470)
subjects.description: Available, with the important question being whether the school runs coursework or the alternative paper. The two need different teaching, and internal deadlines govern the first.

sections.heading: What a near-me search returns here, and what it leaves out
paragraphs: Type the query and you get a map with pins, a few directory listings and some agency pages that name the emirate once. What the map cannot show you is the only thing that matters: which of those pins has taught Cambridge 0620 at Extended tier, or Pearson 4MA1 at Higher tier, in the last three years. Distance is measurable and so it gets measured; specialism is not, and so it gets assumed.

In a city with a deep market the two correlate well enough that proximity is a reasonable filter. Ras Al Khaimah is not that market. The emirate's school-age population sits in a long, thin band of communities, and the tutoring supply inside that band is small. Filtering by distance first and subject second therefore produces a shortlist of people who are available rather than people who are expert, and in the autumn term of Year 11 that distinction decides whether a tier conversation happens at all.

The table below is the version of the local picture that is actually useful. For each part of the emirate it gives the nearest campus cluster, an approximate off-peak drive, the earliest weekday session start that is realistic once the school run is done, and an honest read on local specialist supply. Note that the last column does not improve with proximity to the city; the city has more tutors, not more specialists in a given syllabus.

The practical conclusion is not that local help is worthless. It is that distance should be the last filter rather than the first. Start with the specification and tier, then availability, then timing, and only then convenience. A family that works in that order ends up with a tutor who can teach the course; one that starts with the map ends up with a tutor who lives nearby.

sections.heading: Which subjects can actually be staffed in the northern emirates
paragraphs: Availability transparency is the gap nobody in this market fills. Competitor pages imply that every subject is covered everywhere, and parents discover the truth in week three when the tutor turns out to be learning the specification alongside the student. Our position is to publish the picture in advance, including the parts that are unflattering to us.

Mainstream subjects at both tiers - mathematics, the three separate sciences, both English syllabuses, business and economics - can be matched quickly, usually within a few days, and the trial lesson is with the tutor who would keep the slot. The thin areas are predictable. Additional Mathematics 0606 is the hardest syllabus in this list to staff anywhere in the northern emirates. Co-ordinated Sciences 0654 taught with the correct scope rather than from single-science material is the second. Computer Science with a genuine programming focus is the third. Post-16 Higher Level sciences and Analysis and Approaches are thinner again.

There is also a time dimension that nothing can fix. Between roughly 4.30pm and 7.30pm Gulf Standard Time every UAE family wants the same slot, so a scarce specialist in that window is scarcer still. A family that can take a weekend morning or a 3.30pm session during a lighter school week has materially better access to the right teacher than one that insists on 6pm on a Tuesday.

When we cannot cover something well, the options we will offer are a named wait, a different time with the right specialist, or a plain statement that this is not a subject we can teach properly right now. What we will not do is put a generalist in front of an Extended-tier student in an exam year and call it a match. That costs a term, and a Year 11 student does not have a spare term.

sections.heading: The local fact that matters more than distance: your exam centre
paragraphs: If you are going to be precise about anything local, be precise about where your child sits the papers. Entries are made through a school's examination centre, and that centre is the authority on which series are available, whether a science practical test is offered or the alternative-to-practical paper applies, and when internal and external deadlines fall. A tutor two streets away knows none of that about your school unless they ask.

The zone detail catches UAE centres specifically. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, each with its own version of the timetable, and states that it is essential to use the correct version for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after the wrong timetable was used. That sentence is the reason we never restate exam dates as though they were universal. Ask your school's exams officer which zone the centre sits in and work from the official timetable for that zone.

Deadlines are the other half, and they are where a family loses options without noticing. In the UAE the choice is between the June series and the November series — Cambridge's February/March series is offered to India only, so it is not on the table here — and the administration for either one runs far ahead of the papers. For a June sitting the entries are made in the spring term, months before the first paper, and the forecast grades the centre submits come later again; for a November sitting the entries are settled well before the autumn half-term. We are not printing a day and a month for those, because the exact dates come from your centre's zone timetable and your child's statement of entry, and Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six zones with its own timetable version. Pearson's structure is similar with different dates — its November 2026 International GCSE timetable runs to 19 November 2026 — and Pearson publishes provisional timetables for future series, which is the document to check rather than any date on a tutoring site.

For families not attached to a school - after a mid-year move to Al Marjan Island, for instance, or where a student is studying privately - the centre question comes before the teaching question. Which centre will accept a private entry, by when, for which subjects and with which practical arrangement. Those four answers determine what is possible, and no amount of tutoring changes them.
bullets: Ask your exams officer which Cambridge administrative zone the centre is in
Confirm whether a practical test or the alternative paper applies to each science
Private-candidate entry deadlines fall earlier than school candidates'
Work from the board's own timetable, not from any date restated by a tutor

sections.heading: Crossing emirate lines for school, and who regulates what
paragraphs: Plenty of families in the north do not use a school in their own emirate. A household in Al Hamra Village may drive to Umm Al Quwain or Sharjah; one near Al Rams may have a child boarding or commuting further still; a parent working in Dubai may choose a campus near the office rather than near the house. The moment a family does that, the regulator changes, and so does the place where the inspection report and the fee approvals live.

The map is settled and worth having in one place. Dubai's private schools answer to the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which oversees the quality of private education in the emirate. Abu Dhabi and Al Ain sit with the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools there. Sharjah has the Sharjah Private Education Authority. Ras Al Khaimah has its own Department of Knowledge, which regulates private education in the emirate. Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah sit with the federal Ministry of Education, which supervises private schools in those three.

One detail in that list changes decisions rather than just satisfying curiosity. Ras Al Khaimah's authority, like Sharjah's, approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Curriculum and fee approval sitting with the emirate regulator is why guidance written for Dubai parents does not automatically describe a Ras Al Khaimah school's position, and why a family comparing a campus here with one in Umm Al Quwain is comparing two different regulatory arrangements as well as two commutes.

The federal baseline applies everywhere. Private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. So wherever your child studies in the UAE, those subjects run alongside the Cambridge or Pearson timetable, and content for them is set centrally - in Dubai's published version of the rules, additional or different material may not be used without prior Ministry permission. Count that load when you plan tutoring hours.

sections.heading: Vetting somebody local: a short checklist
paragraphs: If you decide a nearby tutor is right for your household, that is a legitimate choice and this page is not an argument against it. It is an argument for asking better questions than how much and when. Five checks separate a good local arrangement from an expensive one, and all five take a single conversation.

First, the permit. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated: the MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers categories including registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18. Anyone tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. Since it costs nothing and MoHRE states a two working day completion time, a tutor without one has chosen not to have one.

Second, the specification. Ask which board and tier they have taught, and ask them to name a component - the alternative-to-practical paper, the non-calculator paper, the case-study paper. A tutor who answers in generalities about the subject has not taught the course. Third, who else they teach: your child's own classroom teacher is the wrong person to pay privately, and in Abu Dhabi professional-ethics rules for school staff expressly prohibit that arrangement while the permit's code of conduct bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school.

Fourth, what they will not do. A tutor who offers to write, redraft or complete coursework is offering your child a malpractice problem, and two sites competing in this search sell exactly that. Fifth, evidence. Ask what you will receive after each session and what will be compared at week six. A local arrangement with a written error list and a six-week review is better than a remote one without, and the reverse is equally true.
bullets: MoHRE permit: free, two years, two working days to issue - no reason not to hold one
Name a component, not a subject: the answer tells you whether they have taught it
Never your child's own classroom teacher, paid privately
No writing, redrafting or completing assessed work, at any price
Ask what arrives after each session and what gets reviewed at week six

sections.heading: What families in each part of the emirate actually ask us
paragraphs: The near-me searches that reach us from Ras Al Khaimah are not interchangeable. They cluster by area in ways that say something about each community, and knowing the pattern helps a parent work out which conversation they are actually in.

From Al Hamra Village and Al Jazirah Al Hamra, the dominant request is bridging: a Year 11 student with a decent Extended mathematics grade heading into a Diploma or A Level course, and a parent who has worked out that the first term of Year 12 is where the trouble starts. These are usually summer bookings, two sessions a week through July and August, and they are the most clearly effective use of tutoring money we see from this emirate.

From the city districts - Al Nakheel, Khuzam, Al Dhait - the questions are about tier and about group classes. Is Core the right entry, does a centre class work as well as one-to-one, how many sessions a week does an Extended student need. This is the part of the emirate where a parent has genuine local options and is weighing them, which is exactly the right thing to be doing.

From Al Marjan Island and Mina Al Arab the pattern is mid-year arrivals: a student who has moved from a different curriculum or a different board and has to catch up on a specification nobody has taught them. From the northern strip and the inland belt the question is almost always timing - which evening slots exist at all when the school run finishes at six - and that is the group for whom remote teaching changes the answer from nothing available to a fixed weekly hour with the right specialist.

sections.heading: Equivalency, universities and the question behind the grade
paragraphs: Parents searching locally are usually thinking a year or two ahead, and the destination question shapes what the tutoring is for. For families aiming at UAE universities, Ministry of Education equivalency is the process to understand, and the published British-track rule is more specific than most tutoring content suggests.

Students on the British track must show five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Two points inside that rule change plans. Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five required subjects, so a student including them in the tally may be a subject short. And the threshold is stated on both scales - E or 3 - which is another reason to know whether your child sits Cambridge or Pearson.

For the American track the specification is different: English proficiency through a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the SAT reading and writing section, and at least 450 in SAT Math before applying. For the IB Diploma we publish no points threshold, because none has been read on a Ministry source; ask the Ministry or a school counsellor rather than trusting a figure on a tutoring page, including this one.

Equivalency is also not something a tutoring company performs, accelerates or guarantees, and tutoring is not required for it. It is an administrative process run through the Ministry and the emirate's attestation channels. What tutoring can honestly claim is to put the five subjects comfortably clear of the threshold rather than on it, which is a smaller promise and a true one.

faqs.question: Why does the nearest tutor not necessarily suit my child?
faqs.answer: Because distance and expertise are different filters, and in a market this size they rarely point at the same person. The question that decides a grade is whether somebody has taught your child's exact syllabus at your child's tier - Cambridge 0620 Extended rather than chemistry in general. Filtering by distance first produces a shortlist of people who are free; filtering by specification first produces a shortlist of people who can teach the course. In Dubai the two lists overlap. In the northern emirates, for several syllabuses, they do not overlap at all.

faqs.question: Is there anyone in the northern emirates who teaches Additional Mathematics 0606?
faqs.answer: Locally, very few, and that is the honest answer rather than a sales line. The content - calculus, trigonometric identities, series, vectors at IGCSE level - needs a teacher who has delivered the course rather than a graduate who is comfortable with the mathematics, and the course is taken by small cohorts in a small number of schools. It is the single hardest syllabus on our list to staff for families here. We match it remotely where we can, offer a weekend morning when the evening window is full, and say no when we cannot cover it properly.

faqs.question: What should I ask my son's school before booking any tutor?
faqs.answer: Three things. Which examination board each subject is entered with, because several campuses here use Cambridge for some subjects and Pearson for others. Which Cambridge administrative zone the centre sits in, since the timetable differs by zone and the board states it cannot take responsibility for a candidate who used the wrong one. And whether each science carries the practical test or the alternative-to-practical paper. Those three answers shape a tutoring plan more than the choice of tutor does, and the exams officer can supply all of them in one email.

faqs.question: We live in Al Hamra Village. What do families here usually need help with?
faqs.answer: Bridging work, more than anything else. The pattern from this part of the emirate is a Year 11 student with a reasonable Extended mathematics grade moving into a Diploma or A Level course, and a parent who has realised that the first term of Year 12 is where students come unstuck - not for lack of content but because the work becomes independent and the assessment criteria become explicit. Two sessions a week through July and August is the usual shape, and it is the most clearly effective use of tutoring money we see from this emirate.

faqs.question: Our school run from Al Rams finishes at six. Does any slot exist?
faqs.answer: Yes, though not the one most families want. A 6pm or 6.30pm start works and is the busiest hour in the whole Gulf week, so the strongest subject specialists in that window are booked early in the academic year. The better option from the northern strip is usually a weekend morning: easier to staff with the right specialist, long enough to sit a timed paper, and more productive for a student who has already done a full school day and half an hour in the car. We would rather put you with the right teacher on a Saturday than the wrong one on a Tuesday.

faqs.question: My daughter has just moved here from a different curriculum. Where do we start?
faqs.answer: With a comparison of specifications rather than with teaching. A student arriving mid-course has usually covered different topics in a different order, and the first job is to establish what her new school's specification expects that she has not met - which takes one session with the syllabus and her previous work side by side. The second job is administrative: which board she is now entered with, which tier, and whether any coursework component applies. Teaching that starts before those two questions are answered tends to cover ground she already has.

faqs.question: Does it help that a tutor knows the teachers at my child's campus?
faqs.answer: A little, and less than parents expect. Knowing a department's mock style and internal deadlines is genuinely useful, and any competent tutor asks about both in the first session whether or not they have local knowledge. What it cannot substitute for is having taught the specification, because the external paper is set and marked by the board rather than by the school. In a small emirate, insisting on someone who knows the campus often means accepting someone who has not taught the course, which is the more expensive compromise.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to hire someone from my own neighbourhood?
faqs.answer: Not usually, once travel is accounted for. Published market rates for in-home one-to-one across the UAE run roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour including the tutor's journey, against roughly AED 150 to 300 for qualified online one-to-one and AED 200 to 450 for exam-board specialists; group classes at centres sit lower, around AED 45 to 150. Those are market figures from published provider rates, not our price list. In an emirate forty kilometres across, the drive is a larger share of an in-home fee here than in a dense city, so neighbourhood proximity reduces the travel but rarely the rate.

faqs.question: What does a local tuition centre give us that one-to-one does not?
faqs.answer: A room, a timetable and a lower hourly figure, plus the discipline of leaving the house to study, which for some students matters more than any teaching method. The limitation is attention arithmetic: in a class of six, an hour yields perhaps ten minutes of individual attention and the pace follows the group's median student. For a child who shares the class's gap, that can be the better buy. For one losing marks in four specific places - missing method, misread command words, unfinished papers - a group rarely finds them, because finding them requires reading that student's script.

faqs.question: How do I check that a tutor I found locally is allowed to teach?
faqs.answer: Ask about the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, applied for through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system, with a stated completion time of two working days, and the eligible categories include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18. Anyone offering private lessons without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. Since it is free and quick, not holding one is a choice rather than an obstacle.

faqs.question: Can my child's own class teacher tutor her privately?
faqs.answer: It is the arrangement to avoid, and in some emirates it is expressly prohibited. Press-reported professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff in Abu Dhabi prohibit teachers from providing paid private tuition to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. Beyond the rules, there is a conflict worth naming: the person who sets the assessment should not be paid to prepare one candidate for it. A provider offering you that arrangement is offering you a problem.

faqs.question: We are considering a school in Umm Al Quwain instead. Does that change anything?
faqs.answer: It changes which authority you deal with. Ras Al Khaimah's private schools answer to the emirate's own Department of Knowledge, which regulates private education and approves fees, curricula, programmes and assessment methods. Umm Al Quwain, along with Ajman and Fujairah, sits with the federal Ministry of Education, which supervises private schools in those three emirates. Dubai has the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, Abu Dhabi and Al Ain the Department of Education and Knowledge, and Sharjah its own authority. The board your child sits and the entry deadlines do not change; the regulator, the inspection report and the fee approvals do.

faqs.question: Do we need tutoring at all for a UAE university place?
faqs.answer: No, and anyone implying otherwise is misdescribing a regulatory process. Ministry of Education equivalency for the British track asks for five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at a grade of no less than E or 3, excluding Arabic and Islamic education from the five, plus one A Level at no less than E or two AS Levels at the same grade. Tutoring is not a requirement anywhere in that. What tutoring can honestly do is put those five subjects comfortably clear of the threshold rather than on it, and make the post-16 grades competitive for the course your child actually wants.

faqs.question: If you cannot cover a subject, will you tell us or just assign someone?
faqs.answer: We tell you, and it happens. The subjects where this comes up most are Additional Mathematics 0606, Co-ordinated Sciences taught with the correct scope, Computer Science with a programming focus, and post-16 Higher Level sciences. In those cases the options are a named wait, a different hour with the right specialist, or a plain no. The alternative - putting a generalist in front of an Extended-tier student in an exam year - costs a term that a Year 11 student cannot spare, and it is how tutoring arrangements end up abandoned in March.

faqs.question: Can we just buy a diagnostic opinion rather than ongoing lessons?
faqs.answer: Yes, and some families should. Two or three sessions produce a ranked list of recurring errors with rough mark values, a view on whether the current tier is right, and an honest read on whether a target grade is reachable in the weeks remaining. That list is yours and works with any tutor afterwards, including a local one you prefer for other reasons. Parents use it most often in the autumn term of Year 11, when the entry can still be changed and the information is still worth something.

intro.heading: The decision at sixteen is the one that is hardest to undo
paragraphs: Julphar is the old name of the settlement that became Ras Al Khaimah city, and the district that carries the name today sits in the established part of town near the creek, with the Julphar towers, the older apartment blocks and the villa streets behind them. It is long-settled territory. A large share of the families here have been in the emirate for ten years or more, often with older children already through school, and they ask a different kind of question from a family that arrived last August.

The questions that arrive from this district are structural. Should a child take IGCSEs and then A-Levels, or move into the IB Diploma? Which maths route keeps engineering open? Does dropping a science at sixteen matter? What does the Ministry of Education require before a UAE university will consider the certificates? Can a student sit as a private candidate if the school does not offer a subject? These are decisions rather than difficulties, and the cost of getting one wrong is measured in years.

They also arrive at the worst possible moment, which is usually February or March of Year 11, when the school is asking for sixth-form choices and the student has four weeks to decide. By then the useful conversations should already have happened. A subject choice made in a hurry at sixteen can close a degree route at nineteen, and the person who notices is normally the admissions office rather than the school.

The second thing that makes this district distinctive is supply. Ras Al Khaimah has a small private-school set, so not every route is locally available and not every subject runs in every year. A student who wants a particular Higher Level combination may find it is not offered, or is offered only as a single set of four students. Long-settled families know this and ask about it early, which is exactly the right instinct.

The sections below work through the decisions in order: the IGCSE and A-Level route against the Diploma, the two Diploma maths courses and what degree routes expect, the subject choices that close doors, what the Diploma core genuinely demands, what a two-year support plan costs in AED, private-candidate entry, and what happens after results. Tuition for Julphar families is delivered as one-to-one lessons over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a UAE address; home visits are offered only in India.

One local point of orientation. Private schools in Ras Al Khaimah are regulated by the emirate's Department of Knowledge, which approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Programme availability questions, including whether a school is authorised to offer a particular programme, belong with the school and with that authority.

ras-al-khaimah/julphar.programmesIntro: Four routes are genuinely in play for a Julphar family at sixteen. They differ less in difficulty than in shape: how many subjects, how much coursework, and how much of the grade is decided before the final exams.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across six groups, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Breadth is compulsory: a student continues with mathematics, a science, a language and a humanities subject whether they want to or not.
programmes.countryNote: In Ras Al Khaimah the Diploma is offered at the coastal campuses rather than in the city centre, so a Julphar family choosing it is also choosing a daily journey south. Ask the school in the spring of Year 11 which Higher Level sets are actually running for the coming cohort, because a published subject list and the sets that run in a given year are not the same thing.

programmes.name: IGCSE then A-Level
programmes.description: Three or four subjects studied in depth, with AS and A2 structures depending on the board and centre. Narrower than the Diploma and deeper in each subject, with no compulsory breadth and no core requirement equivalent to Theory of Knowledge or the Extended Essay.
programmes.countryNote: For Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track the published requirement is one accredited subject at Advanced Level at a grade of no less than E, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, alongside five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3. Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among those five. Verify the current wording with the Ministry before planning around it.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten subjects examined terminally, with Cambridge running June and November series and Pearson running May/June and November. Tiered entries in some subjects cap the available grade, and the tier decision is made in Year 10.
programmes.countryNote: The IGCSE grades a Julphar student finishes with do two separate jobs: they satisfy part of the equivalency requirement, and they determine which sixth-form route is open. A school will usually require specific grades for Higher Level or A-Level entry in a subject, so the Year 10 tier decision and the Year 12 route decision are connected more tightly than most families realise.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, reported on a 1-7 scale, with an optional eAssessment at the end. It is designed to lead into the Diploma, and the transition is smoother in programme philosophy than in examination technique.
programmes.countryNote: An MYP student in this emirate heading into the Diploma usually needs a summer on technique rather than content: timed writing, algebraic fluency and working without the scaffolding a criterion task provides. Students who arrive in DP1 having only ever been assessed against criteria find the first set of timed papers a shock, and the shock is avoidable.

ras-al-khaimah/julphar.subjectsIntro: At a route decision the subject list matters less for its content than for what each subject keeps open. The notes below cover both: what the subject assesses, and where it sits in a degree route.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The proof and calculus route, and the one most commonly specified by engineering, physics and mathematics degree programmes. Higher Level adds complex numbers and vectors. Marks are lost in unstructured later questions and in the exploration's reflection criterion rather than in the mathematics.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling and calculator-led problem solving, more often accepted for business, social science and life-science routes. Check the published entry requirements of the specific programme, because acceptance of AI for quantitative degrees varies considerably between universities.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0625 and 4PH1
subjects.description: Commonly required alongside mathematics for engineering routes. Fields and thermodynamics are the Higher Level difficulties; the uncertainty and graph-analysis strand carries real marks and is rarely taught explicitly.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0620 and 4CH1
subjects.description: Usually required for medicine, dentistry, pharmacy and most life-science degrees, frequently at Higher Level. Moles and stoichiometry gate the rest of the course, and multi-step calculations lose marks to rounding carried through stages.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0610 and 4BI1
subjects.description: Often paired with chemistry for health-science routes. The highest content volume of the sciences, with extended-response marks awarded for named mechanisms and exact terminology rather than general understanding.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: A common Group 3 choice for business and economics routes. Some economics degrees specify mathematics rather than economics, so taking it is rarely a substitute for the maths requirement. Diagram accuracy and the three commentaries decide most grades.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study based, with command terms doing most of the work in the papers. The Higher Level research project needs a real organisation and a bounded question. Less often a formal entry requirement than economics or mathematics.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Satisfies the Group 1 requirement and, at the right level, often the English language requirement for university entry. Paper 1 unseen analysis rewards a repeatable structure, and the Individual Oral needs a tightly scoped global issue.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Useful rather than usually required for computing degrees, which more often specify mathematics. Trace tables and pseudocode discipline carry IGCSE marks; the Higher Level internal assessment needs a genuine client and a scoped problem.

subjects.name: Arabic as a First Language
subjects.description: Mandatory for Arab students in UAE private schools, taught in Standard Arabic to prescribed content. Note that Arabic is not counted among the five IGCSE subjects the Ministry requires for British-track equivalency, which matters when planning a subject set.

subjects.name: Visual Arts and Group 6 options
subjects.description: A genuine Group 6 choice at some campuses and absent at others, which is one of the availability questions worth asking early. Where a Group 6 subject does not run, students take a second subject from another group instead.

sections.heading: Who lives in Julphar, and why the question here is route rather than rescue
paragraphs: The district carries the historic name of the settlement that preceded modern Ras Al Khaimah, and it still feels like the older part of the city: established apartment blocks, villa streets set back from the creek, long-standing businesses, and families who have been in the emirate long enough to have opinions about individual schools rather than about systems.

That changes the nature of the enquiries that come from here. A family new to the UAE asks who is good at maths. A family in their eleventh year asks whether the Diploma is worth the journey to the coast when the local British route is five minutes away, and whether dropping chemistry at sixteen will matter if their daughter later applies for pharmacy. The second question is harder and more valuable to answer well.

There is also a sibling effect. Households here frequently have an older child who has already been through the process, which is useful institutional memory and occasionally misleading, because route availability shifts. A subject that ran as a Higher Level set three years ago may not run this year, and a published subject list is a statement of intent rather than a guarantee for a particular cohort.

The practical consequence is that the useful work happens a year earlier than families expect. Sixth-form choices are typically demanded in the spring of Year 11, with a few weeks to decide. The conversations that make that decision sound should happen in Year 10: what the student is actually good at on marked evidence, what the intended destinations publish as requirements, and what the school can realistically run.

sections.heading: IGCSEs into A-Levels, or the IB Diploma: a straight comparison
paragraphs: Both routes are respected, both lead to good universities, and the choice should be made on the student rather than on reputation. The honest difference is shape. A-Levels narrow early: three or four subjects, each studied in depth, with no compulsory breadth and no core. The Diploma keeps six subjects running, insists on mathematics, a science, a language and a humanities subject, and adds Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS on top.

That shape suits different students in predictable ways. A student with a clear, narrow strength and a known destination usually does better on A-Levels, because the breadth requirement in the Diploma forces them to spend two years on subjects they have already finished with. A student who is strong across the board, or genuinely undecided at sixteen, usually does better on the Diploma, because it keeps options open and rewards the organisational skills it also demands.

Workload is where families most often misjudge. The Diploma is not harder in content than three A-Levels at the same level; it is more continuous. There is internally assessed work in most subjects, plus a 4,000-word essay and a reflective course, and all of it is spread across two years with internal deadlines that collide. A-Levels concentrate the pressure into terminal papers with less to manage along the way.

The table compares them across the dimensions that actually decide the outcome. Read it with your own child in mind rather than looking for a winner, and check the specific entry requirements of the destinations you care about, because universities differ in how they treat each route.

sections.heading: Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation
paragraphs: This is the single most consequential subject decision in the Diploma and it is frequently made on the basis of which course sounds easier. The two are different in kind rather than in difficulty. Analysis and Approaches is the algebra, calculus and proof route. Applications and Interpretation is the statistics, modelling and technology route, with the graphic display calculator assumed throughout.

The reason it matters so much is admissions. Engineering, physics, mathematics and many computer science programmes commonly specify Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level, and a student who has taken Applications may find the door closed even with an excellent grade. Business, economics, social science and some life-science routes more often accept either, and some specify a particular level rather than a particular course.

What makes this difficult in practice is that the decision is taken at sixteen, before most students know what they want to study, and it is very hard to change later. Moving from Applications into Analysis after DP1 has started means covering a different course from a standing start while the rest of the cohort is a term ahead. Moving the other way is easier and still disruptive.

The practical rule is to choose for the widest plausible range of destinations rather than for the current favourite. If engineering, physics or mathematics is on the list at all, Analysis is the safer choice. If the student is genuinely more capable with data and modelling than with algebra, Applications at Higher Level may produce a far better grade than Analysis at Standard Level, and a better grade in the accepted course beats a poor one in the preferred course. Always check the published requirements of the specific programme rather than relying on general advice, including this page.

sections.heading: Subject choices at sixteen that quietly close degree routes
paragraphs: The costly mistakes are not dramatic. Nobody abandons chemistry while intending to study medicine. What happens is smaller: a student drops a subject they find dull at sixteen, chooses a Standard Level where a Higher Level was expected, or takes a subject that looks relevant instead of the one that is actually specified. The consequence surfaces two or three years later in an admissions requirement.

The most common examples repeat across this district. Economics taken instead of mathematics for an economics degree, where it is mathematics that is specified. Biology without chemistry for a health-science route. A science at Standard Level where Higher Level is required. English at a level that does not satisfy a language requirement. And the quiet one: a subject set that satisfies school requirements but leaves the student one short of the Ministry's equivalency count.

Preventing it is mechanical rather than clever. Write down the three or four degree subjects the student might plausibly apply for, find the published entry requirements for two or three universities in each, and list every subject and level that appears. Any subject that appears on more than one list is effectively compulsory. The exercise takes an evening and is almost never done before choices are submitted.

The table lists the pairings worth checking, with the usual requirement and the common mistake. Requirements change and vary by institution, so treat it as a prompt to go and read the actual published criteria rather than as a statement of any university's rules. And note the second caution: no tutoring is required for admission, equivalency or progression, and anybody suggesting otherwise is manufacturing urgency.

sections.heading: What the Diploma core actually demands
paragraphs: Families comparing routes tend to compare the six subjects and ignore the core, which is where most of the unplanned work sits. The core is three things: Theory of Knowledge, a reflective course with no content to revise; the Extended Essay, an independent research piece capped at 4,000 words with a supervisor rather than a teacher; and CAS, a programme of creativity, activity and service commitments spread across both years.

Theory of Knowledge is the hardest of the three to prepare for because nothing can be learned in advance. It is assessed through an exhibition and a prescribed-title essay, and it rewards structured argument, precise distinctions and willingness to take a position. Students who write fluently and vaguely do poorly; students who write plainly and precisely do well. It is a writing skill, not a knowledge base.

The Extended Essay is where the time goes. Choosing a research question narrow enough to answer and substantial enough to sustain an argument is the single highest-leverage hour in the two years, and it is routinely done in twenty minutes because the deadline feels distant. A supervisor on a small campus may be supervising several essays in fields outside their own, so the student owns the process in practice as well as in principle.

CAS is the quiet scheduling cost. It is not graded but it must be completed, and the commitments land on exactly the evenings a family would otherwise use for study or tuition. Mapping CAS alongside everything else before DP1 begins is what prevents the familiar DP2 autumn, in which three internal deadlines, the essay and the first serious revision arrive in the same fortnight. A tutor can teach the skills each of these needs and give feedback on the student's own drafts; the work itself must be theirs throughout.

sections.heading: What a two-year plan costs, in context
paragraphs: Families at a route decision are also making a budget decision across two years rather than a term, so the useful figure is annual rather than hourly. No rate table has been published for Ras Al Khaimah, and every AED figure in this market comes from a Dubai source, so the bands below carry the provider that publishes them and should be read as a ceiling.

The shape of a two-year plan is rarely constant. Most families who sustain support across the Diploma run one subject weekly throughout, add a second in DP2, and add a short block before mocks and before the final series. Spread evenly, that is less than the headline rate suggests; concentrated into DP2, it is considerably more because specialist rates rise closer to a results deadline.

For wider context, Dubai's private school sector published figures showing 387,441 students across 227 private schools offering seventeen different curricula, with the UK curriculum at 37 per cent of enrolment, Indian at 26 per cent, US at 14 per cent and the International Baccalaureate at 7 per cent. KHDA also confirmed in May 2026 that Dubai private school fees would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year under the emirate's second economic incentives package. Both are Dubai figures; confirm the position for your own school with it and with the Department of Knowledge.
