sections.heading: Sitting as a private candidate, and when it is worth it
paragraphs: A Julphar student can run into a subject the school does not offer, or a subject offered only in a combination that does not work with the rest of the timetable. One answer is to sit it as a private candidate, entered through a recognised examination centre rather than through the student's own school. It is a legitimate route and it carries real administrative weight.

The practicalities belong to the family. A centre has to be found that will accept private candidates for that syllabus, the entry has to be made by the published deadline, and any component requiring supervised practical work or a speaking endorsement has to be arranged with that centre. The first real decision is which sitting to aim at, because a UAE candidate has two: Cambridge's June series, and its November series, which is also the resit route. The February/March series Cambridge runs is offered to India only, so it is not an option from Julphar and a February exam window quoted anywhere is not yours. Entry deadlines then sit months ahead of the papers in either case — spring for a June sitting, well before the autumn half-term for a November one — and the exact day comes from the centre on the statement of entry rather than from a page like this. Pearson shows the same gap with published figures: its November 2026 International GCSE timetable runs to 19 November 2026, and the equivalent November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026, so a private candidate who starts thinking about entries in October has already missed the series they had in mind.

Timetable administration matters more than people expect. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after the wrong zone timetable has been used. A private candidate has to confirm this with the centre rather than assume it.

Where it makes sense is a specific and limited set of cases: an extra IGCSE subject needed for an equivalency count, a resit in a November or January series, or a subject genuinely unavailable locally. Where it rarely makes sense is as a substitute for school provision across a whole programme, because the coursework and practical components of many subjects are difficult to arrange outside a school. A tutor can teach the syllabus and track the board's deadlines; registration and fees remain with the family and the centre.

sections.heading: After results: equivalency, retakes and the next decision
paragraphs: Two things happen after results that a Julphar family should understand before they arrive. The first is equivalency. Certificates earned at a private school here generally need a Ministry of Education equivalency certificate before a UAE university will consider them, and the published British-track requirement is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, plus one subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five.

On the American track the published requirements are different in kind: English proficiency through IELTS 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and at least 450 in SAT Math, both taken before applying. For the IB there is no points threshold published in the sources used for this page, so none is quoted here. Confirm any IB figure on the Ministry's own site or with the emirate attestation authority, and treat the process as something the family completes with the Ministry rather than something a tutor performs or expedites.

The second is retakes. Both IGCSE boards run more than one series a year, so a disappointing result in June does not have to wait twelve months: Cambridge runs June and November series, and Pearson runs May/June and November. For the Diploma, a November session exists, and the decision to resit should be made on the component marks rather than the overall grade, because a single weak component is a different problem from a weak subject.

The sensible order after results is: read the component breakdown, ask the school's examinations officer whether a review or enquiry about results is warranted and what the deadline is, then decide about retakes, then start the equivalency paperwork. Doing those in the wrong order is how families miss a short review window. And no tutoring is required for equivalency, admission or progression; the requirement is the qualification, not the support used to get there.

process.title: Start in Year 10, not spring of Year 11
process.description: Route and subject decisions are usually demanded with a few weeks' notice. The useful conversations need marked evidence of what the student is actually strong at, plus the published requirements of plausible destinations, and both take time to assemble properly.

process.title: Write down the destinations before the subjects
process.description: List three or four degree subjects the student might apply for, read the published entry requirements for a few universities in each, and note every subject and level that appears. Anything appearing on more than one list is effectively compulsory.

process.title: Confirm what the school can actually run
process.description: A published subject list is a statement of intent. Ask which Higher Level sets are running for the coming cohort and how many students are in each, because a single set of four has different implications for independent support than a set of twenty.

process.title: Trial lesson, then commit to the plan
process.description: One session with the matched tutor before any term commitment. For a two-year Diploma plan this matters more than usual, since the point of the arrangement is continuity across internal deadlines rather than a quick repair.

process.title: Review at each internal deadline
process.description: Progress is judged against the next real checkpoint: a mock, an internal assessment submission, an Extended Essay draft. If nothing is moving by the second checkpoint, the match changes rather than the student being asked to try harder.

whyPoints.title: Decisions treated as the main work
whyPoints.description: A route or subject choice made badly at sixteen costs more than any term of weak teaching. Sessions on route choice are deliberately finite and end in a written summary of the options and trade-offs rather than becoming an open-ended arrangement.

whyPoints.title: Published requirements, not general advice
whyPoints.description: Maths route and subject-level questions are answered by reading what the specific programmes actually publish. General guidance, including this page, is a prompt to check the real criteria rather than a substitute for them.

whyPoints.title: Two-year plans built backwards
whyPoints.description: Diploma support is planned from internal assessment and core deadlines rather than from the start of term, so coursework does not end up colliding with the first serious revision in the autumn of DP2.

whyPoints.title: Private-candidate routes explained honestly
whyPoints.description: Where a subject is not locally available, the private-candidate option is set out with who handles each step. Registration, centre arrangements and fees belong to the family; teaching and deadline tracking are what a tutor provides.

whyPoints.title: Coursework boundaries that protect the student
whyPoints.description: Internal assessments, the Extended Essay and TOK essays are the student's own work throughout. Sessions teach the skills and give feedback on drafts the student has written, and never supply text, data or a finished piece.

whyPoints.title: Honest about what IB Gram is
whyPoints.description: An independent tutor-matching platform with no UAE premises and no accreditation from the Department of Knowledge, KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson. Equivalency is a Ministry process, not something IB Gram performs.

faqs.question: Should our daughter take A-Levels or the IB Diploma after her IGCSEs?
faqs.answer: It depends on the student rather than the reputation of either route. A-Levels narrow to three or four subjects studied in depth, with no compulsory breadth and no core, which suits a student with a clear strength and a known destination. The Diploma keeps six subjects running, requires mathematics, a science, a language and a humanities subject, and adds Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. It suits a broad or undecided student who is organised. In this emirate the Diploma also usually means a daily journey to the coastal campuses.

faqs.question: Is the IB Diploma harder than three A-Levels?
faqs.answer: Not harder in content at the same level, but more continuous. Most Diploma subjects carry internally assessed work, and the core adds a 4,000-word Extended Essay, a reflective Theory of Knowledge course and CAS commitments spread across two years. A-Levels concentrate the pressure into terminal papers with less to manage along the way. Students who build steadily and manage deadlines well generally find the Diploma suits them; students who peak in an exam hall and dislike coursework often do better on A-Levels.

faqs.question: Which Diploma maths course does an engineering degree expect?
faqs.answer: Engineering, physics and mathematics programmes commonly specify Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level, and frequently do not accept Applications and Interpretation. Business, economics and social science routes more often accept either. The decision is taken at sixteen and is very hard to reverse, because moving into Analysis after DP1 begins means covering a different course from a standing start. If engineering is on the list of possibilities at all, Analysis is the safer choice. Check the published requirements of the specific programmes rather than relying on general advice.

faqs.question: My son wants to study medicine. Which Higher Level subjects does he need?
faqs.answer: Chemistry at Higher Level is the usual expectation, almost always with a second science, most often biology. The costly mistake is small and common: chemistry taken at Standard Level because it is harder than biology, or dropped at sixteen with the intention of picking it up later. Medical schools differ considerably and set their own rules, so read the published requirements for each one he might apply to rather than working from a general rule. The decision has to be made before DP1 starts; it is extremely hard to fix afterwards.

faqs.question: Can a student in Ras Al Khaimah sit an IGCSE as a private candidate?
faqs.answer: Yes, through a recognised examination centre rather than through their own school, and the administration belongs to the family. A centre willing to accept private candidates for that specific syllabus has to be found, the entry made by the published deadline, and any practical or speaking component arranged with that centre. Cambridge also allocates centres to one of six administrative zones and warns that using the wrong zone timetable can mean a missed exam. It works well for an extra subject or a resit, and poorly as a substitute for a whole programme.

faqs.question: What is Theory of Knowledge and does it affect the final score?
faqs.answer: It is a reflective course with no content to revise, assessed through an exhibition and a prescribed-title essay, and it contributes to the Diploma alongside the Extended Essay. Precisely how those two combine in the award is set out in the current Diploma regulations, so confirm the detail with your child's coordinator. What is consistent is what it rewards: structured argument, careful distinctions and a willingness to take a position. Students who write fluently and vaguely score poorly. It is a writing and reasoning skill rather than a body of knowledge.

faqs.question: How much time does CAS actually take?
faqs.answer: Enough to matter to a timetable, and it is the cost families most often ignore when comparing routes. CAS runs across both Diploma years as a programme of creativity, activity and service commitments with reflection attached. It is not graded but must be completed, and in practice it lands on exactly the evenings a family planned to use for study or tuition. Map it alongside clubs and sport before DP1 begins, because the alternative is discovering in the autumn of DP2 that three internal deadlines, the essay and CAS hours collide.

faqs.question: Is it possible to change a Diploma subject once DP1 has started?
faqs.answer: Sometimes in the first weeks, rarely after that, and the two maths courses are the hardest case. Changing from Applications into Analysis means starting a different syllabus while the cohort is a term ahead, which is possible with sustained support and is genuinely difficult. Changing level within a subject, from Higher to Standard, is usually easier than changing subject. Availability is the other constraint: in a small school set the alternative subject may simply not run. Ask the coordinator what is actually possible before assuming a change can be made.

faqs.question: Do UAE universities prefer the IB Diploma or A-Levels?
faqs.answer: Both are recognised, and the decisive step is usually Ministry of Education equivalency rather than a preference between routes. On the British track the published requirement is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, plus one subject at Advanced Level at E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from the five. No IB points threshold is published in the sources used here, so confirm that figure with the Ministry directly rather than accepting any number from a tutoring page.

faqs.question: What does a full two-year Diploma support plan cost?
faqs.answer: No rate table is published for Ras Al Khaimah, so the available figures are Dubai ones and should be read as a ceiling. Qualified online subject tutors are published at AED 150-300 an hour and specialists at AED 200-450 or more, with monthly package examples of AED 799 online for eight sessions and AED 1,599-1,799 for in-home blocks. Most families who sustain support run one subject weekly throughout, add a second in DP2 and add a short block before mocks. IB Gram quotes after a consultation rather than from a price list.

faqs.question: We have lived here for years. Which local schools actually offer the Diploma?
faqs.answer: The IB continuum provision in this emirate sits at the coastal campuses rather than in the old city, principally the RAK Academy campuses at Al Hamra with a further campus at Khuzam. A Julphar family choosing the Diploma is therefore choosing a daily journey as well as a programme. Confirm current programme authorisation and which Higher Level sets are running for the coming cohort with the school and with the emirate's Department of Knowledge, because a published subject list is a statement of intent rather than a guarantee for a given year.

faqs.question: Can a student take four Higher Level subjects instead of three?
faqs.answer: The standard Diploma is three Higher Level and three Standard Level subjects, and some schools permit a fourth Higher Level where the timetable and the student's record allow. It adds substantial workload on top of a core that is already demanding, and it is rarely what makes the difference to an application. A strong three-Higher-Level profile with good core marks is generally a better outcome than a stretched four. Ask the coordinator whether the school allows it at all before treating it as an option.

faqs.question: How early should subject choices be discussed?
faqs.answer: Year 10, a full year before the school asks. The decision needs three things that cannot be assembled quickly: marked evidence of what the student is genuinely strong at, the published entry requirements of three or four plausible degree routes, and confirmation of what the school can actually run for that cohort. Families who start in the spring of Year 11 are deciding in four weeks with none of those in place, which is how a subject gets dropped that an admissions office later requires.

faqs.question: What happens if a student passes the subjects but does not get the full Diploma?
faqs.answer: The IB awards results for individual subjects as well as the full Diploma, so a student who does not meet the Diploma requirements still has certificated subject results. How those are treated for university admission and for Ministry of Education equivalency varies, and it is a question for the specific university and for the Ministry rather than for a tutoring page. The practical step is to ask the Diploma coordinator precisely which requirement was not met, because a failed core component and a failed subject lead to different remedies.

faqs.question: Is resitting in a November series worth it?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and the decision should be made on component marks rather than the overall grade. Cambridge runs June and November series and Pearson runs May/June and November, so an IGCSE resit does not have to wait a year. A single unexpectedly weak component is a different problem from a subject that was weak throughout, and only the component breakdown shows which it was. Ask the school's examinations officer about review and enquiry-about-results deadlines first, because those windows are short and close quickly after results.

ras-al-khaimah/julphar.closingHeading: Decide once, with the published requirements in front of you
ras-al-khaimah/julphar.closingBody: The useful work for a Julphar family happens a year before the school asks for choices. Send us the marked evidence of what your child is actually strong at, the degree routes they might plausibly apply for, and the subject list the school expects to run. We will set out what each route demands, which maths course keeps which doors open, and where the real trade-offs sit. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, and route sessions are deliberately finite, ending in a decision rather than a subscription.

ras-al-khaimah/khuzam.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover the IB Diploma, the Middle Years Programme and both main IGCSE boards. For a multi-child household, matching also accounts for whether sessions can run back to back in the same slot without competing for the same room.

intro.heading: The school is five minutes away, and the timetable is still the problem
paragraphs: Khuzam sits inland from the Corniche, a mixed district of villa streets and apartment blocks with a RAK Academy campus inside it. For families here the school run is trivial: a short drive or in some cases a walk, children home by mid-afternoon, no causeway and no motorway. On paper this is the easiest place in the emirate to fit tutoring into a week. In practice Khuzam households run into a different set of constraints, and they are the ones nobody writes about.

The first is siblings. The typical household asking for help here has two or three school-age children, often spread across primary, lower secondary and an exam year. That is three different homework loads, three different bedtimes, and one room quiet enough for a lesson in which a child has to speak aloud. A timetable that works for the Year 11 student will routinely collide with the Year 4 one's reading practice.

The second is the after-school programme. Clubs, sport and CAS commitments on the campus run past four o'clock on several days a week, and because the school is so close, families say yes to more of them than a family driving in from Al Dhait would. The result is a week with two or three evenings already committed before any tutoring is considered, which is why the honest answer is often two sessions rather than three.

The third is the homework load itself, which almost no family has actually measured. A Year 9 student with eight subjects and homework set twice a week in each is carrying something close to two hours a night. Adding a tutoring session to a week already at capacity does not produce more learning; it produces a tired child and a cancelled slot in week five. The fix is to decide what the session replaces, not what it adds.

The fourth is proximity to the staff room. In a district where families live alongside their children's teachers, the question of whether a classroom teacher can tutor privately comes up constantly. It has a clear answer, and it is not the convenient one. The sections below work through all four constraints, then cover formats and costs, the exam-session calendar, what to do when a match is wrong, and the practical setup for live video in a shared house.

Tuition for Khuzam families is delivered as one-to-one lessons over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a UAE address; home visits are a service offered only in India. Private schools in this emirate are regulated by the Department of Knowledge, which approves curricula, programmes, courses, activities, assessment methods and tuition fees. That is a different authority from Dubai's KHDA and Abu Dhabi's ADEK, so published guidance written for those emirates does not transfer directly to a Khuzam household.

Two or three children per household is the norm, not the exception
Club and CAS commitments take two or three evenings a week
A Year 9 homework load is already close to two hours a night

ras-al-khaimah/khuzam.programmesIntro: Khuzam households are usually spread across more than one programme at once, which is itself the planning problem. The four below are the ones that appear in the same house.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten subjects examined terminally. Cambridge runs a June and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. Pearson International GCSE runs May/June and November. Entry deadlines sit months before the papers, which is the part families miss.
programmes.countryNote: For a Khuzam household the IGCSE year is the one that dictates the whole family timetable, because it is the only year with immovable external deadlines. A candidate here has two sittings to choose between, June and November, and no third: Cambridge's February/March series is offered to India only, so any February exam window quoted at you belongs to another country. The gap that matters is between the entry and the paper. Pearson's published figures show it plainly — its November 2026 International GCSE timetable runs to 19 November 2026, and those entries are settled long before the autumn term is under way — and Cambridge's June series works the same way, with entries closing in the spring. A household planning around the exam rather than the entry is already two terms behind.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internally assessed work carries a meaningful share of each subject grade, and the terminal papers are sat in the May session at almost every UAE school.
programmes.countryNote: CAS is the quiet scheduling cost of the Diploma in a district like this. Because the campus is close, students take on more commitments than a commuting student would, and CAS hours land on exactly the evenings a family would otherwise use for tuition. Mapping CAS, club and sports commitments before choosing a slot prevents the most common cause of a collapsed timetable.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each assessed against four criteria out of eight and reported on a 1-7 scale. No external papers before the optional eAssessment, so there is no exam mark to read progress from and criterion descriptors do all the work.
programmes.countryNote: In a multi-child house the MYP child is usually the one whose difficulties get noticed last, because there is no exam grade to compare and the older sibling's exam year absorbs the attention. The useful habit is a short termly conversation with the school about which specific criteria are weakest, rather than waiting for a reported number to drop.

programmes.name: IB Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led, transdisciplinary and unexamined. What responds to support at this stage is reading fluency, number-fact recall and written stamina, all measurable in minutes rather than grades, and all improved by short frequent practice.
programmes.countryNote: Primary children in Khuzam are home earliest and are at their best between about half past three and five, which is precisely the window the older sibling cannot use. In practice that is helpful: a household can run a 16:00 primary session and a 18:00 exam-year session on the same evening without either competing for the quiet room.

ras-al-khaimah/khuzam.subjectsIntro: Requests from this district reflect the mix of year groups in one house: primary literacy and numeracy, lower-secondary maths and science, and the exam-year subjects where an external deadline is approaching.

subjects.name: Mathematics (IGCSE)
subjects.description: The most requested exam-year subject. The tier entry made in Year 10 caps the available grade, so it is worth querying early. Extended candidates lose marks in algebraic fractions, graph transformations and the long unstructured problems where no method is prompted.

subjects.name: Mathematics (lower secondary)
subjects.description: The year group where a quiet gap opens and nobody notices, because nothing is externally examined. Fractions, negative numbers, index laws and rearranging formulae are the four weaknesses that reliably resurface in a Year 11 mock three years later.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0625 and 4PH1
subjects.description: Circuits and electromagnetism are the IGCSE blockers; fields and thermodynamics the Higher Level ones. The uncertainty and practical-skills strand carries real marks, is rarely taught explicitly and can usually be fixed inside three sessions.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0620 and 4CH1
subjects.description: Moles and stoichiometry gate everything after them. A student insecure there drops marks across energetics, rates and electrochemistry no matter how well those topics were taught. Organic mechanisms reward drawing precision rather than recall.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0610 and 4BI1
subjects.description: Highest content volume of the three sciences and the one where revision method decides the grade. Extended-response marks go to named mechanisms and exact terminology, which rereading notes never produces.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE first language
subjects.description: Structure rather than ideas decides the band for most students here. Paper 1 unseen analysis rewards a repeatable paragraph pattern under time pressure, and the Individual Oral needs a global issue narrow enough to argue in ten minutes.

subjects.name: English reading and writing (primary)
subjects.description: Reading fluency and written stamina, both measurable in a few minutes and both responsive to twenty-minute sessions twice a week. Children who can discuss an idea but not sustain a paragraph arrive in Year 7 behind, and the gap compounds.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Proof, calculus and algebraic fluency. Marks disappear in the unstructured later questions and in the exploration, where the mathematics is usually sound and the personal engagement and reflection criteria are thin.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling and calculator-led problem solving. Hypothesis testing and regression are the topics students most often meet properly for the first time in a mock, and calculator operation errors account for a real share of lost marks.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy and the three internal assessment commentaries decide most grades. Evaluation that does not refer back to the diagram just drawn stops earning marks at the top band.

subjects.name: Arabic as an Additional Language
subjects.description: Mandatory in UAE private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, taught to the Ministry's prescribed content. Short frequent practice aligned to the school's own scheme works; imported material is not permitted without Ministry approval.

sections.heading: Living next to the school changes which problem you are solving
paragraphs: Most tutoring advice written for the UAE assumes a long school run, because most of it is written for Dubai. In Khuzam that assumption fails. A child here is often home within fifteen minutes of the bell, which removes travel fatigue from the equation and opens a mid-afternoon window that coastal families simply do not have. The useful consequence is that a primary child can genuinely work well at four o'clock.

What replaces travel as the constraint is commitment density. Because the campus is a few minutes away, saying yes to a club, a team or a CAS activity costs a family almost nothing in logistics, so Khuzam households say yes more often. Two or three evenings a week are frequently committed before anyone has thought about tuition, and those commitments are rarely written down in one place.

The second replacement is the shared house. One quiet room, two or three children, and a lesson that requires a student to talk aloud for an hour. Families regularly book two sessions at the same time on the assumption that a laptop each is sufficient, and discover that a child who can hear a sibling being taught stops speaking. Sequencing rather than parallel scheduling is almost always the answer.

The practical first step in this district is a written audit of the week: every club, every sport, every fixed family commitment, and the real homework load per child. Only then does choosing a slot make sense. Families who skip that step pick the slot that looks free and lose it in week five, which is the most common way a tutoring arrangement ends here.

sections.heading: Scheduling one evening across two or three children
paragraphs: The households that make this work treat the evening as a shared resource with a rota rather than as open time. The principle is simple: the youngest child takes the earliest slot because that is when they are capable, the exam-year student takes the latest because that is when they are capable, and the middle child takes whichever evening the other two are not using the room.

Parallel sessions almost never work in a house of this type. Two children on two laptops in two rooms sounds efficient and produces two weaker lessons, because at least one of them is in a space where they can be overheard and will stop talking. Headphones help and do not solve it. Consecutive slots in the same good room solve it completely, at the cost of one adult evening.

Frequency is the second decision, and the honest answer is usually fewer sessions than a family first requests. One child with two sessions a week in the subject that is actually failing produces more movement than three children with one session each in subjects that are merely imperfect. Spreading thin is the most expensive mistake available in a multi-child household.

sections.heading: What the campus already provides after three o'clock, and what it does not
paragraphs: Before paying for anything, it is worth establishing what is already included in the fees. Schools in this emirate generally run some combination of homework club, subject surgeries, intervention groups and revision sessions in the run-up to external exams. These are free at the point of use, run by teachers who know the course, and are systematically under-used because nobody tells parents they exist in a single list.

What school provision does well is structure and content clarification. A subject surgery is an excellent place to ask why a particular method works. An intervention group is a reasonable place to be walked through a topic again. Where school provision is weak is anything that requires sustained one-to-one attention over months: diagnosing an individual pattern of errors, marking eight timed papers per subject, or supervising an internal assessment design.

Neither is a substitute for the other, and the sensible order is to exhaust the free provision first. A family that books two paid sessions a week without having asked whether a Thursday subject surgery exists is buying something the school was already offering, and buying it in the slot the surgery occupies.

The table separates the two honestly. The right-hand column is where paid one-to-one earns its place: the work that needs one adult tracking one student's specific errors over a term, which no group provision can do regardless of how good the teacher is. Ask the school for the list in writing at the start of the year, including who runs each session and on which day, because the provision is usually announced once in September and then assumed to be common knowledge.

sections.heading: Group class, tuition centre or one-to-one: what each actually buys
paragraphs: Al Nakheel, a short drive north, holds most of the emirate's tuition centres, so Khuzam families have real choice of format. The three options are a centre group class, an in-home visiting tutor, and one-to-one over live video, and they are priced differently because they are different products rather than better and worse versions of the same one.

No rate table has been published for Ras Al Khaimah. Every AED figure available in this market is a Dubai figure, so the bands below carry the provider that publishes them and should be treated as a ceiling rather than a local quote. Centres in this emirate generally quote per course or per month rather than per hour, which makes direct comparison harder than it looks.

The decision rule that works: pay for attention when attention is the thing that is missing. A confident student who needs a revision structure imposed does well in a group. A student whose multi-step calculations drift, whose command-term reading is wrong, or who has an internal assessment to design, needs one adult watching one student, and a group cannot provide it at any price.

sections.heading: The homework load by year group, and when a week tips over
paragraphs: Adding a tutoring session to a week that is already full does not add learning. It adds a cancelled slot. The only reliable way to avoid that is to count what is already there, which almost no family does, because homework arrives subject by subject and nobody sees the total.

The counting is quick. List the subjects, note how often homework is set in each, and estimate the time each piece actually takes rather than the time it is supposed to take. For a Year 9 student with eight subjects and work set twice a week in most of them, the honest total is frequently ninety minutes to two hours a night. A Year 11 student in the spring term is higher again once revision is included, and a Diploma student in DP2 is higher still.

Once the total is on paper, the tutoring decision changes shape. The question stops being whether to add a session and becomes what the session replaces. Often it replaces unproductive revision: the hour spent rereading notes, or the homework that is being done inefficiently because a method was never secured. A session that replaces an hour of low-value work costs the student nothing in time and gains them the method.

The table gives workable nightly figures by year group for this district, with the point at which an additional commitment starts doing harm. The right-hand column is the one to act on. Recount it at the start of each term rather than once a year, because the load moves sharply between Year 10 and Year 11 and again between DP1 and DP2, and a timetable set in September is usually wrong by February.

sections.heading: Could a teacher from the school tutor your child privately?
paragraphs: In a district where families live alongside the staff who teach their children, this question arrives early and deserves a direct answer rather than a polite deflection. The general position in the UAE is that private tutoring runs on a permit. Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 introduced the private tuition work permit, issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation and granted at no charge for two years, and registered school teachers are among the eligible categories.

So a teacher may hold a permit. What they should not do is tutor students enrolled at their own school. Abu Dhabi's education authority has issued professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff that prohibit paid private tutoring of students at their own school, and the MoHRE permit carries a code of conduct that also bars serving students affiliated with the teacher's own school. This is press-reported rather than quoted from the policy document, so verify the current wording before relying on it, but the direction is unambiguous.

The reason is sound independently of any rule. A teacher who both teaches and privately tutors the same child has a conflict of interest around assessment, predicted grades and internal marking, and the student loses the one thing a tutor is actually for: a second, independent read on their work. Marketing a child's own teacher as a private tutor is a practice to avoid, not a convenience to arrange.

What a family should do instead is straightforward. Use the school's own free provision for anything that needs the class teacher's knowledge of the course, and use an independent tutor for diagnosis, timed-paper marking and coursework coaching. Ask any individual tutor to show their MoHRE permit before the first lesson. Those operating without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule has been published, so any amount quoted to you is a guess.

sections.heading: The exam session calendar, counted backwards from the published dates
paragraphs: Families plan around exams. Boards operate on entries, and the entry deadline is the date that actually constrains a household. Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level exams in a June and a November series, with Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE exams are available in May/June and November each year.

The gap between the entry and the paper is the whole point, and it is easiest to see as a June-or-November decision rather than a single deadline. Cambridge's June series is the main sitting in Ras Al Khaimah: the papers fall across May and June, final entries close in the spring term several months earlier, and the centre submits forecast grades in the weeks before the first paper. The November series is the other half of that decision — it is the resit route, and the route for a candidate who needs one more term of teaching before sitting a subject — and its entries are settled well before the autumn half-term. We are not printing a day and a month for either, because Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones with its own timetable version and the exact dates reach you on the statement of entry. Pearson is where the published figures are concrete: the November 2026 International GCSE timetable runs to 19 November 2026, and the equivalent November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Either way, a decision about tier or about adding a subject has to be made a term or more before the papers, not in the month of them.

Pearson's recent dates show the same structure. The November 2026 International GCSE final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson also publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, which is why a revision plan should link the live official timetable rather than restate dates that can be revised.

One Cambridge administrative point matters in this emirate. Every exam centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge states it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong zone timetable. Ask your school which zone its centre sits in. No IB session or results date is published on this page: the IB's own calendar should be confirmed with your school's Diploma coordinator.

sections.heading: When the match is wrong, and how to change without losing a term
paragraphs: A proportion of tutoring matches do not work, and the expensive failure is not the mismatch itself but the three months a family spends hoping it will improve. The signals are visible within two or three sessions if anyone is looking for them, and they are behavioural rather than academic.

The clearest signal is whether the student talks. In a working one-to-one session the student speaks for a substantial share of the hour, asks questions, and holds the pen. A student who answers in single words after forty minutes is not engaged with that tutor, however well qualified the tutor is. The second signal is whether the tutor can describe the paper structure and the mark allocation for the specific syllabus code without looking it up. The third is whether the written notes after each session say anything specific.

The remedy is to have agreed the review point in advance. A named next assessment, a date, and an explicit understanding that if there has been no movement the match changes rather than the student being told to work harder. Framed that way, changing tutor is a scheduled decision rather than an awkward conversation, and the handover is easier because the session notes exist.

Changing well costs about one session. The incoming tutor reads the notes, sees what has been covered and what is still insecure, and starts from there rather than re-diagnosing from scratch. That is the practical reason written notes matter in a household like this: they make a tutor replaceable without the student paying for the change.

faqs.question: Our three children are in different year groups. How do we schedule tutoring for all of them?
faqs.answer: Sequence rather than overlap. Put the youngest in the earliest slot, around 16:00, because that is when a primary child works best and when an exam-year student does not. Put the exam-year student at 18:00. Give the middle child a different evening entirely. Two children taught at the same time in two rooms produces two weaker lessons, because one of them is somewhere they can be overheard and will stop speaking. One good quiet room used consecutively beats two mediocre spaces used simultaneously.

faqs.question: The campus runs clubs until half past four. Does a session still fit afterwards?
faqs.answer: Yes, but it changes which evenings are usable, and that is the whole planning problem in this district. Because the school is close, Khuzam families take on more club and sport commitments than families driving in from elsewhere, so two or three evenings are often already committed. Map the activity timetable in writing first, then choose two protected evenings for tuition and leave one deliberately empty. Three sessions squeezed into a week that only has room for two produces cancellations rather than progress.

faqs.question: Is a group revision class as useful as one-to-one for IGCSE maths?
faqs.answer: It depends on what is wrong. A group class is good value for a student who knows the content and needs a revision structure imposed, and it is cheaper per hour. It cannot watch one student's working and notice that their algebraic fractions drift under time pressure, or mark eight timed papers against the official scheme. Pay for attention when attention is the missing ingredient. Many families here use both: a centre class for structure and one-to-one for the subject that is actually failing.

faqs.question: How much homework should a Year 9 student realistically have each night?
faqs.answer: Around sixty to ninety minutes is typical for eight subjects with work set twice a week in most of them, and the honest figure is often higher because pieces take longer than they are meant to. Count it before adding anything. Once the total is written down the decision changes shape: the question becomes what a tutoring session replaces rather than what it adds. Usually it replaces unproductive work, such as rereading notes or grinding through homework with a method that was never secured.

faqs.question: We live a few minutes from the school. Could one of the teachers tutor our son privately?
faqs.answer: A registered school teacher can hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted at no charge for two years. What they should not do is privately tutor students enrolled at their own school. Abu Dhabi's education authority has published professional-ethics rules prohibiting exactly that, and the permit carries a code of conduct along the same lines. Beyond any rule, it removes the point of a tutor: an independent second read on your child's work, free of any role in their assessment.

faqs.question: When do Cambridge entries close for a Khuzam candidate, and which series can they sit?
faqs.answer: A candidate in Khuzam can sit the June series or the November series, and that is the full list — Cambridge's February/March series is offered to India only, so it is not a window open here. For a June sitting, final entries close in the spring term, months before the papers, which fall across May and June; the centre submits forecast grades in the weeks before the first one. For a November sitting, entries are settled well before the autumn half-term. The exact dates differ by centre, because Cambridge allocates each one to a timetable zone, so they come on your child's statement of entry rather than from a tutoring page. The gap is the detail families miss: decisions about tier, about adding a subject or about sitting as a private candidate have to be made a term or more ahead, not in the month of the exam. Always confirm against the board's live timetable.

faqs.question: When do Pearson International GCSE results come out?
faqs.answer: Pearson published June 2026 results to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. Pearson also publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, which can be revised, so a revision plan should link the live official timetable rather than rely on dates copied from elsewhere. Retake decisions are easier if the dates are known before results arrive.

faqs.question: What device does a child need for a live video lesson?
faqs.answer: A laptop or tablet with a keyboard, a reliable connection and headphones. A phone is not workable for a lesson involving shared screen work, because the student cannot see the tutor's writing and their own work at the same time. Headphones matter more than most families expect: a child working within earshot of siblings will stop speaking, and a session where the student stops speaking has stopped being one-to-one teaching. A wired connection or a seat near the router removes most remaining problems.

faqs.question: Can two siblings use the same laptop for back-to-back sessions?
faqs.answer: Yes, and in a house with one genuinely quiet room that is usually the best arrangement. Consecutive slots on one device in one room avoids the overheard-sibling problem entirely and costs a family one evening rather than two. Leave ten minutes between sessions so the second child can set out their own books and the first can finish writing up. Each child gets their own tutor matched to their level and board, and separate written notes after each session.

faqs.question: How do we change tutor without losing a term?
faqs.answer: Agree the review point before the first session: a named upcoming assessment and an explicit understanding that if nothing has moved, the match changes rather than the student being told to work harder. Framed that way it is a scheduled decision rather than an awkward conversation. The handover itself costs about one session, because the written notes from each previous lesson tell the incoming tutor what has been covered and what is still insecure, so nobody re-diagnoses from scratch.

faqs.question: What does IB and IGCSE tuition cost for a family in Khuzam?
faqs.answer: No rate table has been published for Ras Al Khaimah, so the available figures are Dubai ones and should be read as a ceiling. Named providers publish AED 45-150 an hour for budget online tuition, AED 150-300 for a qualified online subject tutor, AED 180-500 for in-home visits with travel priced in, and AED 200-450 or more for an IB or IGCSE specialist, with one premium provider at AED 650. Centres in this emirate usually quote per course or per month. IB Gram quotes after a consultation and arranges a trial lesson first.

faqs.question: Does living next to the school mean we probably do not need a tutor?
faqs.answer: It means you should use the school's own provision first, which many families here do not. Homework club, subject surgeries, intervention groups and pre-exam revision sessions are already covered by the fees and are run by teachers who know the course. What they cannot do is track one student's specific error pattern over a term, mark eight timed papers per subject against the official scheme, or give monthly criterion feedback on an internal assessment. That is the work paid one-to-one is actually for.

faqs.question: Is a Saturday morning session a good idea in Ras Al Khaimah?
faqs.answer: It is the best slot available for anything that needs an uninterrupted block, which in practice means a full timed paper or a session on internal assessment work. On a school night a ninety-minute session competes with homework, dinner and fatigue; on a Saturday morning it competes with nothing. Most families here use one weekend morning for the long block and keep midweek sessions to sixty or seventy-five minutes. Protecting the rest of the weekend matters: a student working seven days does not last the year.

faqs.question: How many subjects can one student sensibly have tutoring in at once?
faqs.answer: One, or at most two, and the common mistake is spreading thinner. A student with two sessions a week in the subject that is genuinely failing moves further than one with a single session in each of three subjects that are merely imperfect. Tutoring works through repeated contact on a diagnosed problem, and one session a week in a subject is maintenance rather than repair. Add a second subject the following term, once the first has moved, rather than starting everything at once.

intro.heading: The school run sets the timetable, not the tutor
paragraphs: Mina Al Arab sits on the southern coastal edge of Ras Al Khaimah, a low-rise mix of villas on Flamingo Villas and Bermuda, apartments on Hayat Island and townhouses backing onto the lagoons. Almost no family here walks to school. Children are driven or bussed to RAK Academy at Al Hamra, to the Indian and Our Own campuses nearer the city, or down Sheikh Mohammed Bin Salem Road towards Al Jazirah Al Hamra. That journey is the single biggest fact about tutoring here, and it is the one nobody plans around.

Work the day forwards. A bus collection on Hayat Island between 06:40 and 07:05 means a child is awake by six. Primary finishes somewhere between 13:00 and 14:30; secondary runs later, and a Diploma student with a sixth-period lesson can still be on campus at 15:00. Add the return leg and the gate at Mina Al Arab opens again between 14:15 and 16:00. A tutoring slot pencilled in for 16:00 therefore lands on a child who has been awake for ten hours and has not eaten properly since a mid-morning break.

That is why a Mina Al Arab timetable usually settles at 17:30 or 18:30 rather than straight after school, and why the choice of start time changes the outcome more than the choice of tutor does. A Year 11 student working two 75-minute sessions a week at 18:30 covers more Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625 content than the same student working three exhausted 45-minute sessions at 16:00. The hours are fewer. The retention is higher.

Driving to a tutor compounds the problem. There is no cluster of specialist IB teachers inside Mina Al Arab, so a family that wants a subject specialist in the room is looking at Al Nakheel, Al Dhait, or more often Sharjah and Dubai. That is a round trip measured in hours on E11, repeated weekly, during the months when a Diploma student has least time to spare. Online one-to-one removes the journey entirely and widens the pool from whoever lives nearby to whoever actually teaches the subject.

This page sets out the practical version: what the day looks like hour by hour, what the drive costs in time, what the market charges in AED, how a visiting tutor compares with live video for a family on this stretch of coast, and how to build a weekly timetable that survives exam leave and Ramadan. IB Gram delivers tuition for Ras Al Khaimah families as one-to-one online lessons. It does not send a tutor to a UAE address; home visits are a service offered only in India.

One framing point before the detail. Private schools in Ras Al Khaimah are regulated by the emirate's Department of Knowledge, which approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. That is a different body from Dubai's KHDA, so advice written for Dubai families does not transfer cleanly, and a question about a school's programme belongs with the Department of Knowledge rather than with an authority in another emirate.

Each has a different weekly rhythm, which changes what an evening slot should be used for.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Assessment is split between internally marked work submitted through the school and terminal papers sat in the May session. The Diploma's difficulty for most students is not the content of any one subject but the collision of internal deadlines across six of them in the same fortnight.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma cohorts in Ras Al Khaimah are small, which has one consequence Dubai families never meet: a Higher Level subject may run as a single set of four or five students, and if the teacher leaves mid-year there is no second set to absorb them. A Mina Al Arab family should ask the school in September how many students are in each HL set, because that number predicts how much independent support the year will need.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Usually eight to ten subjects examined at the end of Year 11, with Cambridge running June and November series and Pearson running May/June and November. Papers are tiered on some subjects, so a Core entry caps the available grade. The syllabus code on the entry form, not the subject name, is what a tutor needs before the first lesson.
programmes.countryNote: Mina Al Arab families often discover mid-Year-11 that two children at two different schools sit different boards for the same subject. One may be on Cambridge Physics 0625, the other on Pearson 4PH1, with different paper structures and different practical arrangements. Check the entry statement the school issues before February, and bring the code to the first session so the practice papers match the real exam.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, marked out of eight and reported as a 1-7 grade. There are no past papers in the IGCSE sense, which is why MYP parents often cannot tell whether a child is on track. The criterion descriptors are the only reliable guide, and most students have never read them.
programmes.countryNote: The MYP-to-Diploma step is where Ras Al Khaimah students most often lose ground, because a child who has been awarded 6s against criteria can still arrive in DP1 without the algebraic fluency a Higher Level maths course assumes. A Mina Al Arab student moving from MYP 5 into DP should spend the summer on technique rather than new content.

programmes.name: IB Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led and transdisciplinary, with no external examinations. Support at this stage is about reading fluency, number facts and written stamina rather than exam technique. Short sessions work better than long ones, and progress is measured in reading age and arithmetic recall rather than grades.
programmes.countryNote: Primary children in Mina Al Arab finish school earliest and tire earliest, so a 16:00 slot that fails a Year 11 student can work well for a Year 4 one. Thirty focused minutes twice a week, before dinner, is the pattern that holds through a RAK term.

ras-al-khaimah/mina-al-arab.subjectsIntro: Requests from this part of Ras Al Khaimah cluster around the subjects where a small school cohort leaves a student without a specialist: Higher Level sciences, the two maths routes, and Economics. The list below reflects what families here actually ask for.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The proof-heavy IB maths route. Higher Level adds complex numbers, vectors and a substantially harder calculus load. Marks are lost in the unstructured Paper 2 questions where students recognise the topic but not the method, and in the exploration where the mathematics is sound but the reflection is thin.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics and technology-led problem solving. The graphic display calculator is assumed throughout, and a surprising share of lost marks come from calculator operations rather than mathematics. Hypothesis testing and regression are the two topics RAK students most often meet for the first time in a mock.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0625 and 4PH1
subjects.description: Electricity and magnetism are where IGCSE students stall; at Higher Level it is fields and the quantum topic. The practical skills strand rewards precise language about uncertainty, which is rarely taught explicitly and is quick to fix once a student sees how it is marked.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0620 and 4CH1
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and energetics carry the most marks and the most confusion. Higher Level students lose marks on multi-step calculations where a single rounding decision propagates. A small school set often means the practical programme is thin, so data-analysis questions need separate drilling.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content volume is the problem rather than difficulty. Students who revise by rereading notes score poorly on the extended-response questions, which want specific terminology and a stated mechanism. Statistics in the data-based questions is the other reliable source of dropped marks.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy and the three internal assessment commentaries decide most grades. Higher Level adds quantitative questions that reward neat working. Students often write fluent evaluation without anchoring it to the diagram they have just drawn, which is where examiners stop awarding marks.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is unseen textual analysis under time pressure, and the Individual Oral needs a global issue narrow enough to argue. Students in Ras Al Khaimah often have strong ideas and weak paragraph architecture; fixing the structure moves the grade faster than reading more texts.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Reading comprehension at speed and the summary task are the two components that separate grades. The writing papers reward register control more than vocabulary range. Speaking endorsement arrangements differ between the 0510 and 0511 variants, so the code matters.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study command terms do the work here. A student who answers 'discuss' as though it were 'describe' loses the top band without writing anything wrong. Higher Level adds the research project, which needs a real organisation and a narrow question.

subjects.name: Mathematics (IGCSE)
subjects.description: The Core tier caps the grade, so the tier decision in Year 10 matters more than any single topic. Extended students lose marks in algebraic fractions, transformations of graphs and the longer multi-mark problems where no method is prompted.

subjects.name: Arabic as an Additional Language
subjects.description: Mandatory in UAE private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum. Progress depends on consistent short practice rather than long sessions, and on matching the school's own scheme, since the Ministry's content requirements are prescribed and schools may not substitute their own.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Pseudocode discipline and trace tables account for a large share of IGCSE marks. At Higher Level the internal assessment needs a real client and a bounded problem, which is where RAK students most often need steering before coding starts.

ras-al-khaimah/mina-al-arab.regionsIntro: Students taught across Ras Al Khaimah come from a narrow coastal belt plus the inland communities. The notes below are the local detail that changes a timetable: distances, school feeds and when a child is realistically home.

regions.name: Mina Al Arab and Hayat Island
regions.note: Villas on Flamingo and Bermuda plus the newer Hayat Island apartments. Bus pickups start around 06:45, and secondary students are rarely back before 15:00. Evening slots from 17:30 are the norm.

regions.name: Al Hamra Village
regions.note: Immediately south along the coast and the location of the RAK Academy campuses. Families living here have the shortest school run in the emirate, which makes a 16:30 slot workable for secondary students.

regions.name: Al Marjan Island
regions.note: Reclaimed coral-shaped fronds with apartment towers and villas. Every school run leaves the island by a single causeway, so a traffic delay there pushes a lesson start by fifteen minutes with no warning.

regions.name: Al Nakheel
regions.note: The commercial heart of the city, with the Indian-curriculum schools and most tuition centres. A Mina Al Arab family driving here for a lesson is making a round trip of roughly 40 to 50 minutes outside peak.

regions.name: Khuzam
regions.note: Residential district inland of the Corniche and home to a RAK Academy campus. Mixed villa and apartment housing, and a common destination for the school run from the southern coast.

regions.name: Al Dhait North and South
regions.note: Large villa districts towards the Dubai road. Families here often choose schools in both directions, which splits sibling timetables and makes a shared evening slot difficult.

regions.name: Al Jazirah Al Hamra
regions.note: South of Mina Al Arab on the way to Umm Al Quwain. Some families here commute to Dubai schools, which pushes a realistic lesson start to 18:30 or later.

regions.name: Al Qusaidat and Al Mamourah
regions.note: Older established neighbourhoods north of the creek with largely Indian and Egyptian curriculum families. Shorter school days mean earlier available slots than on the southern coast.

schoolClusters.city: The southern coast: Mina Al Arab, Al Hamra and Al Marjan
schoolClusters.note: This is the IB-heavy side of the emirate. The RAK Academy campuses run the IB continuum, and families on the southern coast feed into them rather than driving north into the city. Diploma sets here are small by Dubai standards.

modes.description: One or two sessions a week in the same slot, held for the term. The fixed slot is the point: a session that moves around the week competes with football, Arabic homework and the drive back from Al Hamra, and loses. Most Mina Al Arab secondary families settle on 17:30 or 18:30.

sections.heading: The Mina Al Arab school day, hour by hour
paragraphs: A tutoring slot is only as good as the hour it sits in, and in Mina Al Arab that hour is decided by the bus. Pickups on Hayat Island and the Flamingo and Bermuda villa clusters begin between 06:40 and 07:05 depending on the route, because the bus is collecting across the southern coast before it turns inland. A child on the first pickup is dressed and fed by half past six.

The return leg is less predictable. Primary children are home between 14:15 and 15:00. Secondary students, and in particular Diploma students with a late period or a CAS commitment, arrive between 15:00 and 16:00. Add a shower, a meal and the twenty minutes it takes a tired teenager to become a functioning one, and the first hour in which real learning is possible begins at about 17:30.

The table below is the version families recognise. Times are typical rather than any single school's published timetable, and the right-hand column is the one to argue about: it is the earliest slot at which a session produces work worth the fee, not the earliest slot that is technically free in the calendar.

Two details change these numbers for individual households. A child on a late bus route that loops through Al Jazirah Al Hamra before turning back loses fifteen to twenty minutes against the figures shown. And a Diploma student with CAS on two afternoons a week has effectively two shorter evenings, which is the single most common reason a timetable agreed in September has collapsed by half-term. Both are worth checking before any slot is fixed.

sections.heading: Why the 16:00 slot fails and the 18:00 slot holds
paragraphs: Parents book the earliest slot available because it looks like the one that protects bedtime. On this coast it does the opposite. A session starting at 16:00 catches a secondary student within half an hour of walking through the door after a ten-hour day, and the first twenty minutes are spent waking up. The effective lesson is forty minutes long inside a sixty-minute booking, and the tutor spends part of it re-teaching material the student was too tired to hold on to.

The 18:00 slot works because three things have happened. The child has eaten, the school day has been filed away, and the homework that would otherwise compete with the session has either been done or been consciously deferred. A student arriving at a lesson having already attempted the problem set brings questions, and a session driven by the student's own questions covers roughly twice the ground of one driven by the tutor's plan.

There is a limit at the other end. Past 20:45 on a school night, retention falls away and the session turns into reassurance rather than teaching. For Diploma students in the fortnight before internal deadlines, a 21:00 finish is sometimes the only option, but it is a short-term measure rather than a timetable. The useful window in Mina Al Arab is narrow, roughly 17:30 to 20:45, and the families who protect it are the ones still on the same schedule in March.

There is one exception worth naming. Younger primary children run the opposite curve: they are at their best shortly after getting home and are unusable after seven. For a Year 3 or Year 4 child on this coast, a 16:00 start for thirty or forty minutes is correct, and an evening slot borrowed from an older sibling's timetable will produce nothing. Households with children at both ends of the ladder need two different plans, not one compromise.

sections.heading: What the drive to a tutor costs in hours, not dirhams
paragraphs: The honest comparison is not cost per hour. It is cost per taught hour including the journey, and in Mina Al Arab the journey is substantial. There is no concentration of specialist IB subject teachers on this stretch of coast. A family that insists on a tutor physically in the room is looking inland to Al Nakheel or Al Dhait for a generalist, and south to Sharjah or Dubai for a Higher Level specialist.

Run the arithmetic for one weekly 90-minute lesson in Al Nakheel. Twenty to twenty-five minutes each way outside peak, longer between 16:00 and 18:30, plus parking and the wait. That is roughly an hour of car time wrapped around ninety minutes of teaching, every week, usually driven by a parent who has their own working day behind them. Over a 30-week school year it is close to thirty hours in a car for one subject.

For a specialist in Sharjah or Dubai Academic City the figure stops being a scheduling inconvenience and becomes the reason the arrangement quietly stops in November. The right-hand column of the table is the point: the same hours, kept at home, buy a second subject or a protected revision block. That is the practical argument for live video on this coast, and it does not depend on anyone claiming video is pedagogically superior.

The journey also has a hidden cost in the child. A student who has spent fifty minutes in a car arrives at a lesson already depleted, and the same student has to make the return trip afterwards rather than going straight to the problem set while the method is fresh. Removing the travel does not just return the hours to the parent. It returns the twenty minutes immediately after the lesson, which is when most of the consolidation actually happens.

sections.heading: What IB and IGCSE tuition costs around Ras Al Khaimah
paragraphs: No published rate table exists for Ras Al Khaimah. Every AED figure circulating in this market is a Dubai figure, so the bands below are presented as what named providers publish for Dubai, with the source attached. Treat them as a ceiling rather than a local quote: RAK families generally report paying at or below the Dubai mid-band for the same level of teacher.

Two patterns are worth knowing before any conversation about price. First, the in-home premium is real and it is mostly travel: the same teacher costs more when the fee has to absorb an hour in a car, which is exactly the hour the previous section measured. Second, rates rise with proximity to a results deadline, so a Higher Level specialist booked in February costs more than the same specialist booked in September for the same work.

IB Gram does not publish a fixed price list on these pages, because the right figure depends on subject, level and how many sessions a week a student actually needs. Pricing is quoted after a short consultation, and a trial lesson is arranged before any commitment so a family can judge the match before paying for a term. Figures below are market context, not an IB Gram quote.

One useful piece of context for a Ras Al Khaimah budget conversation. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year under the emirate's second economic incentives package. School fees are therefore flat for many families this year while tutoring rates are not, which changes the arithmetic of adding a second subject. Check the equivalent position with your own school before assuming it applies in this emirate.

sections.heading: A visiting tutor in Mina Al Arab against one-to-one online
paragraphs: The question most families on this coast actually ask is whether someone can come to the villa. It is a reasonable question and it deserves a straight answer rather than a sales pitch. In-home tutoring exists in Ras Al Khaimah, it is legal where the tutor holds a MoHRE private tuition work permit, and for a primary child who needs a physical presence at the table it can be the right choice.

What it cannot do on this coast is deliver subject depth. The pool of people able to teach Higher Level Chemistry or Analysis and Approaches and willing to drive to Mina Al Arab weekly is very small, and a family choosing from that pool is choosing on availability rather than on subject. Online one-to-one inverts that: the pool is everyone who teaches the syllabus, and the constraint becomes the timetable rather than the map.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Tuition for Ras Al Khaimah families is delivered as one-to-one lessons over live video; home visits are a service offered only in India. The table sets out the trade honestly, including the places where a tutor in the room genuinely wins, so a family can decide rather than be sold to.

Many households on this coast end up running both, and that is a sensible outcome rather than a contradiction. A Year 4 child who needs someone sitting beside them while they write is best served by a local arrangement. The Year 12 sibling taking Physics HL is best served by a specialist who may be nowhere near Ras Al Khaimah. Choosing one format for the whole family is what produces a compromise nobody is happy with.

sections.heading: A weekly timetable that survives a Ras Al Khaimah term
paragraphs: A timetable fails for predictable reasons: it puts the hardest subject on the day the child has football, it books three sessions in a week that only has room for two, and it leaves no slack for the fortnight when every internal deadline lands at once. Building backwards from the weekly school pattern avoids most of this.

Sunday and Monday are the strongest teaching days of a UAE week. The weekend break has reset attention, and work set on those days has four school days to be revisited before it goes stale. Wednesday is the weakest day in most households on this coast, and Thursday evening is close to useless for new content but good for review. Friday and Saturday mornings are the only slots where a 90-minute session can run without competing with the school day at all.

Two sessions a week is the pattern that holds for most IGCSE and Diploma students. One session is enough to maintain a subject but rarely enough to repair one. Three or more works only in a short block before mocks, and should be booked with an end date so it does not quietly become the permanent timetable and exhaust the student by February.

Leave one evening genuinely empty. Every Diploma student hits a fortnight when three internal deadlines, a mock and a CAS commitment land together, and a timetable with no slack turns that fortnight into four cancelled sessions and a month of catching up. The empty evening is not spare capacity to be sold back later. It is the reason the other four slots survive from September to May on this stretch of coast.

sections.heading: Ramadan, exam leave and the fortnights when the timetable breaks
paragraphs: Two periods in a Ras Al Khaimah school year reliably break a tutoring schedule, and both are foreseeable. The first is Ramadan, when private schools shorten the day. Children are home by early afternoon, fasting teenagers are at their least alert between two and five, and the family's evening restructures around iftar. A slot that worked in January does not work in Ramadan, and pretending otherwise produces three cancelled sessions and a dropped arrangement.

The practical answer is to move rather than pause. Post-iftar slots work well for fasting secondary students, typically from around 20:30, and younger children often do better with a late-morning session on the shortened day. The schedule is agreed before Ramadan begins rather than renegotiated after the first missed lesson, and it reverts to the term pattern afterwards.

The second break is study leave. Once a Year 11 student is on leave before a Cambridge or Pearson series, the school day disappears and the whole day becomes available, which sounds like an opportunity and usually is not. Unstructured days produce less work than timetabled ones. The pattern that works is two fixed sessions plus one timed full paper per subject per week, with the rest of the day planned in writing before leave starts.

A third, smaller disruption catches families on this coast out: the long summer. Cambridge and Pearson both run a November series, and a student resitting in November is revising through July and August when the household is often abroad. Live video handles that, but only if the slot is agreed for the destination timezone before anyone travels. Sorting it in June costs one conversation; sorting it in August costs three weeks of lost preparation.

sections.heading: Who may legally tutor your child in Ras Al Khaimah, and how to check
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE runs on a permit. Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 introduced the private tuition work permit, issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. The permit is granted at no charge for two years, and the eligible categories are broad: teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged 15 to 18.

Anyone providing private lessons without that permit is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule has been published, so any figure quoted to you as the penalty is somebody's guess. The application route is MoHRE's own service, 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing', applied for through the MoHRE smart app, website or e-services system.

Two further points matter for a Mina Al Arab family. Private schools in Ras Al Khaimah are regulated by the Department of Knowledge, which approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods in the emirate, so questions about a school's programme belong there rather than with KHDA. And a tutoring operation with premises and staff is a different legal animal from an individual tutor: that requires an educational services permit from the relevant authority. IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform and holds no regulator accreditation; it should never be described as holding one.

One further rule is worth knowing even though it is set in another emirate. Abu Dhabi's education authority has issued professional-ethics rules that bar private and charter school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit carries a code of conduct along the same lines. Press reporting rather than a policy document is the source here, so verify it against the current wording before relying on it, but the principle is sound: a child's own classroom teacher is the wrong person to pay privately.
